The chapter ends with the recognition entered as a fact about two people in the same building, and with Talla Roke asking which of them is the keeper.

## Chapter 56 — The Reckoning

Tams Quill reads the two columns together for the first time and the room finds the second one harder. The crew's **thirty-eight and a half has not gone up** — it went down, because he is not on the lever, not allowed a bar, and because a man who was on the lever for three weeks is under a stone and is not on the board anywhere — and the boundary's has gone from **forty-six to fifty-one**. He reads the items without rounding them: a day and a half of Jo's shutter route, gone and not recovered; the half-day for the Chapter 50 closure; two days of Ilsa's school; nineteen days of meals, which are not hours and which he is putting in anyway; Mikka's pot twice; a watched flue wall; two hours of the clerk's evenings; and four hours of Renn's own, which she keeps in her head, and which he has now put on a board — and she says *it stays*. The finding is the same and one item longer: **the half that gets counted is the half that is ours.** Sefu gets the leaving sentence read and says the obligation is open in the direction that they are leaving and not in the direction that the work is done. And then **Ilsa Norr asks the question nobody has asked in nine weeks** — *who keeps the Hearthhold rooms* — and explains why it has not been asked, which is that every one of them has been assuming somebody is already doing it, and the walls are nobody's job, and if she had not said so out loud and paid for it there would be a hole under a school and it would be nobody's fault. Nobody answers it. Corva Nye puts the form on the bench flat, does not read it out, and shows the room the shape of what it has: a line for the holder of a route, a line for the charter, a line for the date it was inspected, a line for the keeper of a *workshop*, a line for the office, a line for the guild — **and no line for a woman who teaches nine children and pays for a floor out of her own hand and shuts a door because she decides to.** She writes that in her margin in her own ink and Dalla makes the clerk read it back. Corva then asks properly to see the nine register boxes, and **Ilsa refuses again, in her own words, in front of the same people**, and says what is in the box without opening it — attendance rolls, a fuel book, a lintel that is not a lintel, four inches of copper, ground maps, and one plan rolled on a dowel with a tape round it, on its own box, never opened — and gives the reason: everything else is a thing somebody did and finished, and *that plan is a decision about what this building is*, and she will not open it in the week after a man died under a stair, and if it is a house she has to be the woman who found out. She says yes in three weeks with a name and a date, and one term is that the crew will not be in the room. Talla Roke then says the thing that makes the question more expensive: in eleven Hearthholds in four years she has never seen a vault, and every plan she has carried off the middle gate's survey shelf is drawn like a house, with doors drawn on hinges, and nobody has ever told her why. Nera says she does not know, and says the honest half — she has not opened that plan either, and if Ilsa unrolls it in three weeks she will be the only person in the room who cannot be trusted with it, because she will want it to be a house. Dalla writes the question down with the week and the room and the asker, and no answer under it, and **no word *pending***.

## Chapter 57 — Reading It by Ear

The check does not get worse, and that is the thing Jo says out loud, because a room decides a hiss is the new normal and the new normal is fine. It is a hole with a shape. She gives the two-note vocabulary — a hiss that stays a hiss, and a hiss that gets **thinner**, and thinner is the seat — and asks that it be written in a room that can be frightened and not with *noted* on it. The school runs, because the school always runs, and Ilsa says so in the flat voice and Mikka says so the same way, and a day lost is a day the nine children do not get back, and the corridor is open and the waist is a live post, and **Renn Vale takes it and says out loud what she is and is not before she takes it**. The pump comes off **four minutes early, on the nineteenth stroke**, and this time everybody is off, because the terms were read at the school door, the bearer was named on the day's board, the plinth was read by Ruk Sella, the bell was rung by Bel Ordry, and **the woman from the wash rooms had been asked in advance and had said yes**. Nobody dies. The anteroom clears in a minute and a quarter on foot and the litter sets the number and has not come, and Sefu records that the system worked and the pump did not, which are two different sentences and only one of them is a reason to be pleased. She shuts the route at the top of three steps, on her own hand, for a reason nobody would have thought of: *Jo's hiss has gone thin and I am not a pump hand and I do not know what a thin hiss is, and that is exactly why I am shutting it*, and she says it out loud instead of writing it because she can do both and the harder one is better. It costs a day of Ilsa's school and a pump interval, and the corridor stays shut for the rest of the week, and Renn says that out loud so that nobody can say afterwards a watch quietly stopped. Then **Isel Ferrow puts a bar in Tams Quill's left hand and asks twice and Tams refuses it in front of the room**, and the reason is the best sentence in the batch: when the interval came off early, the first thing that went was the hiss, and a man at a frame with a bar in his hand does not hear a hiss. The tally gives **fifty-eight and thirty-eight and a half**, and Tams reads the same finding again with a shut in the *held* column and the check on the list. And Nera claims her own cost at the end and does not let anybody else carry it: she took the stair's air out of the certification list, a watch is the cheapest thing there is, she chose it, and **a watch is not a smaller certificate — it is a debt that gets paid in somebody's day** — and she will not change it, because the alternative is publishing a number she cannot stand behind and a man going under a lip because of it.

## Chapter 58 — Eleven Feet Down

**The one marked viewpoint shift in the batch, into Nera Oduya.** It opens on the fact that she was **asked** — by Renn Vale, at the top of three steps, in the flat voice, with the day and the hours and the post named, and the right to refuse given and the promise not to ask again this month. Dalla Sen turns the yes into a second question, because the air valve watch does not go to a lip, and Nera's answer is to take the board and the cloth with her, shut the valve, and declare it out loud before she goes: **it is the first time in eleven weeks that the watch has moved and it is not to be done again without the air engineer saying so in writing.** Bel Ordry goes with her as the bearer, because a bearer at the near lip is a person of this boundary. She stands on the fixed first landing with her left boot on the stone and her right hand on the rail, four feet from the rail over the throat, not going near it, and the chapter gives the reader the thing nobody in the room has: **her private count of the turns, forty-one before the shore and more since, of which thirty-four came between one and nine minutes after the lever came off, said once out loud in the thirty-sixth day and refused three times since**, and the two unexplained marks on her board, and the fact that she is the only person in this building who can only say *there is nobody down there* in eleven weeks. At the second minute of the nineteen strokes, from eleven feet down, she hears **a flat, dry, wooden knock with a slide on the end of it** — a bar in a staple, a hand leaving a door frame — and an air push past her with a shape to it, out of the throat's north-east cheek at about the height of her knee. She does not move, and she counts four seconds of breath. Then the turn comes on the second minute of the six, and she says the word and she and Bel Ordry are up the three steps in under a minute, and the terms are the only reason that was a sentence and not a scramble. She tells the room two things and then gives **four conditions**: the post's work is scoped to what can be seen from the fixed first landing and **nobody goes under that stone**; the four treads are **not walked this month**; the throat is **sounded, not entered**, daily at the second bell, with a bar, by a person, and the answer written down whatever it is, **including nothing**; and the review is **brought forward** to the first work-bell after a sound from the throat, a thin hiss, or anybody writing the word *out* on the slate. She says plainly that she is not going down, not publishing a rate, not taking the watch off, and not certifying anything, and that the reason for all four is one reason: she has never certified a room she has not stood in, and she learned that in a place where a room nobody stood in killed thirty people. Renn asks the practical question — *what would a door be doing down there* — and Nera says: where people walk in and out. Talla Roke connects a latch, a door drawn on hinges on a plan, and a plan rolled on a dowel, and says she has been in the building a week and has counted four things nobody has opened and they are all about the same subject, and asks the clerk to write down who wants the boxes and who wants the door, because those are two different people. And in the anteroom on the Wednesday, Marek stands at the bench with the tally board and the plate in his coat pocket, puts his hand flat on the bench either side of it, waits, **gets nothing, and does not write *null*, because there was nothing to write it on and he knew what it would say.**

## Chapter 59 — The Order Withdrawn

Talla Roke withdraws the order in the anteroom, in her own hand, at the fifth bell, after the tally, and asks for it in her words and not the clerk's and for it read back. She withdraws somebody else's order, on a clerk's mark, that she believes was made in good faith for a better reason than hers. The reason is Iven's, given a week earlier: the moment the slab carries a load in a Hearthhold work it is material in use under a guild lien, and **a claim on the boundary's material is a claim on the boundary**; and her own reason is simpler — *a courier's whole trade is that a thing claimed by nobody can be carried by anybody, and the moment I write my order into a boundary's book I put a second lock on the same door.* She refuses to have it recorded as a refusal, and asks the clerk to record the distinction she learned in eleven days: **a refusal is the clerk's and stands and can be appealed; a withdrawal is the courier's and can be made again by anybody with a mark.** Dalla records both, in the clerk's hand as well as the courier's, because in a year somebody will want to know whether this boundary ever got anybody to change their mind, and the answer is yes, once, and it was not about a stone. Then Talla says the cost herself before anybody can be gentle with her and asks somebody else to say it out loud and write it, and **Mikka Hale says it: four households in the second gate carrying water up four sets of steps this winter.** Talla asks for the crew's hours — a named work, a person asking, a clerk to write it down — for the second gate's inlet, in the spring, and Marek says there are **two springs** and promises neither, and then admits to a room that he has been thinking about it at two in the morning on his own with nobody's name on it, and Sefu Aran makes him say it twice and put a time on it, and says the correct answer is to write it in a room because a man who will admit a two-o'clock plan in a room is worth ten men who have not got one. **Sefu holds that the first spring is not the crew's hours and not this year: it is a conversation between the keeper and the air engineer about a named hand-over, and it happens whether or not anybody is leaving, and Nera Oduya is not going to be impressed by a man who has been talking to a courier.** Corva Nye asks, properly and in front of the keeper and Renn, to sit at the top of nine steps and watch a clerk write a number. **Renn refuses**, gives her reasons, says it is both a condition and a refusal on purpose, and adds that if the office wants to know whether the boundary can keep the route then the office can come in the cold, and be asked, and may be asked not, and carry water, and nobody writes a report. The report goes up on foot. And **Iven Tallo says the correct response to a guild page is nothing** — no second page, no seventh line on the slate, because the day the slate gets a line added to answer a clerk is the day it stops being a thing the boundary keeps and becomes a document the boundary defends — and that the boundary's own page was the answer and **the guild's page is the first nail**, and that the wall is four habits and a rope and a clerk who says no, and that it will cost somebody something not written down anywhere. Then Jo Verrick, at the frame, says the seat goes before the cold, names the three things she does not have, and says the man who holds it cannot be Tams Quill and cannot be Marek Venn, because **a seat you cannot feel is a seat you cannot tell has gone wrong.**

## Chapter 60 — A Threshold That Is Not the Last One

Renn Vale writes the shore onto her slate and argues the room into a **seventh term**, which says in her own hand that the lip is not held but packed, that it goes a finger and a half with a man under it and went two inches before, and that **the next time that slab turns somebody will be under that lip with a knee on a piece of wood and their whole weight on it, and it will be Jo Verrick** — and that the room is writing down that it knows, which is not the same as writing down a plan. Talla Roke asks for the ledger to be read to her in full, because she is going to walk out of here and would rather know what this boundary has from the book than from a person, and it is read, item by item, and it is read as the entries that are **new since the fourth of the month** and not the whole of it: the pump and the seat and the check read by ear, with a two-hand correction Jo Verrick insists on — *I did not write and the seat is going; hers is a finding and mine is a rule* — the four air cards and the word *spent* and the reason the room worked, the recovered length received by the keeper with a time on it, the material that does not exist, the route's seven terms, the closure with a name and a date, **the first entry in nine weeks with a stranger's name in it** (Corva Nye, entered on the clerk's own authority, and Renn's refusal of her, both halves), the withdrawal and the refusal/withdrawal distinction and the four households, **the question asked in the tenth week by Ilsa Norr and not answered with no word *pending* on it**, the register boxes refused with a date three weeks out and the crew not in the room, and the throat sounded with a bar and the answer written down including nothing, and the two knocks kept separate in two hands, and a correction entered in the clerk's own hand because a half-day of shutter route had been read out as though it belonged to two closures instead of one. Then **Sefu's closure clause fires for the first time**: the route has been used for **work**, not air and not its own testing, and it goes on the clerk's page with the names of the people who opened and shut it, the reason, and the date — and the room hears what that sentence sounds like, and Mikka says *well* and Ilsa says *about time*, and Renn goes down the three steps and puts her hand on a shore that is not hers and says nothing about that. The maintenance obligation has not ended, and Marek says why out loud: a woman who will not stand on that stair and will not be on that landing, a woman who has a dead mother in a hole and will not be asked, and himself, which makes three of the four who could say it, and a boundary Renn has only just started believing she is allowed to have. Talla goes out at first light with a satchel, a drawing of the second gate's inlet and a copy of her own withdrawal, and has a short conversation with her brother at the top of nine steps about a hand that will open in the eleventh week, and he says *you have a hand* and she says nobody in this room says anything to anybody in a way they did not ask to hear first. On the last morning **Bel Ordry sounds the throat with a bar and writes down *nothing*** and says out loud that that is a real thing he has written down, and the review line is named and read out before it is written and taken apart twice. The unresolved list gains its eleventh item, which is the seat and the check; the post is the tenth: **a post under the near landing's lip, which wants nine foot and a bundle, which is not built, and which is the reason there is a woman under a stone at all.** And the two questions carry on, and the plate did not go anywhere because nobody went anywhere, and the brass rule said nothing again, and a key turns in three weeks, and the chapter ends on a shore that is **not enough**, and that everybody in the room knows is not enough, and that the page says so in Renn Vale's hand with a date on it.

---

# Volume 02, Batch 0002 — Chapters 61–70

## Chapter 61 — A Hand and Not a Fist

Two days after the courier went out, Tams Quill's right hand opens on the anteroom bench at the first bell, and it opens flat and stays open for as long as he asks, which is twenty-two seconds, because somebody in the room would otherwise have counted. The gap that had been a finger and a half is the width of two fingers; the little finger still does not come all the way down. It was a month, said at the time in the seventh week, and it is not nine days, and he says so twice. The room does the arithmetic on its own and arrives at a woman at a frame with a scored bronze seat and no bronze in the building, and Tams says *somebody had better say it before I do and I would like it to be the right somebody.* **Jo Verrick makes him stand at the other end of the room so she can watch his face, and refuses the seat to him — not because the hand is not ready but because she will not cut a repair out of the one thing in the building that is certain to be wrong in four months, and because she said the thing in the ninth week herself, that a seat you cannot feel is a seat you cannot tell has gone wrong.** Then she prices the work in her own hand, before she starts, line by line, read as it is written: eleven inches across the face, two and a quarter deep, set proud at the top and hollow at the bottom; a day and a half of a shutter route she has already lost a day and a half of in the seventh week; a housing open while the pump is not pumping, and while it is not pumping the water in the dip comes up under a corridor two foot eight wide that stands on the shaft; **and no instrument, because there is no check and the only thing she has ever had to know about this pump.** **Sefu Aran names the work and strikes half of his own naming aloud**, because a keeper who strikes half his own sentence and does not say so is a keeper who has learned to write. Tams reads the stores: a scarfed head, one length of five foot nine, a two foot ten and a handful in Jo's basket, and the last of those is not sound. **And Jo says line nine out loud: I do not have the wood.** The chapter ends with the search named and the cold in the window, the check hissing thin, and a boy at the top of nine steps calling the interval eight seconds early with no opinion about timber.

## Chapter 62 — Asking

The cold comes up the nine steps and pushes under the school door, and Nera Oduya says the thing nobody expected: the shaft has stopped being a chimney. The dyed cloth on a stick did not lift at the top of three steps; **it sank**, lay down against the wall of the throat, and came back slowly. Everything she taught the room about the stair was a warm-weather lesson taught in the autumn, and she says so herself, while it is in front of them. **Iven Tallo names the four stops before anybody asks him, and states the rule that makes the search honest: the best wood in a building is almost never the wood anybody can have, because it is the piece that had to survive, and the piece that had to survive is the piece somebody needed to be able to forget about.** Then the walk. **Bel Ordry's two rooms:** a single oak floor-board, his mother's, eleven inches marked in pencil last week and not cut, and Mikka Hale refuses it because he would be cold in his own room by the end of the month and a man who is cold in his own room stops being a person who can stand on a two-foot-eight gap; and then Bel says the sentence the batch turns on — *if I give it and somebody says thank you, then in three months there is a line in that clerk's book with my name on it against a thing this Hearthhold has got, and I will have become a person who gave something to this boundary* — and a man who has held nothing for eleven weeks and been given nothing will not trade that for a floor. **Ilsa Norr's school store:** the two beech lengths are the props under the shelf the nine register boxes stand on, and she says no in one breath and then says she would have said yes if the shelf had been sound, because a person who never admits a better reason is a person who enjoys saying no. **The wash-room door:** Renn Vale stops the party twenty feet short and will not name the room on a list, and the reason is not the floor and not the risk, it is that the woman in there has a mother in the same hole and has said yes twice, and a list of what people want out of her room would be the first thing anybody has ever asked her for. **And under the anteroom floor, the pump's own bed:** two lengths of elm, thirty years in standing water, the best-conditioned timber in the Hearthhold, which cannot be cut because the housing bolts into it and a seat in a crooked housing does not announce itself. **Tams reads the carried column out loud, once, at the moment it decides something**, and Iven hears Oren Sill's method about bearing faces applied to a bed and says that a bed is not a shore and a bed is a *finished* thing, and that those two sentences are the whole morning and both are true. Sefu Aran then says the sentence that becomes the week: **I cannot get a plank to my own pump, and neither can any of you, and that is not a shortage of planks, that is a shortage of reach.** The crew's hours go to forty-one and a half for the first time, the boundary's to sixty-five, and Tams opens a column with no heading for days and leaves it with no heading on purpose.

## Chapter 63 — Thinner

The cold is three days old and the check hisses thin, and eleven people look at Jo Verrick, and she keeps her hand on the frame for eight more seconds and then says the sentence the whole of Volume 02 has been walking toward: **I cannot tell any more.** A hole hisses thinner in cold air, so the two-note vocabulary she gave the room in the tenth week is dead, and she has been hearing it change three times since Saturday and telling herself it was the seat. She does not take the pump out of service, because the dip fills and the corridor's low end is under it; she puts it on **attended**, two people from the second bell to the fifth, with Isel Ferrow at the frame and Mikka Hale taking half his shutter route and refusing payment. Then Nera arrives from a different direction and says what the cold has done to the stair: **for six minutes out of every forty the shaft is a sink and not a vent, and that has never been the safe part, it was only ever the part where nothing moves because the shaft was breathing out.** Somebody would have to stand at the low end of the corridor and watch the water, and she will not name a person, and the crew are barred from the rota, and **nobody in the room offers, which is the correct thing and is entered in the ledger as the first time in eleven weeks a post had been offered to nobody.** At the second bell Bel Ordry's bar comes back with three ticks and a slide on the third — the shape of the knock — **and the same tick in two other places on the same cold wall**, and he refuses to write it as a knock and refuses to write it as nothing, and Nera writes the shape, the cold, the three places and no conclusion, and says out loud that **her own refusal to publish a rate and her own method are standing on opposite sides of the same wall.** It cost Bel Ordry the day he was going to fix his mother's door. And on the fixed first landing Marek Venn puts his palm on the dressed stone in the cold, waits, gets nothing, and **refuses to write *null*** — a null in the cold is a different instrument reading a different room, and a column that has a lie in it is worse than an honest one. Tams Quill opens **a column with no heading** with a one in it, the temperature, and the reason, which is a fault in the reader and not a fault in the building, and says a room that only writes down the half it likes is the guild. The short review is called for the first time in eleven weeks, and Mikka Hale names the thing nobody has said: **in those six minutes the water comes up under the corridor's low end.** And Jo, at the frame: the seat is going, the check has gone, the cold has taken the last thing she had for reading it, and she will be able to tell the room on the morning it goes and not on the morning before.

## Chapter 64 — The Reply

A reply comes up the middle passage on the back of a man carrying a bag, forty days old, carried by **Sabra Kest**, a Cartwright route-custody assessor, who stops at the bottom of the nine steps and enters herself in the ledger on her own authority with a name and a number and the last figure doubled. She reads the reply standing up, lets a woman at a frame interrupt her, and then puts **Form 9-C, route disposition** flat on the bench, because she has learned in eleven years that a form held up is a performance. Three boxes and a person to fill one: **held**, **worked under charter**, or **unattended**. Under the third, the operative sentence: *no officer of this or any chartered office shall be required to enter, inspect, maintain, fund, or answer for any condition arising upon it.* **That is the best answer anybody in that building could have wanted and it is the reason nobody is ever going to help them, and Sabra Kest says so in a room and says she has been carrying both halves for forty days.** Three people could fill a box and the room knows all three. **Then she tells Iven Tallo, in front of everybody and before he can find it in a file, that a suspended bond can be reinstated on a single document, that it is not a bribe, that she has done it eleven times, and that she is telling him because she will not be the person who let him find out from a file.** He refuses, and his reason is the best argument in the batch: *a licensed man who signs a route does not stop being the man who signed it when he leaves the room, and there are five of us who are leaving, and the only way to make me leave is to take my licence.* He says the correct response to a guild page is nothing and he is now arguing for the guild, and he says both of those are the same sentence and he has not changed his mind about anything. **And then Renn Vale reads her own seventh term out to a stranger — the lip, the knee, the packing, Jo Verrick's name — and refuses to put it in the one free-text field on the form that could have put a person in the boundary's corner, and Sabra Kest writes *none reported* about a condition she was told about and says she will be asked and will give the same answer again.** The route goes back down nine steps **unattended**. And at the end, alone, Marek Venn says out loud that he filled one of the three boxes in his head in four seconds with no name in it, that nobody saw him do it, and that he is not going to do it again in a room where it is written down, and he wants that in the book with the time on it.

## Chapter 65 — Both Columns

The short review is held the morning after the assessor goes, with an empty chair at the end of the room chalked and not used. Five items, read out, and the room is short because it has learned to say a thing once. The throat: the sounding continues, whatever is written down including *nothing*, with Renn's new term added in her own hand — **if it turns out to be a door then it is a door in a building I keep, and nobody goes down it, and that decision is made now, in the cold, so that in the summer nobody can stand on this landing and say the words *we did not know*.** The check: the vocabulary is withdrawn, the pump runs attended, and the draw is stopped on a water line chalked on the frame by Leena Orr. The six minutes: the shaft is not a vent, the terms are unchanged, and **that is one of the two things this review is not deciding** — recorded, unresolved, and it will sit on the page with no name against it for as long as it has no name, and anybody who wants to put a name on it in six weeks will have to come past the line that is already on it. The form: nothing is answered, and Bel Ordry asks who will say no if a second one comes up the steps, and Sefu Aran says the clerk will, and not him, because the day a keeper starts saying no to paper is the day a keeper starts keeping a file. And then **Mikka Hale puts a fifth item on the list that is not on it: the fill at the waist went down a hand's breadth in the thaw, under nine children's feet, and it did not complain, and there is no packing for it because the packing that would have gone into the waist went out of the anteroom's four foot eleven and into a shore's head six weeks earlier — both in Tams Quill's column, on the same page.** Tams reads the two lines, one in each hand, and says *that is mine* and asks for his name under it and asks nobody to be kind to him about it. Then the water is read out loud for the first time in eleven weeks, in Mikka's own words, and asked for: **it comes up the middle passage in pails on the shoulders of whoever is coming, and it has never been in this book, and add it to my column with no heading, because it is not a day and it is not an hour and it is a pair of shoulders, and there is no column in this book for a pair of shoulders.** The two columns: the crew's **forty-four and a half**, up twice in a fortnight for the first time since the second week, and not one of the six hours was work anybody in the boundary needed done; the boundary's **eighty-one and three-quarters**, itemised without rounding, with Renn Vale's own four hours explicitly not counted again, with **Tams's own half-day in the anteroom on the stranger's day, in which he said no whole sentence and entered the half anyway**, and with **Mikka Hale's pot struck out of the column as money and not a day** so the list reconciles exactly on the sixty-five, and the finding unchanged — **the half that gets counted is the half that is ours.** And then **Mikka Hale asks the volume's question a second time in a harder form**: *a room is kept by the work in it, a job is a reason for a person to be in a room, and when there is no work to be done there is no reason for anybody to be in the room and nothing is missing and nobody notices the day it stops* — so: **who keeps the Hearthhold rooms on the day there is no work left to do in them, and who notices, and how does anybody find out?** Nobody answers. Sefu Aran then does the owed thing: **the spring conversation is scheduled with a date, an hour, a room and two people**, and he says out loud that it is not about the crew, that it happens whether or not anybody is leaving, and that a keeper who starts saying no to paper has started keeping a file. Nera Oduya gives the hand-over in four sentences: a valve, a grille, a bypass hatch, a board with four cards and two unaccounted marks, and a post at the second bell and the fifth — **and the person is not me and is not going to be me for a year**, and she will say it in that hour, and the person she names will not be in the room, and on the third day she will go and stand at their door.

## Chapter 66 — What the Thaw Took

Frost for three days and then a wet wind off the shaft, and on Thursday afternoon at twenty past five Renn Vale, on the waist with Isel Ferrow and a school corridor's worth of people gone past, puts two fingers on the third wedge and says one word into the waist: **Up.** She reports it from the common landing with the slate under her arm, and Dalla Sen writes it on a bench at the bottom of the nine steps. Two things, said before what she wants: the ground moved again and **it came up through the sole of her boot**, which is the whole of the instrument; and the third wedge has come up a quarter of an inch, and *a wedge in a fill does not come up because it is tired, it comes up because the ground under it moved, and telling you is the whole of its office* — and she adds that she has been standing on moved ground for two hours without putting her hand down, because a person with a hand on a fill has made a decision that the ground is fine. Ilsa Norr says the corridor shuts now and puts her own cost in the same breath — a day of school, nine children, and a day the nine do not get back. **Then Mikka Hale says the water.** It does not come from a pipe and it does not come out of the ground: **it comes up the middle passage in pails, on the shoulders of whoever is coming that week, paid for out of what they are carrying, and it goes down the nine steps and through the school door and along the corridor to this kitchen, and it passes two places that are two foot eight wide and one of them is that waist.** Her number is sixteen and will be fifteen tomorrow, and she does not read out a number she has not written down first. Jo Verrick refuses Marek's *the waist went so the water stopped*: the waist is a fill, the water is a pump, and the pump's seat is going, and the fill was packed out of the dip by her own hand, and in a year somebody will read a cause into a sentence that has three separate things standing next to each other in a two-foot-eight corridor. The closure goes on the clerk's page with Renn's name and thirty-one words in her own hand. And then Sefu Aran puts the week in the air in one breath: **the corridor is shut, the water stops, the school is off, and from Monday the stair is the only way anything gets into this building, four at a time, four minutes, in the pump's window, and it is not for a cart.** Tams Quill does the arithmetic out loud — fourteen pails a day, four to a crossing, **twenty-eight crossings a week against a record of four** — and says he has got no column for it and would like somebody better at arithmetic to tell him what the arithmetic is. The woman from the wash rooms says no, standing on the steps, and does not go up to the covers. And then **Renn Vale says the thing nobody has wanted to hear: *then we do it four days in seven*** — the corridor open on the days she holds the wet seam, shut on the three she does not — and calls it a calendar and not a rota, and puts it in the book in her own words, and says she will stand on moved ground and will not put her hand down, and **will not decide who carries the water on the other three days.** And Ilsa Norr, at the top of three steps, says stop: **the school used to run when I said it ran, and it now runs on Renn Vale's days, and I am not refusing and I want it in the book in my words that nobody asked me and the first thing in eleven weeks this boundary has put on a person's body is a rota made out of a woman with a bad boot**, and asks for her own cost to be read at the fifth bell on a schedule.

## Chapter 67 — Over the Stair

Friday morning, forty minutes, two people who do not agree about anything else: the pot and the crossing. Mikka takes the pot — **twelve on the open days, eight on the shut ones, and I am not sorry about the four** — and Tams takes the crossing and reads the seven terms out of his own memory, including the four treads nobody walks, and gets to **two crossings on a shut day, at the first bell and after the fifth, because a stair period may not fall on a day the school runs or between the second bell and the fourth** — six crossings a week against a record of four, a fifth of the twenty-eight on his board two days earlier. Jo Verrick takes the objection nobody expected, against herself: the rule she made in the ninth week is true and it forbids the water being on the route *instead of* the people, and every one of those crossings is four people and a pail, and a pail does not go through a doorway on its own, and she wants both sentences on one line so that the line which stops a barrow is next to the line which stops her. **Four people offer, and Dalla Sen writes the fact that four people offered before she writes any of the names, and Pell Roke corrects her word *boy* to *fourteen* from the bench.** Renn asks the woman from the wash rooms for the string, three days a week, twice on each, at the first bell and after the fifth, and writes the asking and the answer in her own hand, and **the woman does her own arithmetic standing on the step, finds that a shut day has no school and her covers are at the second bell and the fifth, and says yes — and says she is not taking yesterday back, she is adding to it: yesterday she was right, today she has found a way round it that costs her nothing she had, and that is not being talked out of anything, that is a woman who has been here a month.** Isel Ferrow takes the near lip for six crossings and asks for the word *asked* written next to his name. Bel Ordry takes the threshold bell and says out loud that he did not volunteer because the bell is the easy one and a bell is the only part of that stair that has to be *heard*, and then takes it anyway, and names his cost as a month of his mother's door instead of a day. On the Saturday the first crossing goes and goes badly: fifty-eight seconds off the near landing, worse than the thirty-eight and the best figure in the record for a party with a load, and **the turn comes and the cold has taken the plinth** — Ruk Sella felt it late and says so in her own words and Dalla makes her say it twice, and Pell called it eight seconds early and said he would not be told he had been late by anybody who was not sitting where he was sitting — and the string has the word and Isel does not leave the lip and there is no knee on the stone. Dalla writes down what made the morning: **three of the four instruments on that stair failed in the cold, and the one that held was a person with her hand on a rope, a boot on a stone and a bad hand in a sling who had said yes at the top of three steps.** And Jo announces that she is going to open the housing on Monday with a borrowed chisel, and names the price before she starts — a day of corridor, a day of school, an unfilled pot — and says that if there is nothing to look at then she will have looked, and this building is full of women who did not.

## Chapter 68 — Locally, or by Charter

The argument is had on the common landing **in the gaps between school crossings**, on Sefu Aran's condition, with nine children at a walk and a bell at the threshold, and every sentence gets said in about nine minutes. **Renn Vale: locally**, and she argues it from a document — the sentence the assessor read out, that no officer shall be required to enter, inspect, maintain, fund or answer — and from the fact that this boundary chose *none reported* about its own seventh term. **Iven Tallo: charter, reluctantly and honestly**, and the room does not like it: a waist in washed-out fill on a two-foot-eight gap over an eleven-foot shaft, with ground that has moved twice, wants a survey and a licensed man and a bottom nobody has seen, and there is none of the five things it needs in this Hearthhold, so what locally *is* is that somebody stands on it — **and he says out loud that he said the correct response to a guild page is nothing on the fourth day and is arguing for the guild on the ninth, and that both are the same sentence and he has not changed his mind about anything.** Nera Oduya breaks the argument in half: **you are not choosing between a local repair and a charter, you are choosing which of your two faults you are willing to write down in words** — a charter buys the pump argument, which is a route instrument, and leaves the floor argument exactly where it is, and a floor is not a route and has no form with a box for it. Sefu Aran: a charter is an admission document, and what it buys is reach and what it costs is a name, and a name is a fiction that has to be kept alive by somebody writing to a clerk. And then Mikka Hale ends it: **a charter does not carry pails.** And she announces the batch's second real instrument — **a book of favours, in her own hand, every date, name and number of pails, read out at the fifth bell every week** — because a favour is a loan with no date on it, and this room learned that from Bel Ordry and from a courier and it has been using it ever since. And in the last gap before the bell, Marek Venn says the thing nobody had said: *there is no version of this week where somebody is not standing on that waist; locally it is a person, and by charter it is a person and a form and a name and a person after that.* And **Renn Vale says the choice was not between a floor and a charter — it was between a floor with a name on it and a floor without, and this room has not chosen either, and it will find out what that costs on Monday when Jo Verrick opens a housing with a borrowed chisel.** Dalla Sen refuses *pending* a second time. The landing clears, the school comes through, and the review is called.

## Chapter 69 — One Cleaning

Thursday, first bell, the housing comes off in pieces and the bolt-hole at the back has opened a quarter of an inch, and **Jo Verrick holds the seat up into the lamp so that nine people who have never seen a pump's delivery seat can see one, and asks Dalla Sen to enter that it was held up and that nine people looked at it, because in four years somebody is going to ask her whether she looked.** It is a scored ring of bronze, thin as a coin in one place, with a bright crescent worn into the delivery side. **Put it back** — and the estimate moves, for the first time in eleven weeks, in her own hand, from *two or fewer* to **one**, and nobody is allowed to say it moved because of the look, and she refuses to write zero because zero is a decision and a decision gets made on a day with a man standing in front of you. And she says the honest half: the look cost a day of school and a day of a pot and bought her knowledge that she was already sure of. Marek Venn stands two feet from the bench with the chalk half out of his pocket and does not take it out, because the quarter inch is inside Jo's number and a figure in a full room becomes his in nine seconds. Tams puts the cleaning in **held, not spent**, and says he has had nothing in that column but a shut until now. Then the two costs: **Mikka Hale's number goes from sixteen to fifteen, and she asks for it to be read out loud at the fifth bell every day so she is not the only person who knows**, and — the one that matters — **Leena Orr's litter is on the anteroom's side of the shut waist and the clinic is on the other, and Mikka says she cannot stop a bleed up nine steps in a corridor two foot eight wide with a litter in it, and then says, and asks for it in the book in her own words with the time on it: *I asked for it.*** And the woman from the wash rooms comes up on a day she is not needed, because there is a condition to say out loud: **she shut this route once because she is not a pump hand and does not know what a thin hiss is, and the room has now arranged that she stand on a string at five in the morning three days a week, so the thing she shut the route for is the thing she is personally standing in — and there is no thin and no full any more and nothing to teach her and nobody to ask.** She asks for one thing in her own hand, brought written out because she did not want to do it in front of them: **when I say the word it stays shut until somebody who knows looks at the reason, and nobody is to argue with me at the moment I say it or afterwards, and if I was wrong the cost of my being wrong is mine.** Renn Vale asks for it to be copied into a slate; the clerk says no; Renn says why and the clerk agrees, because it is hers and it is not policy. And at the fifth bell, Tams Quill reads out the week — six crossings, in the cold, with the bar cold and the plinth cold and the check on one note, and on the third of them a plinth reader believed a plinth for half a second because a cold thing under a cold hand does not move the way a warm thing does — and a boy at the top of nine steps says **six is a photograph of six cold mornings, it is not six of anything else, and nobody is to use it**, and the clerk reads it out twice without being asked. The frame hisses all week on one note, the seat goes back in with a bolt-hole open a quarter inch, and on the Friday the water in the dip is four inches from a chalk line that has not moved.

## Chapter 70 — Whose Wood

**Nera Oduya writes a hardwood inventory on the back of a card and reads it out line by line, and nine people take it apart over an hour and forty minutes, and every line is a thing somebody does not have.** Line one, the scarfed head, Renn's, in a shore, no. Line two, the five foot nine with the number still chalked on the end, and the only line anybody asked to be kept. Line three, two foot ten and a handful in Jo's basket, **not sound**, underlined, and Jo asks for it in capitals and Nera says she is not going to shout at a woman about a piece of wood in her own basket. Line four, the five public-works wedges; line five, seven sound wedges and two dead sticks, and Renn makes one dead stick entered as a dead stick so that in four years somebody cannot try to use it. Line six, the anteroom's workbench surface, **the absence of a line of wood**, with the bracket's nine inches entered on Iven's request. Line seven, the school store's two beech lengths, and **Ilsa Norr makes them change *Ilsa Norr's* to *the school, held by Ilsa Norr***, because a thing in a locked box belongs to a room and a thing in an apron belongs to a woman, and in four years a clerk is going to ask who owns a beech lintel. Line eight, Bel Ordry's mother's floor, given, marked in pencil, not cut — he asks for the line to be read aloud and asks not to be thanked, and says the reason in the *no* column and the reason he gave are two different sentences and both of them are true. Line nine, the pump's bed, thirty years in standing water, the best-conditioned timber in the Hearthhold, and the housing bolts into it. Line ten, **the wash rooms**: a rack, thirty years damp, the only piece of wood a delivery seat could sit in and stay put, not anybody's, and the only person who can answer for that room has not been asked, and Renn Vale says the page is not going to be the thing that makes her go. Line eleven, the middle gate, four days away, and the reason is not distance. Line twelve, the parapet slab, refused three times, a sill and not a seat. And line thirteen, what the seat wants — eleven inches, a set face, a hand that has been a hand for a season, somebody to stand with the water line — **and there is no line on that page for a person who has one, and she would rather have a short page than a wrong one.** Then the work is read out as **failed**, and Jo Verrick stops Dalla Sen's reason — *the material does not exist* — and has it changed to *the material exists and every piece of it is in use, and one piece of it has been offered and refused by its owner for a reason of his own*, and the entry is read nine times and is the one she would like left in the book longest. On the common landing Jo measures the lip and gives a range, because Ilsa made her give a range once and it stuck: **a finger and a half to a finger and three-quarters**, up from about a finger and a half, and the shore took a quarter inch off the worst day of her life and gave a bit of it back in a fortnight of frost, and **that is not a fix and the man is still under the lip and it will be Jo Verrick if the slab turns while she is on the lever**, and Renn asks for the number and the seventh term to be read out together at the fifth bell because one is about a person and the other is about a stone. The spring conversation happened on the second day at the fourth bell, one hour, the leaving not mentioned once, and it produced one thing that is not in the ledger: Nera Oduya said a name, in her own hand, and the person does not know yet, and the air engineer went and stood at their door. The blank on the review page still has no name against it and is read out every day without comment. And Marek Venn, at the fifth bell, understands that the whole of what he has to bring to a boundary is one sentence, eleven words long, that he has never once in his life said out loud in a room; the brass rule is in the coat on its hook and says nothing; he puts a slate down blank side up and leaves it, because the only thing he had to record belonged to a woman at a frame; and then he goes and asks Jo Verrick, out loud, in a corridor, who is going to stand at the low end of the corridor in the six minutes after the lever comes off, and she says a name, and does not say it, and says it.

## Chapter 71 — The Terms

The thirteenth week opens with **Ilsa Norr emptying her own school store**, nine boxes down nine steps carried by nine-year-olds in twos at a walk, the two beech props under the dressed-stone shelf lifted first, and **a day of school named before the work and in the same breath as it** — after which Sefu Aran flags the anteroom over its rating and sends six people down the nine steps to listen. Box four has a corner held on by a strip of crate board and four nails and Ilsa says, to nobody in particular, that it is eleven weeks old and has done more work this month than a great deal of the timber they have been counting, and nobody laughs. **Nera Oduya then says the sentence that governs the batch, before anything is unrolled: she will be the only person in the room who cannot be trusted with what is on it, and she wants it said out loud at that hour and not afterwards** — and gives the reason, which is that she is the only one of the five who knows what a plan is for, and that she has wanted a document to tell her something since the seventh week, and that this is not a noble thing to walk into a room with. Bel Ordry says then we do not open it; she says we open it, because refusing a work on the grounds that you would like to be the one doing it is the one thing nobody in this building has ever done. **Ilsa's terms, in her own words: the school store is the room; the key is hers and turns on her date; five of us, and the five of them are not in the room, and the reason is that a document you have not been in a room with is a document you can still argue with; the plan does not leave the store, is not copied, drawn or traced; what leaves is a description in the words of the five of them, corrected by her in the same hour; and if one of them cannot carry what is in there, that person says so out loud on the way out, in the anteroom, and not in a store and not in a margin and not in a letter.** The five go in at the third bell. Marek Venn stands on the other side of a foot and a half of dressed stone with a slate he does not use, hears the boxes come off the shelf, and hears **a dowel turn for forty seconds**, and knows exactly what the next four seconds of a professional life are and is not in the room to do them, and works out that being sent out of rooms is a thing he has turned into a virtue and that a virtue is something a man who is leaving should not be doing in a building where a clerk has just written a word she did not know she was writing. Tams Quill counts the boxes twice and enters, in his left hand, that he counted them twice because he had been told once and had not believed it. The door opens at a quarter past the fourth bell and Ilsa Norr says that she has not got anything to hand anybody and she has not got anything to keep, and begins.

## Chapter 72 — Nine Rows

The description is read out, corrected and re-read, and it is **not a drawing of a building.** A hand-wide sheet on a dowel, **nine lines, three columns**: how many people (a number; nobody's names, not even initials, and Ilsa says so before anybody goes looking); when (**a condition in longhand — wet, dark, cold, first, last — and not one number and not one day of a week anywhere**); and what is done, which is **empty on six of the nine lines**. Mikka Hale makes the clerk correct her own line (four is a room, not a pot) and Ilsa Norr says out loud that **there is no treasure on it: it is a schedule of keeping a place to live in, and schedules are not maps and they do not show you rooms, they show you that somebody expected to be here.** **Leena Orr stops the room and asks whether it is to a scale**, because a page with nine rooms on it and no way to find one of them is the most dangerous kind of old document there is, and the room had assumed a description. Nera Oduya answers that it is, having fitted eight of the nine lines to this level by eye and by memory and checked twice — and then says the sentence the batch turns on: **the ninth line is not in the order because it is not in this level. It is down. Four steps.** It is below the ninth tread of the stair behind the rail, at the bottom of the four treads nobody has walked and is not walked this month on her own condition, and it has **a one** in the count, **none** in the when, and **nothing at all** in the work, and *none* appears nowhere else on the page. Then she says the misreading out loud and asks for it to be in the book: **this boundary has been keeping that room since the ninth week, by crossing it** — six crossings a week, four at a time, with a bearer on a lip that is packed and not held — *and I want it to be true, and that is the sentence I asked to be written at the second bell this morning, and this is me finding out what it is for.* **Renn Vale says stop**, and does not come down three steps, and says in her own hand that a room is not kept by crossing it, that a room is kept by somebody going into it, that the day somebody goes down those four treads the keeping begins and it will not stop, and that the choice of a page from before any of them were alive is not her; **the eighth term is not withdrawn, the ninth line is not *held*, the ninth line is *none*.** Nera adds what is not on the page and it is the reason the document cannot answer anything: **there is no air on it at all** — no vent, no shaft, no grille, no rate — *which is not the same as saying they did not have any, and I have spent eleven weeks teaching this room the difference and I am not going to be the one who drops it today.* Dalla Sen closes the day by making the finding legible: eight rooms kept because people work in them, one room at the bottom of four treads with a person in it and nobody near it, and **the only thing anybody has ever done about it is walk over the top of it and call it water**, to be read twice a day, with no name ever to go on the ninth line.

## Chapter 73 — Wet

The consequences land on an ordinary week. **Ilsa Norr touches the corridor wall at the height of a child's shoulder and works out that the plan's *wet* and Renn Vale's wet-seam days are the same four days in seven** — and that she has been reading one as a rota and the other as weather, and that **she cannot tell which of the two wrote the other one down**, and therefore cannot say in this room that the school is hers. She enters it in her own words and asks for it to be read at the fifth bell **on the last day of the week, once**, having had her cost read on a schedule before and refusing a second schedule. **Then Mikka Hale finishes and reads out the book of favours and admits what she did with it: she copied the shape of the plan onto it — how many, and when, and what is done — and filled in the third column with *water* forty-one times in three days, and then sat down and understood that she had built a page with a room on it and a count and a condition and no work in it.** She says the whole reason she started the book was that a favour is a loan with no date on it, and that she has gone and put a date on it, and *the day I head it, it becomes a unit.* Mikka names **Pell Roke** as one of the four or five who carried water, says out loud that she made him do it, and then does not look at him while she says it. **Renn Vale objects to the *when* and not to the book**: the wet days are her days, so a book of favours now has a rota in it made of her boots, and *a condition has stopped meaning the weather and started meaning a rota, and that happened on the sixth day of the twelfth week and nobody wrote it down* — and Dalla Sen writes that down, and notes that the kitchen's book and the ninth line of a locked-store document now mean the same four days out of seven. **And a boy of fourteen closes it**: the ninth line has got a one in it, and if *none* means there is no day, then that is not a room nobody works in — **that is a room with a person posted to it and no work** — and the room has spent two hours arguing about whether anybody does anything in it.

## Chapter 74 — On the Step

**Renn Vale writes the day on her own slate, in front of the clerk, and nobody gives her one**, because the last time somebody handed her a date for a thing she had refused to do she did it in a hurry and it cost a person a morning. She says her terms out loud in a full room: she goes alone, she knocks, she stands on the step while the woman says whatever she is going to say **including no**, and afterwards the whole of the room is told what she said in her words and the woman's and none of the room was in it — *and that is her arrangement and it is older than any of us and I am not the one who is granting it.* She asks Dalla Sen to enter the asking as it is and not softened: **she is asking for a piece of wood**, and she wants the word *wood* in it and read out whatever is said. She is gone forty minutes. Marek Venn stands at the tally board with the sentence he has spent eleven weeks learning — *I am asking for your afternoon, and I want to know what it is like* — and does not say it, because a man who asks a woman for her afternoon is asking for a room, and the room is not his, and the woman has been asked for nothing in eleven weeks and has said yes to two things, one of which put a dead man's mother under a slab. **She says no**, and gives the reason, and it is not that the wood is hers: the wood is on the rack because a rack is what you put things on when the floor is bad, and if you take the piece of wood off that rack then the rack is empty and the floor is still bad, and *that room is a room with a bad floor and an empty rack in it, and it is emptier than a room with nothing in it, because a room with nothing in it at least admits it* — and in about a year somebody will come down that corridor with a list and see an empty rack and write down that there was nothing in that room, **and there is her, in it, every second bell and every fifth, lifting the covers, and that is what the piece of wood is standing up for.** Her condition, given as a condition: **the wash rooms are kept by the person who lifts the covers and by nobody else; there is no work in them; nobody is to be sent down that corridor to do anything, ever; the floor is refused and stays refused; it goes in the kitchen's book and not the route's book; and no name is to be put against them, by anybody, including by accident in four years.** She asked one question at the door — *is anybody going to have to come down that corridor to keep the record true* — and Renn said no. Her **eleven words are not copied into any hand** and she gives the reason: *that one is about when you say the word; this one is about the room.* **Jo Verrick closes the hunt: six owners, six reasons better than hardness, the hunt is over, there is nobody left to ask, and the price of the twelfth week's look is not coming back** — and the only thing between that machine and the dip is her and Isel Ferrow and a chalk line. The fifth bell now reads four things together: the lip's range, the seventh term, the wood she would not have, and a room kept with nothing in the third column of anybody's book, discovered this week, four doors down, by the person nobody had asked.

## Chapter 75 — A Supervising Holder

**Wen Pask**, twenty-two, three years apprenticed to Iven Tallo, comes up the middle passage on the Friday of the thirteenth week with a bundle and a fold of guild paper and a leg that went at the service bend, and says four sentences: the office has read a master's suspension into the roll on the ninth day; an apprentice's bond is his master's bond; **his bond went with his, and a man with no bond cannot be entered on a register, cannot be paid trade work, and cannot be signed against a route**; and he walked four days with it himself because there is nobody at the middle gate to send. **Iven Tallo reads the whole notice out and then reads the fourth paragraph again**: *an apprentice under a suspended master may continue in the trade for a period not exceeding one year under the supervision of a named holder entered against a named route, in a register kept by the office, on payment of the annual supervision fee.* And then: **that is the whole of the charter that I have been arguing about for thirteen weeks, on one line, in a notice about a boy, and I have never once seen it in a form I could read.** The middle's store will not release a stick of timber on his word either, so the only yes this Hearthhold ever had is now blocked twice, and Sefu Aran says reach is a road and can be argued about and **permission is a person, and a person can be found.** Wen Pask then says the thing that costs Iven everything: he was suspended by the argument, by the same argument, in the same words, made by the same man, *and it did not even have to be him to do it.* Iven says **yes, it holds, I am not going to stand in this room and be told I was wrong, because I was not wrong about the page** — and refuses to be forgiven, and refuses the boy's obvious wish to work here for nothing, **because the crew's page empties in the spring and he would have taught him the sentence and broken it for him four doors from where he learned it, and because it would be a favour with no date on it and he is not adding a thirteenth to this building's list.** Sefu enters him: **a man of this boundary, arrived, refused a trade, refused by a work, and kept** — not paid, not on a rota, not owed. Mikka Hale says out loud, from the frame, that the most selfish thing she has said all week is that he will be the only pair of hands in here that is not somebody's. Ilsa Norr says four words from the school door and goes back up the steps. **Marek Venn works out, and says none of it, that the danger was never a name on a page: a boy with no name on the roll has been suspended anyway, because the page needed a date and a sentence and a stamp forty days away.**

## Chapter 76 — The Word Maintainer

**The dependency, in physical form, on the Saturday.** Isel Ferrow is on his shutter route — the half-day lost at the pump frame in the twelfth week was never replaced and a man with a shutter route will always be somewhere the shutter needs him — so the first crossing does not go at the first bell, the water does not come in, and **Mikka Hale's number goes from fifteen to fourteen in a day, and the reason is a man going to earn his living instead of standing on a stone in the cold** — and it stays at fourteen until the second Monday of the next week, when a fourth day is shut at the waist and it goes to thirteen. Then Sefu Aran has the notice read again and Bel Ordry asks the clerk to look at her own hand: since the fourth day of the eleventh week the book has held a hardwood inventory with an owner against every line, a pump maintainer's estimate in her own hand with a time on it, a schoolteacher's rota and three items of her own cost, a keeper's calendar called a calendar, four mornings of a bar with no conclusion, a count of six crossings in six cold mornings, two columns that both reconcile, a cook's book begun this week, a closure with a reason in a woman's hand, and **nine hundred years of somebody's care described into a page of this one** — and a notice that says the trade will supervise a boy for a year if a named holder is entered against a named route. **Dalla Sen says the thing nobody in the room had said: this is the only object in this Hearthhold that a person forty days away can hold, and in a term's time a notice goes into a roll, and it does not need my name in it, it needs a record that a route was kept, and I have been writing one of those since the sixth week of the sixth month.** Renn Vale says it goes in, all of it, in her words, and adds that the first time a refusal has got itself onto a page in a form that could be carried out of this building, it has been the clerk's, and she did it eight times a day out of duty, **and that the best person in this Hearthhold at writing is now the dangerous thing about her.** Then Sefu comes off the wheel, which he does not do, and names the shape: **in thirteen weeks the people this boundary keeps have become the people this boundary keeps.** The nine children are the ones who cross; the clinic is the reason the water crosses; the kitchen is the reason the stair is used at five in the morning; the woman who lifts the covers is the string. And Bel Ordry says the word **employs** and says he did not enjoy it and is going to write it down anyway. **Renn Vale says no, and gives the callback: two weeks ago the choice was not between a floor and a charter, it was between a floor with a name on it and a floor without — and it is now the choice between water with a name on it and water without**, and *a date is half a name and a hand is the other half.* And then the sentence nobody was going to be kind about: **ask who was maintaining this in the twelfth week, and this book will say nine people in their own writing, and every one of them is a beneficiary.** Nobody fixes it. Dalla Sen enters that it was not decided but arrived at over eleven weeks by nine people doing nine kinds of work correctly, that it cannot be un-arrived at without somebody deciding to, and that the clerk's own assessment is that the boundary has now built the evidence for an instrument it never applied for — and reads it out twice.

## Chapter 77 — The Third Time

**The third slump happens on the Sunday, the last day of the thirteenth week, on a day nobody was standing there**, because a post is only a post while its condition is happening and the waist is not a post on the days the corridor is shut. Bel Ordry's bar also ticks on that Sunday morning, and on the Monday — the first day of the fourteenth week — the two facts go on the same page with a date on each and **nothing between them, on purpose** — Nera Oduya will not let a Tuesday exist where a bar said something and a floor did something and a person put the two next to each other with their eyebrows — and Dalla Sen enters the reason for putting them near each other **so a reader in a year cannot make it into a finding.** Renn Vale reports it from the landing in eleven seconds: a hand's breadth again, along the left side, over five foot this time, and the third wedge up **a quarter and a bit**, which is not a number and is the same quarter with a bad temper. The corridor is shut, and *nobody goes over it*, and she says she is not standing on that fill and will not put her hand on it, because a person with a hand on a fill has made a decision that the ground is fine. **Which leaves the water**, and Mikka Hale puts the pair-of-shoulders column into the ordinary week: two people, one at a time, at a walk, past a fill that has moved three times, on a day the school is not coming. Two names go into the book before any name, and a third goes in and **Iven Tallo strikes it out in his own hand** — a man with no trade does not go on moved ground so that a room can feel better about itself, *that is what a body is for in a bad argument.* So it is Isel Ferrow and Jo Verrick, and Iven refuses the framing — *on the stone I hold a rope and go back; on that fill I put my feet on washed-out stuff over an eleven-foot shaft* — and the carry goes at the second bell on the Monday with the eight pails a shut day gets, in two crossings of four, and takes an hour and fifty minutes, and he prices it in his own hand: **a day and a half of a shutter route for Isel, a day of his own unpaid trade, a day of school, and a day of a pot — and the number is thirteen, and Dalla Sen enters that the last time the number went down by more than one in a day was the thaw in the eleventh week, when it went from nineteen to sixteen in one Tuesday afternoon, and that was worse and it was three.** **Marek Venn goes down on the second Tuesday of the fourteenth week, inside the terms, puts his left palm on the throat's far wall at bar height, gets nothing in four degrees, and then spends ninety seconds on the common landing refusing to write *null* and then writing it** — the eighth — because he has been wrong about the cold for a fortnight and it belongs with the other seven. **Tams Quill moves it into the column with no heading, with the temperature and the reason, and says the column now has two in it and a column with two in it is a column, and he is not going to head it.** Bel Ordry then enters a sentence on purpose in order to be caught: *slump, third event — measured: nothing. Measured by: nothing*, and Jo Verrick catches it, and it is read out, and it is the truest thing on the page in a fortnight. And the chapter closes on the corridor giving up its one crossing on the Thursday and shutting again, and a bar that has said nothing three times and something three times with a slide on the end of the something, and **the page that says all of it with a second page laid against it, dated, and nothing between them.**

## Chapter 78 — The Column With No Heading

**On the last day of the fourteenth week Tams Quill reads a fortnight, and he calls the days by their weeks because there are two Mondays in it.** **The crew's column has not gone up at all** — forty-four and a half, unchanged across the whole of the thirteenth and fourteenth weeks — and he reads the things that were not work and refuses to put an hour against any of them: a wall on the first Monday, a corner of a room on the first Tuesday, Iven Tallo's own trade on the second Monday and the fact that he is right that it is his choice and not the crew's column, and a bar on a cold wall and a hand on a cold wall on the second Tuesday. And then the batch's arithmetic, and its finding: **that number has never been a measure of us; it is a measure of whether this boundary needs us — forty-four and a half is not a quantity of engineering, it is a quantity of *asking*, and three weeks is the longest run since the second week of the whole time and the longest in which we were not needed, and a man with a board who has thought the board was about us has just been told by the board that it is about them.** And then the refusal, at his own request and entered in his own hand: **a column that does not go up is the first evidence this Hearthhold has produced toward the end of its own obligation, and I am the man who could stand up and say *we are finished*, and I will not say it on a figure, and a man who could end an obligation with arithmetic and does not do it has to say that he knew he could.** Dalla Sen records that this is the first entry in thirteen weeks in which a person has declined to be relieved of something, and that the declining is now in the only object in this building a stranger can hold, and that she said the same thing on a page in this room eight days ago and is having to say it twice in eight days. The boundary's column is read without rounding and reconciles exactly: **Ilsa Norr 1.5, Mikka Hale 2, Jo Verrick 1.5, Renn Vale 1, Dalla Sen 1, Bel Ordry 4 — four mornings at the bar, the last of them the Sunday, and the sixth morning anybody has put that bar against that wall — Isel Ferrow 1.5, Nera Oduya 1, thirteen and a half on eighty-one and three-quarters, which is ninety-five and a quarter** — and **Wen Pask's ten days and ten nights and his leg and his bundle are in the column with no heading and in nothing else, because he is not on a rota and is not paid and is not owed and is not a post and there is no column in this book for a man who is kept.** Mikka Hale's two carries the two hours she put the fourteen-year-old at the top of nine steps, and Tams Quill has them in her book and not in his, at her request. The column with no heading is the fullest on the board and holds seven lines, four of them six days old — and one of the seven is **a bone in a stranger's pack, refused a line**, because the man it belonged to is under eleven feet of dressed stone at the near landing and is not coming up, and there is nothing of him in this building to put anywhere — and he takes back four weeks of insisting that it get a name: **the day I head it, it becomes a unit, and a unit is a thing you can total, and a thing a room can be praised in.** And then the ninth line: he could put it in **held** in four seconds and it is the only thing he has ever wanted to put in that column that is not a piece of wood and not a cord. **Renn Vale says no — the ninth line is not held, the ninth line is *none*, it is a condition, and I will not have a page from before any of us were alive make this building frightened on a Sunday, and I wrote that on a slate at the end of the first week of this fortnight and I am not withdrawing it because a woman read a one out of a page in a locked store and everybody in this room heard her read it.** Dalla Sen enters that a boundary now has **two ways of saying *not on any day*** and that the two are not in agreement and nobody has asked them to be. Mikka reads the book out at the fifth bell: **six lines, the three shut days at eight pails — the Sunday and the two days after it — and forty-one writes of the word water in the third column, and then the line in her own hand on the first Wednesday night that says the word *when* means boots.** And the batch's own sentence, arrived at by accident, as a warning: **a room is kept by somebody going into it, and a book only records that somebody went.** Close: **six nulls in a column and two in a bucket, which was eight in all**, and no usable reading anywhere, and a brass rule silent for six weeks in a coat on a hook.

## Chapter 79 — Asking

Dalla Sen reads the third item on the review page at the fifth bell with a blank against it, as she has for three weeks, and nobody fills the space after it. Then **Marek Venn says Jo** — and admits he has had the name for a fortnight and has neither written it down nor said it in a room, and has been walking about like a man ashamed of a piece of paper, which is a thing he has done for thirty-two years. **Renn Vale stops him before he goes, because a post is a thing she hands out, the air engineer put it there and would not fill it, and if he goes round the keeper then in six weeks somebody will say he did and they will be right.** So Renn goes with him as far as the clinic return and sets out the post in full on the landing in front of the clerk: the six minutes after the lever comes off, the water in the dip, the two-foot-eight low end over an eleven-foot shaft, no instrument to read it, and **a shout into a shut corridor is a shout into a wall.** Then he goes alone and says what the post is before he asks for it, badly, and knows he is saying it badly. **She says no.** And he says the rest of it — *I would rather it be a no that is on the page than a nothing that is on the page* — and she tells him to say something else. Then she gives the answer, in ninety seconds, on her own step: **she cannot read a chalk line and cannot hear a hiss on one note, but she knows what that corridor sounds like when it is filling faster than it usually fills, the way a person knows their own kitchen at night** — and so **I will not stand at that low end six times a week; I will come, any day, at any hour, the moment that sound changes, and I will come once and I will look and I will shout if there is anything to shout about, and then it is over and I go back up to my covers** — on three conditions: **no name against it, ever, including by accident in four years; it is not a rota and nobody is to make it one, and if it becomes one she will stop; and do not send anybody to make it true, nobody down that corridor to check on her and nobody down it to check the water.** Nera Oduya confirms from the top of three steps that **a sentence in a hand is a better thing than a name in a column**, and Bel Ordry raises the other thread, and **Nera refuses, in a full room, to be asked about the air valve hand-over name** — *a person finds out about a post from the person who is handing it over, on a day when the handing is a choice, and not from a page in a week when it has already been decided* — and Dalla Sen enters that she has been asked to record a **refusal to be asked**, which is a hole in the record and she will not paper it over with a line. Then **Wen Pask**, eleven days in and eleven nights in a school store and not asked for an hour of anything, produces a scrap of paper: **forty pails over four days up the middle passage, four or five people, the same four or five every day, four of them the people who stand on the stair, and one of them fourteen and should not be carrying anything** — and he has the rule from a woman at a counter and has checked his own total twice, twelve on an open day and eight on a shut one, two of each, and he will not head it, because he has watched the count do that. And then the thing that makes the rest of the book: **there is a hold on the middle gate's timber, the water-lock keeper has sent the same message up the middle passage three times to two different people, and the message is not about wood. The message is: has this Hearthhold said it will not come.** Nobody in eleven rooms in eleven days had ever found it in a book. Marek Venn understands that the sentence he has to say in the morning is not about a floor or a lip or a post, and that the answer will cost this Hearthhold the only piece of wood it has ever been able to name.

## Chapter 80 — What This Hearthhold Will Not Do
