**Nobody in the anteroom has ever heard the question put out loud, and four people start to answer it at once and stop.** *Has this boundary ever said out loud that it will not come for the middle gate's timber?* And Sefu Aran says **no**, and gives the bad reason out loud because a room that cannot say the bad reason has not got a good one: **if I say we will not come, I have said we cannot come, and the day the word *cannot* is in the air a courier comes down the middle passage with a charter and a bed and a man who can do something about it, and this Hearthhold has spent thirteen weeks refusing a man who can do something about it — I have been holding a door shut by never saying what is behind it, and a twenty-two-year-old with a scrap of paper has just told me that the other side of that door has a woman at a counter who has said the same sentence three times and slower the third time.** Jo Verrick says the shape of what happens next: **if the keeper says we will not come, then a piece of paper goes out of this building saying that this boundary declines four hundred paces of seasoned hardwood, the only thing in this Hearthhold that has ever been a *yes* anywhere, and the room that has spent a week being frightened of its own book is going to write down the one thing it has ever wanted, in the one form that can be carried out of here. And it will cost us the plank.** So the keeper names it, and puts the price on it before he signs it, and **puts the stair outside it in front of the room: the stair is not in this work, the stair is not in any work, and the keeper is not bringing it into one in the fifteenth week.** Renn Vale changes *received* to **received by this boundary and not held by it**, because received is how a gift is written and she has watched this room learn the difference between a gift and a lock. **Wen Pask does the last carrying, on terms, asked for by name, in the middle of four with a pail, and puts it on the stone when he is told and does not put it down anywhere else.** **The work is done and entered as *finished* — the water, and not the seat, and not the stair, and not the waist — and the crew's column goes up by two hours on a named work asked for by name, the first such line since the eleventh week — **and the work is not the water and the crew are not on it: it is reading the water's terms and its price at the top of nine steps and entering them in this book.** Then, on the Friday, in the cold, Dalla Sen writes the release and the keeper and Wen Pask and the clerk all read it out: **This Hearthhold declines the middle gate's timber** — it will not come for it, does not ask that gate to hold it, does not ask that gate to send it, and asks that gate to **stop holding it and put the water-lock in front of the people who live behind it**, and **no date is attached because a date would be a promise**, and it goes out with a courier, four days up the middle passage to the middle gate and forty days on to the guild file, and not with a man of this boundary, because a message a man of this boundary carries is a message this boundary can be asked about twice. Then two things said at the sixth bell. **Sefu Aran says the crew's obligation is not discharged and says *not yet* in his own hand, with a condition instead of a date — the first day of the month the pot stops falling — because if he says it in the fifteenth week the crew are not needed in the fifteenth week and this Hearthhold is being kept by people it has not asked.** And **Ilsa Norr says the thing nobody has asked the right question about: there is not one name on the plan.** Nine rows, counts and conditions and six empty work columns and a *none* and a one at the bottom of four unwalked treads, and *not one name anywhere on the page*, and he wrote down how many people, which is harder to write down than a name, and the weather, which you only bother about if you intend to be there for all of it — **and in a fortnight this Hearthhold has written down forty-one writes of the word water in a cook's hand and forty pails in a young man's and a woman's *no* at a door and a woman's *no* at a landing and the word *maintainer*, which a clerk put in her own book on the Saturday of the last week and did not know she was putting it in** — and she cannot say which of those two books is safer, and she is not going to pretend a woman who has run a school under a collapse for eleven weeks can look at nine hundred years of somebody's care and say *we have it right.* Nera Oduya: **nobody can, and that is the answer and the whole of it, and it cannot be settled in a fortnight in a cold month by eleven people and a pot of thirteen days** — and she asks for it to be written at the fifth bell so that in a year she can read it out and be believed. The anteroom goes back to being an anteroom. **A person is still under that lip**; the post under it has never been built; the packing is a knee and the knee will be Jo Verrick's. The wrapped bundle on the shelf is unopened and unidentified and unconnected to anything. The brass rule has said nothing for seven weeks. **The plan came off the dowel on the first day of the thirteenth week in front of five women and went back onto the shelf in the same hour, and its fourth row is the anteroom, and its count is the highest on the page, and its condition is *wet*, and its work column is empty, and that is the whole of what anybody knows.** And the last line of the book, in the clerk's hand, because the keeper named it and a clerk writes what a keeper names: *Reviewed on the first day of the month the pot stops falling. Named by this boundary: Dalla Sen, clerk. In the room. With the reason.* — which is a threshold, and it is not the last one.

## Chapter 81 — The Road

**The release goes out, and the road is carried as a road.** At the second bell on the first day of the sixteenth week, four people stand at the top of the nine steps and watch **Hesk Ammery**, fifty-eight, a courier of nineteen years, carry one sheet folded in three and nothing else up the middle passage. He refuses the terms of the room first: *I am not paid to carry a no* — and writes on the back of his own hand what the keeper told him to say if anybody asks what the notice costs, because a man who has carried paper for nineteen years has never once lost a page. Sefu Aran gives the terms: do not explain, do not argue, and if anybody asks what a Hearthhold is, say that too. **Marek Venn does not go, and cannot, and works out that the first act of foreign policy this Hearthhold performed was carried out by a person whose name will be in no book here, and that the only part of it that was his was agreeing with a sentence somebody else wrote.** Then Renn Vale asks the question nobody asked: *we did not ask*, and Dalla Sen enters it in her own hand with the time on it, and the keeper does not take it back, and the room is told that asking now would not bring the page back and would not have stopped it. The far end gets into the room through Wen Pask: **Corin Bexley**, the middle gate's water-lock keeper, named for the first time in this boundary's book, and **Nell Ferrin**, the woman behind the counter who said the same eight words three times and slower the third. The chapter's last fact is a road nobody in the building can date: a page that has gone out, and four hundred paces of seasoned hardwood still standing in a store four days up it, and behind that wood a dry lock and four households carrying water up four sets of steps.

## Chapter 82 — The Third Column

**The public maintenance plan is begun in a kitchen and stops at its third column.** Mikka Hale clears the only table in a kitchen of nine people and one litter and asks, in her own words, the question nobody has asked: not *how* the boundary keeps itself, but *what it is that it does.* Renn Vale says no before the argument starts — a page with a rota on it is a rota, and she has watched the boundary's own keeping become her boots — but she supplies the shape: a notice that says what a boundary will not do is half a thing, and somebody four days up a road is going to ask for the other half. Nera Oduya comes down two steps and gives the plan the dowel's three columns: **how many people (a number, no name anywhere), when (a condition in longhand, never a number, never a day of a week), and what is done.** And then she stops, because the third column is the one nobody can fill. **The boundary has kept a record of its people for fifteen weeks and not one line of its work**, which Dalla Sen states out loud and Tams Quill asks to be written down. Jo Verrick gives the pump line and prices her own estimate of *one* onto the same line. Mikka Hale refuses to fill the third column at all and gives the reason: *a column you fill in before you know is a promise you have not made yet.* Ilsa Norr's count for the wash rooms is struck and replaced with a dash. Leena Orr stops the room with the sentence that governs the sheet: **a list is not a location.** The plan exists on butcher's paper in a teacher's hand, with two columns filled and one empty, no charter agreed and nobody asked to hold it. Marek Venn is the man who would have written it and cannot hold a pencil flat, and it is the first time in his life that being the right man for the work has turned out to be the wrong thing to be.

## Chapter 83 — Eleven Minutes Early

**The pot falls to twelve, and the condition holds, and nobody will ever know whether the sound changed.** Wen Pask is asked, out loud, with the terms read back and repeated, to be the second pair of hands on the pump frame — the frame is not a watch, he is not on a rota, he is not paid, and the hour goes in the column with no heading. On the Wednesday the clinic needs Mikka Hale and the frame loses two people, and **she says out loud that she has been putting this off since the second day** and goes. Jo Verrick takes the frame alone and does not start the pump: *a frame with one person on it and a lever in it is not a pump that is run attended, it is a pump that a man has said yes to.* The water comes up over the corridor's low end for as long as the pump stands off, eleven minutes early, over a floor two foot eight wide on the edge of an eleven-foot shaft, with nine children and a schoolteacher at the anteroom end of it and a bell rung once. **Nobody is sent down that corridor** — the woman from the wash rooms' third condition, enforced by Renn Vale in front of a full room at a cost to the road — and **nobody in the building will ever know whether the sound changed while she was lifting a cover.** The corridor is shut for the rest of the week for a reason that is not the ground. The water arrives two hours late, eight pails go over the waist by hand, Iven Tallo prices it and calls it an ordinary day, and the school runs on Renn Vale's condition and not on a rota. **Mikka Hale's number goes from thirteen to twelve, in a hand that has the words *on my own* against it.** And Marek Venn, alone on a bench, works out that the failure was never in the design: the number of hands a room needs is a load, and he priced the load in timber and air and drainage and never once in people who are not there.

## Chapter 84 — Not In Agreement

**The two ways of saying *not on any day* are put side by side, and the ninth row is argued about and nothing is done about it.** With the corridor shut and the road unavailable, Dalla Sen reads Renn Vale's eighth term against the word *none* from the ninth row of the dowel. Renn refuses the reading: *a promise can be broken by a person and a condition cannot, and I will not have this room frightened of a piece of paper the way a room gets frightened of a person* — and then says the first thing in five weeks she does not know: whether the page is right or her slate is. Nera Oduya reframes the row: **the ninth line's one is the only number on that page that is not an occupancy, and it may be a staffing, and a staffing in an occupancy column is either a mistake nine hundred years old or something nobody in this building has thought of doing yet** — and refuses to say which. Ilsa Norr makes the honest argument: copy the row, because a schedule that admits a room it has not worked out is the most honest object a boundary can make. **Nera refuses, and the reason is the volume's argument in a sentence: a blank row in an old document is a mystery and a blank row in a new document is an omission, and a stranger reads an omission as the worst thing they can think of, which about that room is that we have posted somebody there and are not paying them.** Renn decides on nothing, in her own hand, and names herself as the person who decided; refuses any mark cut in the stone, because a mark is a claim; and asks for it all to be read out. Leena Orr notices that Marek has said nothing for forty minutes and asks to have it checked in a week. Nera then refuses to ask the crew for anything and says she will ask a man with a board, in a room, on a day when he can say no. The school runs **one day out of seven** in the sixteenth week, and Sefu Aran opens the road again on the least respectable reason available: a cook's number and a school that lost a week of itself in three days.

## Chapter 85 — No Column for a Person

**Iven Tallo refuses the guild's fourth paragraph and Wen Pask refuses the boy's trade, and the boundary learns that its scarcest thing is a column.** In the school store, with Ilsa Norr standing in the doorway because *a store with a man sleeping in it is not a store*, Iven Tallo has the boy read the notice out and reads the fourth paragraph again. **The argument holds** — and he refuses to be forgiven for it — and then he says the reason nobody expected: there is one route in this Hearthhold, and the paragraph wants a named holder entered against a named route, and the only route that could be entered is the one the boundary has spent five weeks getting out of every file. He does not fill it in, and the reason is not the argument: *I do not know whether I would still say no in the spring, and a man who cannot be sure of his own no in the spring has no business putting his name on a form about a boy.* **Wen Pask refuses the year's trade himself**, because the paragraph is a door with a year's price on it and neither of them can pay it, and because Iven's name in a guild register would be the reason his trade exists. Then Tams Quill finds the batch's own fact off the back of the refusal: Nera Oduya's inventory has **twelve lines that all say *no* and a thirteenth under them that has been sitting unwritten for six weeks, and the column it wants is the column for an owner, and a person is not an owner** — a man cannot be *owned by*. Bel Ordry says the page needs a column that says *whose work is this* and not *whose wood is this*, and Tams says there is one, on his board, with nothing over the top of it, and he is not going to head it, **because a wage is the one line in this book that must never be a thing a room can be praised in.** Marek Venn works out that nothing here is a shortage of wood: it is a shortage of a place to write a person down.

## Chapter 86 — What the Middle Gate Asks

**The release comes back, in two hands, and the boundary cannot say how old its own notice is.** A courier comes down the middle passage with two things from two people. **Talla Roke's question**, on the back of a store's issue slip, in her own hand and under her own name: the Middle cannot put the water-lock in front of the people behind it, the hold is off, the timber is theirs, the Middle has no carpenter with a bond, and **what is this boundary's answer in a form a person at a counter can be given** — and if the answer is that nothing comes, somebody has to say it out loud in a room in front of four households, because a page read twice at a counter is not a lock kept dry. She adds the only part of it that is hers: *write the answer so that the bottom of those steps is in it, and not only the top.* **Corin Bexley's five words**, on a scrap of painted board sawn off something bigger, with no name on it: *Who will tell the four houses?* Tams Quill's finding is the batch's: **nobody in this building knows how old the notice is**, because the courier was not told and the keeper's best sentence — *no date is attached, because a date would be a promise* — cost a day and a night of somebody's winter. Renn Vale refuses the crew's hours for a work in another Hearthhold, and a keeper comes off the wheel and says the answer to the second question is *him*, and that a page is the cheap half of saying a thing. Nera Oduya refuses to answer the first with a list, because **an obligation written on paper is an obligation an office can call in**, and gives six sentences instead. Pell Roke says three words and is not asked for any more. Marek Venn understands that he would have got it wrong if he had written the notice himself, because he would have written an answer into it — and that he could not have gone, and the reason he could not go is a hand that will not close and a corridor two foot eight wide over eleven feet of shaft. Mikka Hale starts the schedule again in her kitchen on a butcher's sheet that is now in four parts.

## Chapter 87 — Forty-Eight and a Half

**The arithmetic is collected, the ninth null is written, and the keeper's condition is proved harder by the keeper's own notice.** Sefu Aran asks the crew for the two hours himself, in the anteroom, at the first bell, on a day when they can be refused, and Renn Vale enters the price before anybody says yes: the work is at the rail and not on the stair, the eighth term is not touched, and **the stair has now been outside every work since the fifteenth week and is inside one, and the price is that the eighth term and the work are both in the book and are not in agreement.** Marek Venn and Tams Quill go down in the pump's window and come back with **four sentences, three of which are that they do not know**, and with a **ninth null** on the throat's far wall at bar height, which Tams Quill moves into the column with no heading — six in the ordinary column and three in his, nine in all, and nothing usable. Bel Ordry's seventh morning at the bar is *nothing* and he enters that it is a seventh morning. Tams reads the crew's column at **forty-eight and a half** and **refuses to quote the boundary's total** because he has not walked the board; he then separates the two refusals — *mine is a refusal of arithmetic, his is a refusal of a number* — and does the arithmetic of the keeper's condition and tells the keeper on the spot that **the pot cannot stop falling while the only road water comes up in is a gate that has been told in writing to stop waiting on us.** Sefu Aran does not move the condition and says why, and then says the other half: the notice made it honest, not harder, and he gave away the only yes this boundary ever had and it has not cost a day of a cook's count. The column with no heading takes a **page** — the first thing in it that is not a person — and Tams says the honest name for it is *out of our sight* and refuses to write even that, and says what the refused line is, once.

## Chapter 88 — What He Was Asked

**Nera Oduya asks a man to hold the air valve, and is refused a yes and given a spring.** She tells the room in the anteroom that she is going to ask Bel Ordry herself, at the valve, and that the asking is hers, and that no clerk writes the name anywhere until it is done — and Marek Venn walks as far as the turn and stops, because a man who is asked to witness an asking is a different thing from a man standing in it. **Bel Ordry says no, and gives three reasons that are not noble:** the bell cannot be left and a valve cannot be given to the man on the bell; he has been *good* at holding nothing for fifteen weeks and the day he holds something every sentence he has put into the air becomes something somebody has to check him about; and the air engineer did not tell him what the valve was before she asked him, which is the one thing she does not do to anybody. Then **he asks her what it is**, and she tells him all of it, including the six minutes, the shaft that stopped being a chimney in the cold, the sink, the school corner's shut mouth and the air that is not accounted for, and she claims her three costs for refusing to publish a rate and admits that she chose him **on purpose** and that the reason is that she could not think of a better month. Bel's answer is not yes and not no: **asked, and not answered**, with his name against it, because a name against *asked and not answered* is a fact and not a holder, and he will answer in the spring, when the boundary knows whether it is keeping itself or being kept, because a man who answers in the cold has answered a different question. Dalla Sen asks whether she has papered over the hole she entered as a refusal to be asked, and Renn Vale answers for the room: **a hole with a rim** — and asks that the blank line with the woman's two sentences be read out immediately after the valve line, every fifth bell, so that the two are heard in one breath.

## Chapter 89 — The Middle Gate Answers

**A competent office answers a notice nobody asked it for, and the answer costs this boundary half its water.** **Nell Ferrin** comes down the middle passage herself, sits on the bottom step, and brings three things: the office's answer, a copy of the release sent back, and a store's issue slip with a column headed *pails up* and a second column with no heading at all, which Tams Quill recognises as the same disease as his own board. The office accepts the notice and is not sorry. **The hold is off, the timber is the Middle's, and the Middle cannot use it.** And the second answer: **the office has halved what it puts up the middle passage**, because a boundary expecting a plank is not a delivery and the expectation is gone — and the slip the office has been counting for a season is the middle's own side of the road. Tams Quill names the shape before Jo Verrick can say the number: the slip counts what comes up the passage, the work counts what reaches the kitchen, for five weeks they were the same number, and **the difference is what the middle has stopped sending, and this boundary has no well and no tested seam and no second pair of hands in a place to get any.** Six pails a day is one crossing of four and one of two, and **Sefu Aran strikes his own page in his own hand and makes the clerk read it out and read the seventh term with it.** Mikka Hale says the number will not move today and will move on a day she will not be asked to name. Nell Ferrin, the only person in the room who is going back up the road, finishes the sentence Mikka did not say and puts the batch's question on the table: *you have got a page that says you will not come, and a page that says you have one work, and a page that says there is nothing else, and not one of them is a page a person at the bottom of four sets of steps can be helped by.* Then she proposes the **fourth column** — *put in it what this boundary will do* — and Nera Oduya refuses it as a list of obligations, and Renn Vale refuses the opposite column as a list of refusals a judge can be handed, and the fourth column is written and left empty and unheaded.

## Chapter 90 — The Fourth Column

**The plan is handed to a man, in his own hand, half-done, and the volume's question is sharpened rather than answered.** Nine people say no, one says nothing, and **Bel Ordry says yes on conditions**: a count and no name in the first column, because a name is a holder and the guild's fourth paragraph wants one; a condition and never a day in the second, because a rota is a register with the words *person* left out; a third column he will not fill where the work is not yet known; and a fourth column that stays empty and that he will not head, **for a different reason than the count's** — a column of refusals with a name on it is a list of things the boundary owes somebody. Sefu Aran rules, in his own hand and on the same page as the water-carrying: **a keeper of a page is not a holder of a route** — and then says the bad reason out loud, that he is writing a sentence in a book in order to keep a person out of a file, which is the first thing he has ever put in it for that purpose. The third column has three lines in it: the pump, in Jo Verrick's words with her estimate of one on the same line; the seventh term; and the woman from the wash rooms' two sentences, entered in the clerk's hand with no name against it after Bel Ordry checks all three of her conditions out loud and Dalla Sen reads them back. The wash rooms get a row with an empty third column and Renn Vale's reason. The ninth room gets **no row at all**, refused by both women, because a blank row in a new document is an omission and an omission reads as an accusation. Tams Quill reads the board: **forty-eight and a half** for the crew and **a hundred and three and a quarter** for the boundary, eight added since the fourteenth week, and the list adds exactly. Ilsa Norr asks her question a second time — three books now, and nobody can say which is safer — and Bel Ordry answers: the one with the most empty in it, because a page you can pick up is a page somebody can carry out of the room it is about. The plan has **no name and a date**, and the anteroom's row is empty because the anteroom's work is a knee. **A person is still under that lip.**

## Chapter 91 — The Same Pail

**The water is found by a boy who counts pails, and the room is more frightened of it than of the thirst.** The pot falls from twelve days to **eleven** on the Sunday between the seventeenth and eighteenth weeks and Mikka Hale reads it out first thing on the Monday. **Wen Pask**, twenty-two, twenty-six days in the boundary and not paid, has been counting pails for nine days and has found that the four pails that come down the middle passage are not the four that go up: the pail that stands on the ledge at the bottom of the nine steps is the office's except that it belongs to this boundary and is never washed, and it has a crust under the water line, and **the crust is lime, and you cannot get lime out of a pail unless it came through stone**, and the middle gate is a road and a counter and four days of passage and has no stone in it. The objections are staged in the room's own order — Jo Verrick that the pumped water was never for drinking, Nera Oduya that nothing is drunk until it is found, tested and recorded in that order with somebody able to object to a line, and Mikka Hale that he told her on the ninth day and not the fourth and that she is not angry about it. **The clerk asks the question nobody had got to — *what is it that is a room*** — and Jo Verrick answers with the haunch where the outer service door's frame bears on the dressed stone, which is the one place in the Hearthhold a person has to put a hand every day to know the door is bearing, and which has been warm since the cold came, and which she called warm and never wrote down. Marek Venn puts his left palm in it and gets **nothing**, the tenth null, and **Tams Quill puts it in the ordinary column and does not move it**, because the other three went into the unheaded column because Marek went and found them on a cold wall on his own and this one was asked for by a person in a room: **seven in the ordinary column and three in the count's, which is ten in all.** The chapter ends on Mikka Hale refusing to let the wall's warmth be a reason for the pot to move, and on Renn Vale saying that the outer service door is in the anteroom's rating and not in her terms, that she cannot hold both, and that somebody has to ask her to stop it being used.

## Chapter 92 — The Door Off Its Hinges

**The cost of the water is a door, a room's rating, and a woman on a litter going down nine steps.** Bel Ordry asks Renn Vale to stop the outer service door being used, in a room, in front of the clerk, and **she says no** and gives four minutes of reasons: her terms are the lead line and the shore and the road, the outer service door is in the anteroom's rating and not in her terms, and she will not hold two sets of terms on one room quietly, *and she would rather be the woman who is inconvenient than the woman who is careful.* The door comes off its four rusted pins at the third bell in the pump's window, and behind the frame is a lime-mortar joint with four threads of water and a stain the shape of a leaf, and **nobody in the room had ever looked at it and every one of them had walked past it**, and Jo Verrick says out loud that she has had her hand on that haunch every day for fifteen weeks and called it warm. Nera Oduya comes down four steps and reframes it: **a wall that has been taking water for months is not a wall, it is a route; air and water go the same way and one of them is quieter about it** — so the unaccounted air in this Hearthhold has been arriving in the wall of the room with the highest count on the page, and she says she had the direction of that air wrong since the collapse and refuses to say the word *sink* in a room where a man has been standing at a bar for a week. The anteroom is emptied in the pump's window with Renn Vale counting the corridor from the school door, and the air engineer says the pump has been running for five weeks **on the evidence** and that nobody wrote the water down because there is no column for a wet wall. The rating is suspended in Renn Vale's own hand, the school is told it will run in a worse room, Leena Orr's litter goes down the nine steps, and **nobody drinks anything.**

## Chapter 93 — Three Readings

**The water is tested, recorded in five hands with one word struck out, and put in the pot — and the pot does not go up.** Three readings, three vessels, three hours: the pot at the fourth bell on the second day, a pail at the first bell on the third with the pump **off**, and a jar at the fifth bell with the pump on its window. The record is read out and challenged on two specific lines. **Mikka Hale strikes the clerk's word *clear*** — *clean is a word you have got to be able to prove every day of your life and I have proved nothing* — and writes *no colour, no smell, not drunk* on all three lines in her own hand, and the clerk repeats the correction and then repeats the strike, because a clerk who repeats a correction without repeating the strike has corrected nothing. **Nera Oduya objects that the page is not wrong but incomplete** — two of the three readings were taken inside a pump's window and one was not, and an incomplete page about water is a page that lies by being silent — and she adds the hour, the pump's state and the vessel to all three, and is told that this is the first instrument in eighteen weeks anybody could carry out of the room, and answers that she is writing three lines of a page that already exists in the hand of a person who will keep it. Bel Ordry reads the order out loud — found, located, tested, recorded, in use, **and not before** — and Jo Verrick adds the two jars a day. The water goes in at the sixth bell. **The school corner's mouth is opened a hand's width at the fourth bell for one bell with the pump stopped**, and the air out of it is **warm and going into the throat and not out of it**, which is the opposite of what seventeen weeks of assumption said, and the cold current off the four unwalked treads is **not the same current**, and no rate is published. The mouth is shut. The outer service door goes back on packed with rubble, **holding and not fixed.** The pot goes to **ten** and the cook refuses to add the jars to the pot: *if I add them then I have one number and it is a sum of two things, and the day one of the two stops I will not be able to say which.*

## Chapter 94 — Where The Work Is Known

**The third column is filled where the work is known, in the hands of the people who will keep it, and the fourth column is given a reason on the page instead of a heading.** Bel Ordry lays the plan out in four parts, weighted at the corners, and reads it out with the rule that everyone who wrote a line stands and says yes. Four new lines: **Jo Verrick's seam** (found by a man counting pails nine days late, four threads in dressed stone and lime mortar, three vessels, one reading taken with the pump off, recorded in five hands, one word struck out in a sixth, in use from the sixth bell and not before, two jars a day, and the word *clean* struck in a cook's hand and I wrote it first); **Renn Vale's outer service door** (four pins off and on, packed with stone and clay, holding and not fixed, the rating restored only when the word *door* is said in a room, six people down nine steps with a litter); **Ilsa Norr's school** (run at the school end of the corridor with the door shut at their backs — *it ran, it was a worse room than the anteroom, and I am not going to have it written as though we were moved*, and Nera's word *moved* is struck in the clerk's hand); and **Nera Oduya's school corner's mouth** (a hand's width, one bell, shut, and three *I will not*s written on a page). The two rows that stay empty stay empty and the room does not argue, which is now the finding, and **the anteroom's row is no longer empty** and does not contain the word *person*, which Bel Ordry read the whole row out to check. Then the fourth column: three reasons in three hands, Bel Ordry asks for the chalk and **the clerk refuses him in front of the room**, he gives the reason to Renn Vale and not to the clerk, and she writes it — *the fourth column is empty, nothing has been put in it, it has no heading, this is true as at the day in the top corner, the keeper is permitted to put something in it and the person who does it has to be in the room.* **Nera Oduya objects to the word *none* — a promise not to fill a column is a promise an office can call in — and it is struck and replaced in her own hand, and it is the first line on the page anybody here has corrected and left corrected.** **The clerk is wrong out loud about the crew's figure and stands in the correction herself** — she had told the room on Tuesday that the water would not move it, it moved on Tuesday, it moved again on the Thursday morning, and she was right about the water and wrong about the week, and the count did not tell her so because the count had named no day. Marek Venn then says *on Friday* out loud, takes it back before the count answers, and says he has been putting his hands on work to see whether it would hold and then on a calendar, and Tams Quill says he was going to let him have it because he has wanted to hear a date said out loud by somebody else since the twelfth week.

## Chapter 95 — The Man With The Counter

**The guilds are competent, sincere, bounded, and not defeated, and they bring a document.** **Harlan Merrow**, a Cartwright bond assessor, thirty-eight, twenty-one years in the office, **the man who signs the fourth paragraph**, introduces himself in the anteroom before anybody asks and asks for all of it to be entered, including the part about the road having no date on it either. His store's order is for timber this boundary released in writing and the release stands, and he brought it anyway *because a man who brings only the paper he agrees with is not a counterparty, he is a supplicant.* He reads the guild's counter-draft: six heads, a maintained water, air, corridor and stair's near side at a price, continuous timber against the work, attendance recorded and shown at the first of the month with the work lost if it is not, the fourth paragraph verbatim, withdrawal on one term's notice, and no withdrawal that is not given in a room with a person in it. **He states in the room that he wrote one, two, three, five and six and did not write four.** The objections are written out loud before anybody picks up the chalk: Bel Ordry that a named holder is a person the office can be sent to; Nera Oduya that there is nothing in the network a holder can hold and if a clause must be entered it should be the timber, which is the only honest sentence in the draft; Renn Vale that a boundary that cannot produce its record at the first of the month loses the stair, and a room with no name on it is a room with nobody to answer for it. **The guild's answer is good and Harlan says so**: a holder is a name the office has promised not to use, and a document that cannot be sued is a document that cannot be blamed, and a thing nobody can be blamed for is a thing nobody has to fix. Marek Venn says out loud, for the book, that it is the best case against him and that he has not got an answer, and that the jar of water and the six empty lines are not an answer to a man under a lip. **Harlan Merrow then says the office will put the same draft to four other Hearthholds, three will accept, three will have timber, three will be able to shut a route when a clerk says so and will think they are being careful, and this boundary will be cited, and he will recommend the charter and not expect it to be granted.** Iven Tallo will not sign and gives a reason that is not the argument, Wen Pask refuses, and the two disagree in public about the order in which they said it in the sixteenth week and **the clerk writes nothing**, because a man does not have to be believed twice.

## Chapter 96 — In Her Own Hand

**Talla Roke starts a courier route outside the guild system, the boundary's contribution to it is a sentence, and the apprentice is paid a wage in a column with no heading on it.** A single sheet arrives in her own hand with three other names under hers. **Bel Ordry refuses to hold it** — the moment he takes it, it is a page about this boundary, and it is about a woman at a counter and four households and three people who are not in this building — and has the clerk read it out standing, and it goes back down the passage. It says: paper and small goods, four days' road to four households and the Hearthholds past, no guild counter, no bond, no register, not a house, not asking this boundary for anything, written so that a paper with their mark on it is theirs and a paper without it came from a counter, **and that the boy is not on it and is not coming**, and that she will carry two sentences and will not put a third on for anybody. The boundary's contribution is **two sentences with no name and no signature on them** — the way up the middle passage is not shut against the people who live behind it, has not been shut since the second week, and will not be shut for a delivery, and nobody will be asked for anything to come up it; and at the bottom of those four sets of steps there is nothing and we have not sent anybody and we have not got anything and we are not going to say otherwise at a counter — and Mikka Hale stops them on the word *nothing* and makes the clerk say what a cook means by it. **Wen Pask asks out loud whether it carries people**, and the sheet answers no, not this month, not as a favour, not to a boy, because a boy without a bond on a road with a woman he has not met is a thing a woman has to carry, and she carries paper, and the four households cannot get paper up four sets of steps if the paper stops halfway. Iven Tallo says the hard thing: **you will be paid and you will not be a carpenter, and both are true, and being kept is not being trained.** The wage — food, bed, and hours entered as work and not a favour at the cook's own rate — **goes into the column with no heading, the first wage ever in it, and Tams Quill still refuses to head it** for a new reason: a column with a name on the top of it that holds wages is a column somebody can point at, and a wage that can be pointed at is a wage that can be stopped, and the man who stops it will not be the man who is owed. Renn Vale and Sefu Aran both enter that the crew's hours did not move for the water: *a good week is not a work.*

## Chapter 97 — The Charter

**The charter is signed, it is not the guild's, it is not a page, and it does not put a holder against the route in a register kept by the office — and the reason why not is written in the document.** It is on the back of a butcher's sheet in the cook's hand, has an office's number at the top of it, and **has no name on it**, and the cook says why before anybody reads a line: *a charter with a name at the top of it is a charter with a holder.* Dalla Sen reads the whole of it out and the room does the thing the release was done with: **it objects, out loud, line by line, before anybody picks up the chalk again.** Bel Ordry's clause four becomes *when the office asks, in a room, to a person*, with the keeper's promise to show the empty fourth column written in. Sefu Aran rewrites clause two against himself so that it binds the office and not only the boundary. **Nera Oduya strikes the woman's covers out of the reason clause** — *the covers are not the boundary's and the woman has never been asked whether her covers may be used as an argument* — leaving three things: a stair, a lip, a valve. **Mikka Hale takes the second gate's water-lock out of the charter** because it is not a thing to put in a document a kitchen hands out, and the sheet and the page now disagree by one number and she would rather they disagreed. Clause nine says the ninth room, the four treads, the wash rooms, the school corner's mouth and the blank line are **not in it, and that is deliberate**, and the keeper says out loud that a document about a room travels. **Iven Tallo will not sign**, in four words, and is not argued with; he gives the real reason half an hour later on the bench — there is no word in it he has to swear to and he has had a bond suspended for eight months and does not know what he swore — and it goes in a book of Marek Venn's own and nowhere else. **Marek Venn refuses in nine seconds** because a signature by a man who is leaving is a name against a route. **Harlan Merrow says the office can neither grant nor refuse it**, that a boundary instrument needs nothing from them, that what the office does with it is receive it, file it and cite it, and that clause four is the whole of what the boundary has given away. Seven signatures, the keeper first and six under him, and the air engineer is not asked because the air engineer does not sign anything in this Hearthhold. At the sixth bell the plan comes out of the coat in four parts and Renn Vale reads the seventh term off her slate.

## Chapter 98 — What She Is Asked

**Nera Oduya is handed a work instead of a decision, the room does without her visibly for four hours, and the hand-over is onto a page rather than into a coat.** On the day a stranger is to be shown the plan she is at the clinic return with a lamp and a board, and the anteroom runs its pump, its rating, its school and its shaft for four hours without her, and she arranged it, and she enters the arrangement: *so that when I go in the spring there is something here that is not waiting for me.* **And she states the price of the arrangement, which is that the room now knows it does not need to ask, and the day it stops asking is the day there is a real question about the air and she is four hundred miles from it.** Bel Ordry reads the six things at the fifth bell and then asks her for a piece of work rather than a decision: to write, for nobody, what she thinks is most likely to go wrong in the anteroom before she goes, so that it goes in the third column. **She is asked at the fifth bell, four bells after she went out, and is in the room when she is asked; she is never in two places in one bell.** She writes it in nine minutes: the anteroom holds ten on a door that is packed with rubble and not repaired, and the rating depends on a word, and **a rating that depends on a word is a rating that a tired person at the fourth bell in a bad month will say the word to**, and the two ways out are that the door is made good or the word stops working. The keeper rules a third way — the ugliest one, and the only one that has cost nobody anything: **the word is said in a room, by the person who is going to be in the room, and the clerk repeats it, and nobody says it to a door. It gets said to a page.** The air board is not given to a man: it goes onto the page, because a board in a hand is an office and there is exactly one road up this passage. **The thirteenth line stays unwritten and the reason goes on the page in her own hand**: the column it wants is the column for an owner, and a person is not an owner, and anybody who wants to know what the air is can come to the valve at the second bell and hold the release themselves, and there is a man on the threshold who will not stop them. The keeper enters the price of holding a page — that every refusal anybody hands him becomes a line in a thing he carries — and the clerk notes that it is four days since the fright and the fear looks nothing like the virtue now. Marek Venn closes the chapter: the work went to the one person who is leaving, it went into the column that says *what is done*, **and he does not know which of the three of them was right.**

## Chapter 99 — One Room

**Marek Venn reaches the Reader stage, out of a page and a charter, and it costs him his left hand for a night and half his judgement for an hour.** On the fourth day of the nineteenth week, with the plan out of Bel Ordry's coat in four parts because a stranger is coming to look at it, he puts his left hand on the middle part, on the fourth row, without deciding to. **Instead of nothing, a place.** Not a force and not a direction: the anteroom, and it is the most definite thing he has ever got off any surface, and he is frightened of it. **Then it costs him**: the left hand clamps and shakes, the headache comes behind the left eye with a floor to it, and the anteroom's count arrives as a sound — ten people breathing, under the check on the pump, the two noises one noise — and the table moves or the room does and he sits down. **He says it in a room as a fact before he has decided anything, and that is the failure mode and the room takes ninety seconds to notice.** Nera Oduya asks how he knows; he says because the fourth row is empty; she says that is a hole in a document and not a reason, and makes him say what his hand did. He cannot say it twice, and does not know whether he would have got it standing in the room. **Tams Quill enters it as a claim, not a reading** — a null has a room and a temperature and a wall and nothing at the end, and this has a plan and a hand and a man bleeding out of one eye — with the condition that it may not be built on until somebody can do it again, and it is **the eleventh**, in the ordinary column, in Marek's own hand, and the count does not move it. He tries again at the third bell and gets nothing, and the counting noise follows him up the nine steps and is still there at the seventh bell in a room he is not in, and the clerk enters that she does not know whether that is a fault and will not guess in a book. At the sixth bell **the clerk takes the brass survey rule out of the coat's pocket because his right hand cannot open the pocket**, and it lies on the table saying nothing, and it has said nothing for ten weeks, and nobody looks at it. Then the anteroom runs its own full drill at its declared number, and **Jo Verrick finds a finger and a bit out of the head of the frame**, because clay shrinks as it dries and the frame is now bearing on a packing of stone and clay put in by a woman with a knee; there is no timber to hold it with and none is coming. The air engineer's rule on the page is the right rule and the wrong room's rule, and the clerk enters both side by side. They shore it with stone and lime and a wedge; it holds and it is not a repair. **Marek Venn is not asked to be in it and is not in it, and says the whole of it out loud: it did not save anybody, it was worth an afternoon, his left hand closed properly this morning and does not close tonight, he can hear ten people breathing in a room he is not standing in — and it was one room, and there are eight others on that page and he does not know one of them, and anybody who comes and asks him to read a boundary is going to be told no.**

## Chapter 100 — Not On A Figure

**The Cartwrights begin competing for the new network, the four houses are answered out loud, the crew's obligation is discharged on a sentence and not on a number, the next volume's question is asked and refused an answer, and a person is still under that lip.** A **halfpenny sheet** comes up the passage: the Cartwrights' maintenance undertaking, offered at the middle gate's store to any Hearthhold whose keeper applies, timber in the month after next, the fourth line in the same words as the fourth head — and Nell Ferrin's true sentence is on the back of it, that the office printed a hundred and counted them, and that the office is doing this because the first one of them said no, and that she has watched a thing like this twice and both times it worked. Tams Quill walks the board twice and **names no day**: the crew are at **fifty-two and a half** (forty-eight and a half at the end of the seventeenth week, plus four: two on the second day **at the door and the haunch behind it**, two on the fourth and fifth days on the fourth column and the counter-draft, **every one of the four a work and not one of them a jar of water** — the water's record and its three readings are in the boundary's column with the cook's name and the clerk's on them, *a good week is not a work*), and the boundary is at **a hundred and seventeen and a quarter** (a hundred and three and a quarter, plus fourteen, and the list of ten names adds exactly), and both columns reconcile. **The keeper refuses to use his own condition.** The pot stopped falling on the third day of the eighteenth week and has been ten days for twelve days, and he says the condition has been met in the strictest reading and that **a condition you can satisfy is not a condition, it is a date with a number on it**, and that his was satisfied by luck, and it stays where it is and nobody is released on it. When the clerk asks who does release them, **he names himself, out loud, in the room, with the reason**: the boundary can do it, and the proof is the last three days, none of which was done by a person who came up a shaft; and the reason is not a number, it is that a boundary that cannot be left alone is still a rescue. **Tams Quill's refusal of arithmetic stands and is not withdrawn** — his is a refusal of arithmetic, the keeper's is a refusal of a condition, neither has moved, and the obligation ended on a sentence with a reason that had nothing in it that could be measured. **Nobody leaves and nobody is asked to.** The keeper then gives the office's answer to the four houses out loud, in a room, before the first of the month, and it is not good: *nothing comes; the timber is the office's; the office has no carpenter with a bond; the four households have their own water and their own four sets of steps and did not ask this boundary for any of this; and this boundary has two jars a day out of its own wall and is not sending them, and the true sentence is that it looked after itself while four people carried water up four sets of steps, and one of those two things was this boundary's choice.* **And the air engineer asks the volume's question out loud and refuses to answer it**: a halfpenny sheet, a clay packing that shrinks, a word that has to be said in a room and a frame that goes a finger a week is how a door becomes a toll gate — not a gate with a man at it, a gate with a **rule** at it that a man forty days away can be handed — and a page in a coat is **not a system, that is a man**; and she has had a theory since the fourth day of the eleventh week about why the oldest book in this building has kitchens in it and classrooms in it and beds in it and no treasuries, **it is worse than not knowing, and she will not say it in a cold month to a room that writes things down, and she will say it when this boundary is keeping itself.** **Marek Venn's answer has two halves and both are the argument: the open road is not worth a line, because a road is a road, it will be a road in a bad month too, and nobody can point at the thing that built it — and he refuses to let that answer run together with the eighth line of a column, which is worth having, and which is a page in a coat worth having exactly as much as the man in the coat.** He also says the road is open and **that is a fact and not a system.** And the last line is the volume's: the brass rule silent for ten weeks, the wrapped plate unopened on the shelf, the pot at ten days and never once gone up, a charter that is not a page, two sentences going up a road with no name at the top of them, Talla Roke owed a spring by nobody, and **a person was still under that lip.**

## Chapter 101 — Under The School Floor

**The school corner's floor is wet, and the water is the boundary's only drinking water, and the batch refuses the cheap answer.** On the first day of the twentieth week, a Monday, with the corridor shut — which is the only reason the school corner has an empty morning in it in twenty weeks — **Ilsa Norr finds it at the second bell** and says the sentence the next nine days are about: *a schoolroom floor is a floor and I have been standing on the answer since the eleventh week.* **The finding is staged in the room's order and not one step before the one before it**, and Dalla Sen says the order out loud — *found, located, tested, recorded, and not before, somebody say where* — because that is the order this room does things in and she is not going to be the person who reorders it in a hurry. **It is not a puddle**, and that is the first thing three people try to make it into and the first thing she will not let it be. Renn Vale gives away the shape of the floor in one sentence — *a wear surface is a use* — and Dalla Sen asks for an objection to the word before she writes it, because she has learned that word twice this month and was wrong the first time. **Jo Verrick locates a bed joint** under the floor that runs six feet along the party wall to the anteroom's haunch, and says the water does not climb, it spreads, and a spreading thing finds the low side of a floor nine children have worn dished toward a door. **Nera Oduya says no in public, on the reasonable ground that a course of dressed stone is what a course of dressed stone is for, and is wrong**: Jo finds a stone out of that course and a stone back in it in lime about a finger wide, the joint runs out of the bottom of the patch, and **the course is not continuous**, which is a fact about this building nobody in it knew. The correction is entered in Nera's own words beside her own words, unsmoothed, and she asks for it entered that **she said no before she looked**, and the clerk repeats the correction and then the strike. Nera then crawls the wall to the anteroom door in ninety seconds and gives the finding the room actually needs: **it is a line and not a hole**, the seam has not gone anywhere and has not increased — and when she calls that a nuisance, **Mikka Hale strikes the word and puts her own name on the real one**, a wet floor in a schoolroom that nine children will stand on tomorrow. **The room then finds out where the water wants to go, and it is the worst place in the building**: Nera offers to lead it into the covered channel in the dip, and **Jo Verrick refuses her with the canon's six minutes** — the dip takes the pump for six minutes after the lever comes off, and then the water stands in it two foot eight wide on the edge of eleven feet of shaft, and there is a chalk line on the pump frame that a woman in a sling drew and it has not moved — and Nera refuses to take back half of a true thing: *it is not a drain, this room is not a cistern, and I do not know what it is.* **The clerk's line reads *from* and Nera strikes it for *in a joint that runs to the haunch*, because *from* asserts a cause and the page has a place.** **Marek Venn then says the stupid thing out loud — *then cap it* — and the cook will not let him get away with talking about clay**: a cap of clay takes the only drinking water this boundary has found with it when the clay lets go, and the jars are her separate numbers and not the pot, so the pot would not go up, it would stop being topped, and **she would find that out at the fifth bell, on her own board, in her own words, and not from him.** **Renn Vale adds the other half so the room has both** — it is the ordinary fix, right for a wall and wrong for this one, because a joint with water in it is carrying something and this boundary has never found out what, and a change to a room people use is written by the person who will keep it, and *I keep this room's floor and I have not been asked* — **and Marek Venn says out loud in a room that he has nothing left but the one thing he cannot do twice, and will not use it on a floor, and the clerk enters that she did not understand it and is not going to guess in a book what it means.** That is the fourth time this building has written down a person not understanding something and the first time it has been the clerk. **He then reaches for the crew's hours, and Renn Vale stops his hand the way she stopped it on Friday, and tells him what a favour is.** He says *the floor is the problem and not the water*, and the clerk enters the cost: **the school does not run here tomorrow either.** At the haunch he gets nothing for the **twelfth** time, and **Tams Quill enters the twelfth entry as a null in the ordinary column in his own left hand, in the ordinary column because a woman told him where to put his hand**, and the board becomes **twelve entries — eleven nulls and one claim, nine in the ordinary column and three in the column with no heading.** Ilsa Norr asks the question nobody had thought to ask: *then what is the school going to do on Wednesday.* **No closure is added in this chapter, the pot does not move, the seam keeps giving two jars a day, maybe three, and the mouth in the shut wall has been shut for twenty weeks and is not opened.**

## Chapter 102 — Two Rooms

**Three candidate rooms, three refusals in the right hands, and a boundary that ends the day with no room at all.** **Sefu Aran refuses the anteroom standing up, deliberately, because a keeper who refuses a room from the wheel has made the wheel into the room's terms**, and the reason is the room and the word: the anteroom holds ten including one litter for no more than two hours, its second way out is a sentence said in a room, and nine children for a school day is a queue. **Nera Oduya refuses it on air**: the anteroom breathes in and out at the service door, the school corner's mouth has been shut for twenty weeks and is going into the throat, and *a room whose other door is a word has the word as its only ventilation shaft, and on the day I am not here it is nine children and one door.* **The cook refuses it last and most plainly**: *nine children in the anteroom means the anteroom's second way out is nine children, and a second way out that is nine children is a queue.* **Ilsa Norr empties her own school store herself, in the shape she emptied it in the thirteenth week, and refuses it** — *the school is not going into a store* — and Dalla Sen adds the reason she did not give: **the nine register boxes are the boundary's record, and a room you teach in is a room you sit on the record in.** The two parts of the plan come out of the store into Bel Ordry's coat and he says out loud that a coat is a worse place than a locked store. **Renn Vale stops the conversation twenty feet short of the third room**, in the same shape she stopped a party in the eleventh week, and gives no reason beyond that the explanation is nine hundred years of women saying no to a room in this building and every one of them was right; **the refusal goes into the ledger in four lines with no name against it and nothing struck out of it, the floor is not approached, nobody is sent, and the covers stay struck out of every instrument.** **Marek Venn offers the crew's hours to move the school and is stopped a second time, by Renn Vale, with the sentence that the column is a quantity of asking and not a debt and not a rota** — it moves when a person in a room asks the five of them for a work, with the terms said out loud and a person named who can be told no — and nobody has asked, and a favour is a loan with no date on it. **The crew's hours do not move.** The chapter's interior beat is his: twenty weeks ago he had five people who would go up a shaft because he asked, and now there is nothing underneath the discharged debt except that four people in this Hearthhold are better at this than he are. The day ends with a third room nobody has offered — at the kitchen-line end, past the dip and past the waist, and a worse room, and the only one left, and on the other side of a fill that has moved three times and that three people have agreed never to measure.

## Chapter 103 — The Last Walk

**Nine children cross the waist, on a walk, in two parties and a fifth, and they stay on the far side.** The school does not run in the school corner at all this week; on the third day, a Wednesday, with the corridor open, the school goes down the corridor to the room at the kitchen-line end. **The crossing is staged the way a crossing is staged in this building**: four at a time, at a walk, in the pump's strokes and not in the six minutes when the low end stands in water, a bearer at the near lip, two readers, and the plinth reader's word a warning and not a stop. **Renn Vale says out loud that she is not going to put her hand on the fill and says it before she does not**, and gives the reason the book has been giving for twenty weeks: *a person with a hand on a fill has made a decision that the ground is fine, and a person with a hand on a fill keeps their hand there.* Iven Tallo takes the crossing on his own terms and refuses to have the hours put on it. **Isel Ferrow stops a party at the waist for eleven seconds so that a person can say out loud that nobody has touched the third wedge, and nobody puts a hand on the wedge.** **Nera Oduya comes down four steps to give the air rule** — it goes at a walk, a walk is the only speed at which a body is a stable object in a moving current, and the fifth child goes with a bearer who is not his mother, and **Ilsa Norr has the sentence ready and does not get it out in time.** Two parties and a fifth, **nine minutes and forty seconds, entered**, and the clerk enters underneath it that the terms say four minutes and the terms were written for six pails a day and not for nine children, and the room has to decide whether to write new terms or break these ones every Wednesday, and Renn Vale will not write new terms on a Wednesday. **Leena Orr is at the clinic on the far side of the waist, is not asked to do anything and is not asked how she is, and says one thing about who gets carried back in a month.** **Pell Roke reads the plan's first column aloud at the fifth bell from the bench at the top of the nine steps — ten, four, eight, ten, six, nine, five, two, and a dash — and does not go down the steps, into the corridor, or over the waist.** **Ilsa Norr's condition goes on the page in her own words on one line: the school is on the far side of a fill from the clinic and from me, and I am not going to pretend I have agreed with that, and I am going to make it happen anyway, and both of those are true.** **And Renn Vale says one sentence nobody answers: there is a way to shut that room.** The clerk enters that the sentence was said and that nobody answered it, the third time in twenty weeks.

## Chapter 104 — The Cheapest Answer

**The safe closure is proposed by the right person, is correct, is cheap, costs nothing, strands nobody, and passes — and the chapter's question is what it teaches the boundary to do.** On the fourth day, a Thursday, with the corridor shut, **Renn Vale proposes taking the school corner out of use as a room and shutting it, and she has had it on her slate already**, and the clerk enters that a woman who arrives with a thing written down has been thinking about it when nobody was watching her. **The condition is a condition and not a date, because her terms do not take a number**, and it is opened again when the floor has been dry under a lamp through a night and a morning, and **the person who can stop it is the woman who keeps the room and not the man who wrote it**. **Mikka Hale objects to the object rather than the closure: say what shutting it does** — and the answer is **nothing to the water**, because a door does not touch a bed joint, and **it was never for the water; it is for the floor.** Renn Vale asks the room to find an objection to the closure and **not one of them does**, and she says so out loud, and the clerk enters that she asked. **Marek Venn asks the question nobody asked — what did we just stop being able to do — and gets two answers that are not good.** Renn Vale's is about the room: the school now has three days in seven on a fill and three days in seven nowhere at all. **Ilsa Norr's is about the building: they have stopped being able to be wrong in a room with children in it, every argument this boundary has had for three weeks was easier because nine people were going to be in it, and she is not defending the room, she is defending the argument.** Renn Vale writes nothing on her slate and says why: her slate is a room with a floor and a fill and seven terms, and what Ilsa Norr said is about the building. They shut it in eleven minutes and **Jo Verrick puts the wedge in herself and says plainly that one of the three at the school-door head has gone into it, so the school door has two where it had three, and there is nobody on the far side of that door to be pushed against anything, and it is a move and not a use.** The condition goes on the slate and **not on the plan**, because the plan's second column already carries a condition with no number and no day and a room does not need the same instrument twice, and the clerk keeps it on a separate page so that the two pages now disagree on purpose. **Renn Vale then walks the corridor and counts what is shut, as her terms make her do every day, and her slate has fifteen things on it, and she asks the room to hear the sound of it getting longer.** At the fifth bell **two people read four marks and a groove on the lintel above the shut mouth and read them two different ways, and neither of them says what they are, and nobody cuts a mark in the stone** — and the clerk enters that and underlines it, which she does not do, and Bel Ordry asks her not to. **The arrangement is untouched: shut on the first, second and fourth, open on the third, fifth and sixth, school on the three open days, and this closure is a room and closes no corridor day**, and the clerk enters that with the reason so that in six weeks nobody has to argue it again. Marek's one line in his own book that night: *a room kept safe by being a room nobody is in is a thing this building now knows how to do, and I do not think anybody above the Cinder Steps has worked out yet that this is cheap.*

## Chapter 105 — The Line Above The Steps

**The batch midpoint: a competent inspector arrives on a lawful permit, the charter does not cover her, and the boundary has to write a rule about a stranger — which is the first thing this Hearthhold has ever done for an audience that is not in it.** **Hollis Ashe**, forty-one, sixteen years, Stonelight Compact route inspection, is in the anteroom at the second bell on the fifth day, a Friday, with the corridor open, and **nobody in this building saw her come in.** Her permit covers a line of stations on the surface above the Cinder Steps and the approach to it, **and it does not cover this, and she says so before she asks anything**, and she leaves her tally on the table so that they can read it. **Clause four of the charter binds the Cartwright office and does not cover her, and Bel Ordry says that out loud in the room before he decides anything.** The four sentences are **argued, not printed**: Renn Vale on the first (*a rule that lets this boundary say no is a rule a stranger can use to shut a room — put the other half in, or the sheet is a door with manners on it*), Renn again on the second (*two is wrong in the way that gets people hurt; a document that says a thing is refused is worth more up a road than a document that shows a page*), Dalla Sen on the fourth (*we cannot keep this, and I would rather write it and be caught keeping it than leave it out and be caught having thought about it*), Mikka Hale on the third (*there is a man in this building who has spent twenty weeks keeping a page in a coat so that a stranger could not carry it out of a room, and I want him in the room for this sentence*). **The clerk's copy is read back against the original, word for word, and Bel Ordry says out loud that it is not a very good check and that it is the one he has.** She asks to see the plan, gets the third column and not the first and not the fourth, asks for a copy, **and is given the third column written out in words in a clerk's hand — and the third column leaves the building, and it is the first thing this Hearthhold has ever sent a stranger that a stranger could file.** She asks what the anteroom's second way out is and is told **a word**, and writes it down, **and Marek Venn understands four seconds too late that he has just described a rule that can be handed to somebody, and does not warn the room, and it happened about four feet in front of nine people who did not see it either.** She asks about the stair, is told *not a route and not in anything*, and writes it down; Nera Oduya adds that four treads on the far side have nobody on them and nobody is going to, and that she has refused to certify the shaft's air for eighteen weeks, and the inspector says she will write that down with the air engineer's office on it, which is more than she was offered. **Then she asks, in a room, who is the person that answers for the school on the waist, and there are eleven seconds of silence, and Marek knows the answer and does not say it, because the second he says it that arrangement becomes an office** — and Renn Vale answers the question that was actually asked, that there is no person, and the inspector writes that down as a worse answer than a name. She offers to write *refused* and the room makes her write **not covered**, and she tells them what that will cost her own office. **At the sixth bell the clerk discovers that there is a chalked inspection line above the Cinder Steps and that it has been there for nine seasons, and that this boundary has been having its whole argument about the middle gate's pails under inspection the whole time, and nobody fills the space after it.** Marek tells Bel Ordry to his face what he is — *a man who can be found is a man who can be checked, and a man who cannot be found is a man who has to be trusted* — and Bel Ordry does not defend it and does not take it back. **And at the last bell Sefu Aran comes off the wheel and says he is going up the middle passage to keep a promise he made out loud about four households, four days to the middle gate and then on, and he will not say when he will be back, and the room does not argue with him and does not thank him, and he leaves the two sentences with the clerk to be read to whoever would have to act on them.**

## Chapter 106 — The Wheel Goes With The Keeper

**A boundary with no elected keeper in it runs perfectly well, and that is the finding, and it is not a comfort.** On the first day of the twenty-first week, a Monday, with the corridor shut and the school not running, the boundary discovers **it has been carrying the wheel in four other places for twenty weeks and had not noticed**. **Sefu Aran went up the middle passage at the first bell the Friday before with two true sentences in the clerk's book and nothing else in his hands, and nobody walked him out past the waist because the corridor was open that day and four pails were going over it in the pump's window — which was an accident of the calendar and not a decision, and Dalla Sen entered it as an accident of the calendar, and entered that she would remember it in a month.**: Renn Vale holds the road, Mikka Hale the pot, Dalla Sen the book, and nobody holds the wheel, because the wheel goes with the keeper and the charter does not say what happens to a boundary whose elected keeper is carrying two true sentences up a road. **The pump runs attended, the sixth minutes come and go with the post on the review page still blank, the pot is read at the fifth bell by a woman who was not waiting for anybody, and nothing goes wrong — and by the fourth bell the room is in a bad mood about it.** **The keeper's two true sentences are read out at the third bell, standing, in the anteroom**, because he left them with the clerk to be read to whoever would have to act on them, and the clerk says so before she starts: *nothing comes, this boundary is not sending anybody and has not sent anybody and will not; the four households have their own water and their own four sets of steps and did not ask this boundary for any of it; and this boundary has found two jars a day out of its own wall and is using them and is not sending them, and the true sentence is that it looked after itself while four people carried water up four sets of steps, and those two things happened at the same time and one of them was this boundary's choice.* **Mikka Hale asks for them to be read again at the fifth bell** and gives the reason without explaining it, because a true thing heard once gets repeated wrong by the fourth person who hears it. **Renn Vale decides that they stand and are read and decides nothing else**, because a room that decides what to do about four households' water is a room that has started sending somebody. **Wen Pask, from the fourth step, with no standing in that room and some anyway, asks what the point of reading them is, and the clerk cannot answer it and says so, and gives him the reason she can give: not for them, but for the fourth person in the room who has not been here for all of it.** **Renn Vale opens the chapter by finding a hole in the charter that is nobody's fault and everybody's**: clause four says *the keeper* and there are two men in this building it can be — Bel Ordry, who keeps the plan, and Sefu Aran, who signs first on everything — and the two of them agreed without ever having to say so, *and that is not a rule, that is a thing two men happened to be doing.* Bel Ordry will not reopen a signed instrument over a noun, and Renn Vale's answer is the sentence the chapter turns on: **she is not frightened of the boundary stopping, she is frightened of it being the only thing that stopped because he was in it.** **Marek Venn then does the thing nobody has done since the obligation was discharged: he goes and finds out what would happen if the keeper never came back, and finds three things that want a keeper's word, and he finds them at three stations in scene.** **One, the wheel** — Renn Vale stands at it for a bell and a half, comes off it, and reads out of the book in the keeper's own hand the only reason she can stand there (*the road is not the paper, the road is a way up a passage and I hold the cord and the wheel and the bell and none of those are paper*), and says she is not a keeper but a woman holding a wheel because a man said out loud that a wheel is not paper, and *the difference is going to matter the first time somebody wants me to do something I do not want to do.* **Two, the water-carrying** — the seventh term read out in Renn Vale's own words from her own slate, every figure on it hers, and then the sentence that made the day: *it is right and it is mine, and I have been saying it is the boundary's for five months because the boundary is a nicer word than mine.* **Three, a signature** — Dalla Sen finds at the fourth bell that the second sheet has seven hands on the charter and one of the seven is four days up a road, and records three answers she will not decide between, including Isel Ferrow's unasked-for *a sheet with two names on it is a sheet two people can be sent to.* **And then Marek says the fourth thing, which was not a gap**: the plan is a page in a coat in a room with a man in it, and he has watched that man do less and less of the loud things for three weeks. **All three had a substitute, and not one of the substitutes was a keeper.** He says out loud that he has wanted to be needed in this building for twenty weeks, that he has been needed twice in the last week, and that both times it was a floor and a wet joint and a woman with a rule who knew where to put her hand. At the sixth bell the count walks the board, names no day, and **gives the reason out loud that the crew's column is a quantity of asking and has not moved because nobody has asked the five of them for anything**; the boundary's column stands at a hundred and forty and a quarter, and **the column with no heading gains forty-one days and forty-one nights and is not headed for the fourth batch running, and he asks the room to notice that a man with a better reason each time is a man who is running out of reasons.** At the seventh bell Marek writes **the first entry in his own book that is about him and not about a plan**: a room can hear the true thing about itself and go on to the fifth bell, that is the boundary working and not the boundary being all right, he is the last man in this building that needed it to, and he does not know what to do with an evening. **The shut school corner is still shut and nobody has opened it to look.**

## Chapter 107 — The Second Sheet

**A charter with three objects of care has quietly become the wrong shape for what this boundary has become, and the amendment is a second sheet and not a change.** On the second day, a Tuesday, with the corridor shut and the keeper on the road, **the four sentences lie face up on the anteroom table where anybody in this building can read them, and Dalla Sen says she chose that and will not let anybody else bring it up first** — a rule in a drawer is a rule nobody has to look at, and this one has a stranger's hand on the other side of it. **The charter names a stair, a lip and a valve, and the boundary now has a fourth, a wall with water in it.** The room argues it out loud, in four hands, and nobody marks anything until it has been argued: **the air engineer puts the fourth in** — a stranger will ask what this boundary's objects of care are, and if the answer is not on the page then the answer is in somebody's mouth, and a thing in a cook's mouth is a thing a stranger writes down, and she said it badly to a stranger in a corridor on Friday and has not stopped hearing it; **the cook against it** — a document that names three things is a description and one that names four is a claim, and the three in the clause are all of them a person being in danger, a man on a stone, a man under a slab, a hand on a handle, and the wall is not a person being in danger but a thing giving us something, and a wall that gives us something is a wall somebody in four days writes *source* against; **Renn Vale for the cook's side and against her own habit** — the charter got smaller and safer between two strikes and is signed by seven people, and she would be putting a claim on a wall with her own hand on a Tuesday because a man from the surface asked a question on Friday; and
