**Bel Ordry on the shape** — a second clause is a document with two things that can be argued about separately, and the second of them will be argued about by somebody who has never been in this room. **Dalla Sen rules the tie is a person and refuses to be it, and it is the air engineer and the cook, and it is two hands and not one.** **Dalla Sen rules that it goes under — a second sheet, and not a second clause — and is told it is dated in the top corner, and Bel Ordry refuses the date out loud**: a page with a date in the top corner is a record of what a building was doing on a day, he has one date in this building and it means *as at*, and if the sheet has no date on it then it says *now* and *now* is the only honest thing a second sheet can say. **The reason is written on the sheet in the clerk's hand in the keeper's words: it has no date because it does not record a day, the first sheet is dated, and the two are not the same kind of thing.** Bel Ordry then cannot sign, because the second signature below the keeper's belongs to a man on a road, **and a name taken off is a name somebody can put back.** **Nera Oduya strikes the woman's covers out of the second sheet in nine seconds and says the reason out loud instead of writing it** — nobody has asked her, not once, not in twenty weeks, not by her — **and nobody in the room can produce one sentence in which anybody has ever asked her whether her covers could be used as an argument.** **Renn Vale names the price and will not argue against it:** a charter with a sheet under it is two things and the part that is easier to hold is the part somebody keeps, and in a year somebody will read the second sheet on its own because it is shorter and newer and has a wall in it that gives them water, and they will not read clause nine underneath it — **and the alternative is that a wall with the only drinking water in it is on nobody's paper, and she has watched a cook in that room have to describe that wall out loud to a stranger in a corridor on Friday, and a page that can be read wrong is better than a secret that has to be told.** Bel Ordry writes the price onto the sheet in the room's words and lets the charter and the sheet disagree by one object of care on purpose, as the cook already made them disagree by one number. **The sheet is written in two hands with no date and no name at the top of it, signed by the cook alone and by nobody else, and it does not replace the charter, does not erase a clause, and does not touch clause nine.** **Iven Tallo is not asked to sign it, notices, and says something about the first charter and not the second** — he was in the room for the first one and was asked and said no in four words; tonight he is not asked, nobody is surprised, and a man who is relieved to be left out of a document in a bad month is a man who has been taught what a relief feels like, and he has taught it. **And at the fifth bell the clerk does the thing this room has owed a man for a month: she asks Bel Ordry for his coat in front of nine people, counts the four parts, makes him say which is which without looking, and enters that the fourth column is empty and the third has eight of nine filled and that he did not say which and she did not ask; and then she enters that the clerk thinks what he wrote on Friday was very good and that she has no way to check it and has not looked for one, and enters those two sentences in that order, and nobody objects.**

## Chapter 108 — Nine Children In A Numbered Room

**The school moves, the corridor is shut on a day the arrangement had open, and one of the three open days is gone.** On the third day of the twenty-first week, a Wednesday — **a day the standing arrangement has open** — **Renn Vale closes the corridor at the first bell and gives the reason before anybody argues**: the waist has moved three times and is not measured by three people on purpose, there are nine register boxes and a shelf's worth of slates and nine children and a teacher, and there is no second window, because the low end stands in water for the six minutes after the lever comes off twenty-six times a day and the only window is the strokes in between. **Dalla Sen refuses the room's request to hold the closure and the lost day apart for an hour and says out loud that she is going to put them next to each other with a reason beside them and nothing between them, and that the reason is not going to be a reason.** The school crosses in three parties, in the pump's strokes, with a bearer at the near lip; **Wen Pask carries four boxes in a party and a fifth and says nothing about it, because he was asked in a room with the terms out loud and because being asked is a different thing from being thanked.** **The count column has to be read before each party because the only page in this building with a count in it is the plan, and the anteroom's number is ten and the anteroom is empty, and Ilsa Norr refuses to cross the fill on the boundary's arithmetic and counts aloud at both ends instead** — *ten is not how many are in that room, and I am not walking across that fill on your arithmetic, Renn, and I say that with love.* **A boy of about eleven asks, in the middle of the dip, at a walk, where the number comes from, and the teacher says *we will find out*, and nobody follows it up.** **The two beech lengths are the props under the shelf the nine register boxes stand on, and a carpenter tells the room before he is asked and then says no when he is asked** — *the props stay; a boundary that loses its record in a week is a boundary a stranger can rewrite in a month* — **and Ilsa Norr says she was not going to ask and wants that written down.** **The props stay, the school goes without a shelf, and the nine boxes go on the hearth stones, which are dry and higher than the floor, and a cook says yes to that before she is asked.** The school runs two bells and then does not run. **The trade is entered on the room's own page and not on the plan's, in a schoolteacher's words: the school is in the worst room in this building and it is dry, and I did not agree with that, and a room shut with a wedge is not the same as a room taken from us, and I want the book to be able to say both of those sentences without one cancelling the other** — and Bel Ordry reads it out with the rule that everyone who wrote a line stands and says yes, and **the plan has no row for this room, and that is a finding, not a decision.** **The day was lost, nothing is paid back, and Ilsa Norr will not have it written as moved or as paid back and was not told which of the two is the independent one and did not ask.** The clerk puts the closure and the lost day on the page side by side with a reason beside them and nothing between them, on purpose, so a reader in a year cannot make them into a finding. And **at the last bell a courier comes up the middle passage with a folded paper that has no date on it, from the second gate, with a clerk's mark on the form and not a name, and it says the water-lock is closed for survey and is attended** — and Dalla Sen reads the word back and says the room has read it four hundred times and has never once read it the way it is written there.

## Chapter 109 — Behind A Good Reason

**The batch climax: a competent office closes a correct structure, four households are behind it, and the boundary's two instruments are both about this building.** On the fourth day, a Thursday, with the corridor shut and the keeper still on the road, **Dalla Sen reads the notice at the first bell**: the water-lock at the second gate is closed for survey and is attended, a person may attend on giving notice at the counter, notice must be given in person, **the notice is not dated**, and **the office will provide a butt and a hand-pump at the counter, on the day of the survey only.** **The cook reads that last part back and says what it is doing: the man is behind the door, the water is in front of it, and the four of them are behind the door with the man.** **Renn Vale says it is not their door, that she has been trying for two days to find the mistake in it, and that there is not one** — a competent office, on a clearance, for a good reason, with a man in a hut, and a door, and two brothers and their sister and one house that only carries behind it. **The four-sentence procedure comes off the anteroom table and is used inside the boundary for the first time, and Bel Ordry reads it off the clerk's copy, and he drops half of the second sentence and the tail of the third, and Renn Vale notices** — *you have read the whole of one and a half of them* — and the two pages agree with each other and the reading did not, and the clerk enters that the clause he dropped is the one about *what a thing is and not what it is for*, next to the anteroom's rating and the word *door*, because they are the same sentence, and Bel Ordry says a rule that only works in the hands of the man who wrote it is a rule with one holder. **Bel Ordry also refuses to amend the four sentences, and gives the reason: they were written in a room with nine people in it about a woman who stood on a step, and a document that gets amended every time it is inconvenient is the guild's counter-draft with better manners.** The boundary then does the small true things and refuses the large one in the same breath: **the water-carrying is unchanged and nothing extra goes down the passage**; **the two jars are not sent, and the cook says no before she is asked**; a copy of the two sentences goes up the passage as paper, **unsigned and undated, and Bel Ordry does not put his ring on it and says why — a ring on a sheet is a mark on a sheet, and a mark on a sheet is a thing a person can be found by, and he is not going to be the first to break that in a bad week**; **and the clerk enters that a piece of paper in a courier's hand is not the keeping of a promise and cannot be stood in for, and that the room knows the difference.** Nobody sends after the keeper, and the room enters that it considered it and refused it, and the reason is not cost. **The cook states the cost in her own words and it is the longest line in the clerk's hand in twenty-one weeks: this boundary found two jars a day and kept them, four people are behind a gate, both of those are true at the same time, one of them was this boundary's choice, and I would do it again on Friday.** **Marek Venn asks to go and gives four reasons and cannot** — the road, the two-foot-eight corridor over eleven feet of shaft that is packed and not held, nine children on the far side of a fill, and then the one he is ashamed of: **to go up that road he would have to be a person somebody at a counter could send for, and this boundary does not put people in registers, and a boundary that does not put people in registers cannot go and get anybody, and he has spent twenty-one weeks teaching it to be that and it is the correct thing to be and it has cost four households a counter they cannot reach.** **And then he refuses the Marker out loud, in a room, with the ordinary means for the anteroom frame named and exhausted — no timber, no mortar of the right kind, six sound wedges and two dead sticks, a right hand that will not close — and says there is one thing left that is not a reading, and that it is a different sentence from *anybody who asks me to read a boundary is going to be told no*, and that he is not going to do it, and he wants the room to hear him say no while he is standing there.** **Dalla Sen writes all of it down and enters that she did not understand the second half of it and is not going to pretend she did and is not going to ask him at the sixth bell.** He writes one line in his own book and it is the worst line in it.

## Chapter 110 — The First Column

**The batch aftermath: the plan's first column is read aloud and the boundary finds out it has been writing down a nine-hundred-year-old permission instead of a population — and a room with nine children in it has no number at all.** On the fifth day, a Friday, with the corridor open and the school running at the far end, the six things are read and then **Dalla Sen says *Numbers***, and **Pell Roke reads the plan's first column aloud at the fifth bell from the bench at the top of the nine steps**: *ten, four, eight, ten, six, nine, five, two, and a dash* — and nothing fills the space after it, which is what the numbers are for. **The check is made in front of the room, in chalk against the slate, over forty minutes, and it checks three explanations and all three of them are possible and the true one is not any of them.** It is not a miscopy: the slate is the clerk's hand and the page is the plan's, and **what her hand is on is writing down numbers that are said out loud in front of her, eleven times, and nobody has ever asked her what the numbers are numbers of.** It is not a misheard voice: the number is said out loud every time anybody comes through that door and it was ten in three mouths. It is not a miscounted room: the anteroom has never held under ten and never over ten, and empty is not a number anybody here has had to shout. **And then a voice comes up the nine steps from the lower level, because nobody in this building can shout up nine steps, and Leena Orr says the sentence the book has been carrying since the seventeenth week: *a list is not a location, and a count is a list, and this page has been calling a permission a population since the day anybody in this building first picked up a chalk*** — and it is used once, and it earns the discovery. The school store is open, which it is only because the register boxes are on hearth stones, and **the anteroom's ten on the nine-hundred-year-old dowel is the highest number on the dowel**, and Nera Oduya says one professional sentence — *a number somebody set is not a number anybody counted* — **and does not say her theory**, and asks the clerk to enter that the fourth thing bound to *when this boundary is keeping itself* was approached in a room and not met. **Dalla Sen asks her for a piece of work and not for an opinion — write down what the second column is for, nine rows, nine conditions, no number and no day on any of them, and the fourth of them is the word *wet* — and it is done in four minutes when it should have taken nine, and she says she had a great deal more to say and that nobody asked her for the rest of it, and the clerk enters that nobody in that room is going to ask.** And the finding's second half: **a room with nine children in it has no row on the plan at all, and a blank row in a new document is an omission and an omission reads as an accusation, and that is the first time the clerk has understood why the ninth room has no row, and it is not because two women are stubborn.** Tams Quill walks the board twice, names no day, and **the crew are at fifty-two and a half and the boundary at a hundred and fifty-three and a quarter, and the count's list of thirty-six adds by the day it was done, and both columns reconcile**; **forty-five days and forty-five nights go into the column with no heading, it is still unheaded for the fourth batch running, and the reason is worse than last week's: a heading is a claim about what a column is for, and the day it can be checked is the first day one of its contents does not fit, and the one that gets left out will be somebody.** **The twelfth board entry stays a null.** And Marek Venn says the last thing in the room in three parts: a page can keep a number after the people have gone, and he is not going to write a theory about it this week and that is a decision and not modesty; **we have learned how to keep a room by making it a room nobody is in, the price was a wedge out of a school door, it worked, everybody in that room voted for it, he was the only one who could see it was the first of a series and he did not say so**; and **he does not know the other way, and the person who has to work it out is him.** And the last line is his: **a page in a coat is not a system, that is a man, and the man is on a road** — with the brass rule silent for twelve weeks, the plate unopened, the pot at ten days and never once gone up, the plan in four parts in a coat that does not leave the building, the dowel back in a locked store with the key in the room, four treads dry behind a rail that nobody has been on, and a person still under that lip.

## Chapter 111 — The Terms Of The Asking

**The twenty-second week opens with the anteroom emptied for the first time in twenty-two weeks, and the emptying turns out to be the more interesting half.** Dalla Sen sets it in the pump's strokes with a reader at each end and Renn Vale reads the seventh term out loud in her own words, and Iven Tallo answers the one question nobody had thought to ask — **that the head of the frame is not failing, it is doing what a head does, because the clay is drying and the head is the only soft thing in the frame.** He lays the rule against it and has three rule marks on the jamb that prove the head has gone out after every pack in this building's history. **Nine people go out at the second bell and the plan's first column says ten, and the clerk writes ten down while the room is empty, and the page is right and the room is right, and the number did not go anywhere when the people did.** **And for the first time in twenty-two weeks the word *door* is not said, because a room with nobody in it does not need a second way out** — the clerk enters that she did not say it and did not repeat it, and Renn Vale puts the one sentence on it: *a room nobody is in does not need a second way out, that is the reason it does not have one, do not let anybody in here find that out before the rest of us has*, and the clerk writes it once. **Then the boundary does the thing it has not done since the fifth day of the nineteenth week and asks the crew for something.** Dalla Sen asks in a room with the terms out loud and a person named who can be told no, and Renn Vale corrects nothing, and Iven Tallo accepts on his own terms — one hour, no signatures, the answer in the carpenter's words in the room and not on a landing. **The crew's column moves for the first time since the fifth day of the nineteenth week, from fifty-two and a half to fifty-three and a half**, and the reason is a person and not a favour, and the count declines to give it because a clerk gave it better. Iven's four findings are entered: the head is not broken, there is no way to fix that with anything we own, stone in lime would do it and there is no stone in lime and no bond and no apprentice, and he has never in his life seen a man hold a frame with anything except what the frame is made of. **A man of twenty-two is forty-six days into a count that is his own.**

## Chapter 112 — The Head Of The Frame

**The Marker stage, and it is not granted and not requested and not asked for.** Marek Venn had said in a room on the fourth day of the week before that there was one thing left that was not a reading and that he was not going to do it, and he says on the second day of the twenty-second week that he has been not doing it since that day, and that a man who says he has been thinking about a thing sounds braver than a man who has been arguing with himself. **The anteroom is emptied for the second time in two days and Jo Verrick objects to the habit before anybody asks her.** Before anything is done they go and stand in front of the four marks and the groove on the lintel above the shut school corner's mouth, because he will not put a mark on a stone in this building without having looked at the marks already on one, and **Nera Oduya and Renn Vale read them two ways and neither will say, and Jo Verrick puts her rule against the jamb, and the clerk enters the one sentence that had to go in that day and was not about the frame: a mark will hold on anchorstone, and there is none here we can reach, and what we have is dressed stone, which is not the same thing and is not nothing either.** Then he tells the room the whole of the only rule he has — one direction, one limit, and the limit has to be said out loud in a room afterwards or he is not allowed to do it at all — and **Renn Vale stops him for a minute on her own terms, and the objection that stops the room is not *a mark is a claim* but *a mark cut in a stone is a claim that outlasts the person who agreed to it*, and so the mark is not cut: it is chalk and gland grease on the dressed face of the jamb at the height of a hand, where anybody coming through that door can see it.** **Renn Vale agrees, and writes the condition in her own hand with no number on it and no day on it** — *the mark is on while the head of this frame is out of true, it is off when the head has not been further out of true than the line on this jamb through a night and a morning, and I take it off and nobody argues with me about it* — and she says out loud that she took three weeks to be able to write a condition and have it be a condition, because a man can wake up on a Tuesday having done nothing and come back on Wednesday having done a great deal and the line will be the line. **Nera Oduya is named as the second person who can stop it**, because the anteroom's air comes in at the service door and leaves at it, and the two of them can be stopped by each other. **And then the air engineer does the first of the volume's five acts of trust: she writes the limit in her own mouth and hands the sentence to the man to say, and says out loud that she has done it on purpose, and gives the reason — he got nothing twice off a wet wall in a schoolroom and wrote it down both times, and the room will take a limit from him and not from her, and a mark whose only keeper is the man who made it is a claim and not a mark.** The limit is that the head is carrying nothing and the mark is being asked to carry the *absence* of a load. **He does it at the fourth bell with his left hand, in nine minutes, and nobody helps him.** The anteroom's count arrives as a sound under the pump's check and he knows what it is and knowing does not stop it, and **the clerk enters twice that he saw nothing.** His hand does not close. **Tams Quill enters the thirteenth board entry — a mark is not a reading, not a null, and not the claim, on its own terms — and the arithmetic becomes nine in the ordinary column and four in the one with nothing over the top of it, and he refuses to head that column for the fifth batch running and says he has run out of reasons.**

## Chapter 113 — Four Marks And A Carpenter

**The frame has held since the second day of the week before last and Jo Verrick does not like it, and the floor in the shut school corner has stopped getting wetter, and nobody touched anything.** The crossing took nine minutes fifty seconds, the school ran at the far end, and **Wen Pask put the lamp down and went away without being told twice.** At the first bell Jo lays her rule and a hair from one of the nine's heads against Renn Vale's chalk and says it has not moved by a hair, and then says she does not like that, because a thing that has gone out a finger and a bit in a fortnight and then has not moved overnight is not a thing that has stopped. **Jo Verrick finds, by putting a hand flat on the flags through the shut door's gap and sliding a slate under it, that the low corner is no darker than it was on the first day of the twentieth week, and Iven Tallo says the only sentence that quiets the room: the water has stopped coming up, and it comes up that joint from the patch in the course at the haunch, and the frame is the thing with the chalk on it — and asks for it to be entered that nobody may say the school corner dried because a man put grease on a jamb without the sentence about the drain.** Then the argument that the morning turns on is about a number: **Renn Vale cannot say *further out of true* without a figure, and the only figure anybody has for that room is a ten, and a ten is a permission.** Nera Oduya says a ten is not a distance, not a thickness, not a load and not an angle, that it will go on the slate next to *further out of true* and in six weeks a clerk will not know which is which, and that she has not said the next half of it and nobody is going to ask. **A road hand going on to a survey camp comes up the passage at the fourth bell with the guild's survey notice — a route-clearing crew is working a survey of this boundary's sector under a clearance the charter does not mention, the promised timber is not coming because it is in the store the survey is camped in, and the boundary's own record is what the finding will be compared against** — and he stands in a doorway for four seconds on his way up the nine steps and sees the mark on the jamb and does not stop and does not ask, and the clerk enters the whole of it, including that this boundary will not hear from it. **Bel Ordry is asked, in a room, with the terms out loud, what the four marks and the groove are, and he is not asked to read them, and he gives one craft thing about the groove and then the sentence the room needed: five marks in this building now, four cut and one four hours old, and in fifty years a woman will stand in front of that jamb and cannot read a line of chalk and a smear of grease at all, and nobody in this building has ever stopped anything by deciding it would not happen.** A man of twenty-two is forty-eight days in.

## Chapter 114 — The First Of The Month

**The one scene in this volume told from outside this building, in Sefu Aran's viewpoint, on the first of the month, and nobody in the chapter says which day of the week that is.** The counter room at the second gate is eight feet by eleven and **Wenna Dray, who has been at that counter for eleven years, tells him to stand there and not lean on the counter and offers to be in the room when he says it** — and he asks for her to be in the room and *not* to write it down, and she tells him exactly what that is worth at a counter: a thing four people heard and nobody has, and in a year he will be asked whether he came and there will be nothing to point at. **He goes to four doors, because there is nothing there that can summon anybody: two brothers, Ansel and Peth Dunmow, their sister Hessa, and the fourth house, which is Marda Skell, sixty-one, who has not walked to a counter since before the cold closed.** He says the two true sentences to their faces, the second one being that this boundary found two jars a day in its own wall and used them and sent none of them, and that the true sentence is that it looked after itself while four people carried water up four sets of steps, and that one of those two things was its choice. **Marda Skell asks for the other half and gets it, and then asks the whole of the week: *will it be open again* — and he says *I do not know*, and she says *then you came a long way to tell us a thing we had already worked out*, and he says *yes*.** She tells him his own second sentence has already gone further down the road than he thought, on a route that is not his and not a guild's, and refuses to say who told her, and he does not ask. **The water-lock's survey is still on: the butt and the hand-pump at the counter are for the day of the survey only, the sheet is not wrong, and Wenna Dray tells him plainly that nobody is going to be cruel about it and nobody is going to hurry and at the end of it the water is still a step away and down a slope, exactly as it was before anybody surveyed it — and that nobody did anything wrong.** He shows her the boundary's copy of the two sentences, unsigned, unringed, undated, and she tells him what a piece of paper is worth at a counter, and writes one line of her own: that a keeper came on the first of the month and said a true thing to four households and would not have it written. The chapter's last note is that a clerk four days back down the passage wrote a man of twenty-two up by one, and it is not a register and it dates nothing.

## Chapter 115 — The Floor Is Dry

**The school corner's condition is met, the room is opened, and the school does not go back into it, and all three of those facts go on the page side by side with a reason beside them and nothing between them.** Renn Vale reads her own condition, nine minutes with a boy holding a lamp and a woman with a rule on the flags, and reports it dry **at two places and not the middle** and says a condition you improve when it is met is a condition you were hoping to fail. She opens the room and then says the school is not going into it: *I wrote that condition for a wet floor, and the floor is dry, and the reason it is dry is a thing two women can take off a wall, and when the mark comes off that head will start going out again and the joint will start feeding that floor again, and I would have opened a room to nine children on a grease mark.* She refuses to leave a met condition sitting on a page looking met. **Ilsa Norr says it from the far end of the corridor with nine children behind her and is not consoled: we were moved out of a wet room and we are not being moved back into a dry one, and if you had asked me on Monday I would have said yes and would have been wrong, and you did not ask me, and I am not thanking anybody for it because the reason you did not ask is a rule older than me.** **Marek Venn hears it and does not say *I did that*, and the chapter says what he cannot say: that the boundary has now learned two ways to keep a room safe by making it a room nobody is in, and he cannot tell which of the two sentences frightens him more, and the honest answer is the first one.** At the fifth bell **Pell Roke reads the first column, the second, the third and then the fourth, and says *there is nothing in it*** — the first time the empty column has been read aloud as empty — and the clerk enters that a boy read an empty column out loud and said there was nothing in it, and that a column empty with a reason on it is the only decision on purpose in this building, and that he said in four words what a fortnight of pages had been saying. The board is walked, the unheaded column is referred to and not itemised, and the count gains his reason for not heading it for the fifth batch. **Renn Vale decides that the boundary will not write down how long the keeper has been gone, because a number of days is a thing a room can be wrong about.** A man of twenty-two is fifty days in.

## Chapter 116 — The Bench Is To Be Kept Clear

**The sealed archive answers one question, asked in a room, by a person, and the answer is a fact about a room and not a cause.** Bel Ordry drafts the question and the room argues it into shape for four bells — Nera Oduya insists a sealed room will answer the easy half, Mikka Hale replaces both with *I want to know whether a room in a sealed archive has ever been written down as being one thing while it was plainly another, by somebody who had been in it, and I want to know what they called it, because the calling is the part* — and Renn Vale insists the asking be **by a person in a room, not through a child, with a person who can be told no**, and Bel Ordry agrees and **refuses to put a figure on how long the answer will take.** Dalla Sen then goes into the school store for a blank sheet and comes out with nothing: **there is no blank paper in this Hearthhold, and a clerk has just gone through a locked room with a nine-hundred-year-old schedule in it looking for a piece of paper to ask a question on.** The question goes out on the back of a day-board. **The answer comes back on a courier's hand, undated, in the Middle's own route keeper's hand, and it is four lines and the second is a line off a sheet nine hundred years old: room eleven of the lower row is entered in the inventory as a records room and it is a records room, and under the entry on the same sheet, in a hand nobody can date, there is one more line and it says *the bench is to be kept clear* — and there is no bench in room eleven, and there never has been in any inventory, and the keeper stood in it himself.** He refuses in writing to say what it means. **Nera Oduya is in the room for the whole of it and says four words — *a room is being maintained as a bench* — and then stops on purpose, and asks the clerk to enter that the fourth thing bound to *when this boundary is keeping itself* was approached in a room and was not met and that she was in the room and that nobody asked her anything, and that a room that lets a person stop is a room keeping itself better than any of the rooms that are shut.** **Marek Venn has the question in his mouth for a minute — the fourth he has wanted to ask her in twenty-two weeks — and puts it down, because she has just said *nobody asked me anything* in the tone of a woman who has been counting.** The clerk then puts three facts side by side on purpose with a reason beside them and nothing between them, and invites the room to join them, and nobody does. A man of twenty-two is fifty-one days in.

## Chapter 117 — The First Form

**The market route's first form arrives on a road and the first toll on it is not money; it is two lines for a name.** Pettin Rahl, a road-clerk who reads forms for a living, says what he is before he is asked, and says the form **is not a toll, does not cost anything, is not voluntary, and the word in it for not doing it is *attended*** — the same word the water-lock notice used four days ago, and the same word this boundary reads four hundred times a day. The form goes on the anteroom table where anybody can read it and stays there. **The room reads it out line by line and objects to five of the seven, and does not mark anything until it has argued.** Renn Vale on *a person with nothing is not on this form at all, and the four households at the second gate carry water up four sets of steps*. **Mikka Hale on the line for a name: a document about a room travels, this is a document about a man on a road, and there is no date on it either.** Bel Ordry on the count line — *it is the only line on this sheet I believe* — and on the line for the person responsible, and on the signature: **the fifth line and the sixth line are the same line, and there are two of them, and a form with a line for a name and then a line for a name again is a form asking twice on purpose.** **Iven Tallo says the sheet is a good sheet and that the spacing is right and somebody thought about the order, and that if he were a guild clerk writing it he would want somebody to sign it, because a road with a load on it and nobody responsible is a road where the next thing that happens is a man is killed and there is nobody to ask — and he does not argue with it, because he knows what it is like to be a trade nobody asks.** Renn Vale finds one good line and stops arguing. **Nera Oduya's objection to the line for what is carried is the first thing this Hearthhold would put on it is *water*, the second is *nine children*, the third is *nothing, passing through*, and all three are true on the same morning; and the fourth thing is *a mark*, and she does not say the rest of it.** Then the fifth objection, from the man who keeps the page: **clause four names one office, the boundary has now had two bodies come to it that the four sentences do not name, one of them said out loud she would write a procedure of her own, and he is not going to write a second procedure in a fortnight for a second office, because a document that gets amended every time it is inconvenient is the guild's counter-draft with better manners.** Renn Vale reads aloud, out of a book, her own Chapter 100 line about how a door becomes a toll gate, and says she wrote it down and did not read it since. **Two sentences are drafted in answer with no name and no signature — the cook's is that if a person is going to write a name at a gate they should write the water first and the people second and the mark never — and they do not go that day, because a man on a road has to be asked by a person and a sheet on a counter is not a person, and they will go on a market day, and there is no market day this week.** Pettin Rahl's parting line is that the form is not compulsory, it is *attended*, and that four gates in a month have printed that word and none of them has ever asked anybody what this boundary means by it. A man of twenty-two is fifty-two days in.

## Chapter 118 — Stopped In A Room

**The mark's condition is met, the mark comes off a jamb, and the anteroom's second way out is a word again, and eleven people in the room do not see it.** Jo Verrick's rule and a hair from one of the nine's heads go against Renn Vale's chalk line, and it has not moved, and she says she does not like it and that being wrong about being worried is the best thing that has happened to her in three weeks. **Found, located, tested, recorded, and not before** — and the test is done after the condition has been said out loud and not before, because that is the count in this room. **Renn Vale takes it off with a cloth, in front of eleven people, in forty seconds, and Marek Venn is not allowed to touch it, and the reason she gives out loud is that if the man who put a thing on a wall is the one who takes it off, then in a year there is a man in this room who can put things on walls and take them off and there is nothing on the wall to stop him.** Dalla Sen entered that nobody had thought of it. **The burning stops; the hand does not close that night, closes on the second morning, is serviceable on the fourth, and is not what it was, and the sound in the room stays.** He says so plainly and asks for it to be entered unkindly, and says he does not know what the sound is and has had since the second day of the week before last to guess and has not guessed. **The clerk starts to ask him for an explanation, stops herself, and enters that she chose to keep the sentence rather than have the explanation, because an opinion is not a piece of work and the mark is now off the wall and the sentence in her book is a sentence about a thing that is not there any more.** The board is walked and **the mark is not taken off it** — the count's reason being that the mark stopping is a fact about the mark and not about the entry, and the day he takes things off this board is the day it starts being a record of what this boundary has done rather than of what has happened to it — and he says for the first time in five batches that he has run out of reasons, and the clerk enters the omission. **Nera Oduya goes into the school corner and leaves a strip of dyed cloth in the mouth at a width she would not have set, and says she has left it because she does not trust a figure she did not take, and would rather the mouth was set by somebody who has to keep it; Renn Vale goes down and narrows it to what she would have set, and Nera says *Good* and nothing else, and nobody is thanked.** At the seventh bell the anteroom is exactly the room it was for twenty-two weeks and Bel Ordry says the word is back. **And the chapter ends on the four facts Dalla Sen did not put side by side** — a frame a finger and a bit out of true whose second way out is a sentence; that sentence written down in a stranger's hand; four instruments and no procedure for two of the bodies not named in them and a third on the way; and a mark off a jamb in a room that has not changed — and on the fact that the clerk who has spent five weeks putting facts next to each other on purpose had the chalk in her hand and did not do it, and has never given a reason.

## Chapter 119 — The Office Writes A Rule

**A mark that is off the wall is still in a book, and a rule on a table is read in four seconds by a stranger, and both of those are permanent.** **Hollis Ashe comes up the middle passage with a form**, introduces herself again, leaves her tally on the table, and says before anything else that her permit does not cover this, that she has no power over this room, and that what she has is a form with five lines and a man who saw something and wrote it in a book, and that neither of those is a power and both of them are permanent. The five lines are an inscription observed, a date, a condition, a limit, and **the person who keeps it** — and the clerk finds she had written *the holder's* into her own ledger on the second day of the week before while copying the four sentences out fair, and enters that she found it and did not look for it. **Nera Oduya strikes the wash rooms out of the form in nine seconds on her way past, and this time she does not give the reason, and when Bel Ordry asks her why she looks at him and he puts his hand down.** Then **Hollis Ashe reads the market form off the anteroom table, all of it, standing up, without being asked and without touching it, in about eleven seconds, and nobody in that room stops her** — and she says that the moment a form like that is left face up in a room where a person from another office is standing, it stops being yours, and that she did not take it off the table because it is not her table. **Dalla Sen says she chose to put it there and then says the thing the morning turns on: she was talking about her own comfort and not about a table, and she is not putting it away, because this boundary is going to be read from outside whether it is on a table or in a drawer, and the only thing it gets to choose is whether a stranger finds it in a room with people in it.** The mark is then asked about and answered with a condition, a limit and no name, read out of the clerk's hand, and Hollis Ashe fills in three of five lines and says what her office will do about the other two: **the date is the only lie on the form, and line five is worse empty than filled, because her clerk has already filled it once with a title — *the person who keeps the anteroom's terms* — and a title is worse than a name, because a name is a person and a title is a post, and a post can be asked for by a body that has never met the person who holds it.** **Renn Vale says she would rather be named and refused than titled and found, that she does not know which of the two she would survive, and that if a body on a road sends for a post this boundary will answer that there is nothing here to be sent for.** The board is not walked at the sixth bell, for the first time in twenty-two weeks, because there is a woman in the anteroom from another office, and the clerk says so in front of her. A man of twenty-two is fifty-four days in.

## Chapter 120 — The Survey Is Right

**The guild survey's finding is that this boundary's sector is stable, the survey is right, and being right is the worst thing that has happened to it in a month.** **Harlan Merrow brings the sheet himself**, says what he said last time — he recommended the charter and did not expect it granted — and then says the thing he has come to say: **he would rather it was not**, because a sector with nothing in it does not get a crew put in it again. He gives four findings and asks for all four to be entered in a clerk's hand as he says them. **One: the narrowing between the dip and the school door has moved three times, there are three wedge holes in it and they are not the same date, the total movement is between a finger and a hand, it is seasonal, and it is not a fault** — which is the answer to twenty-two weeks of three people deciding on purpose never to measure it. **Two: the doorframe is a bad repair on a sound wall, not a fault, and the timber the halfpenny sheet promised is in the store the survey is camped in, and he put it there, and he says he will do it again and would like it written that he enjoyed making it.** **Three: the school corner's floor is not a fault, it is a use — the first sentence anybody from his trade has said in this building that the air engineer has written down, and a surveyor telling this room that in a building this old the difference between a use and a fault is a matter of whose floor it is.** **Four: the sector is stable, nothing he surveyed would take a closure, and he would recommend in writing that the boundary be left alone for a season** — and then he says the two facts that belong in the same sheet: a stable sector is a sector nobody has a reason to fund, and he thought about it and put them together anyway, because the finding is the finding. **Bel Ordry's answer is the answer he gave in the twentieth week and he gives it before he is prompted: a record written by the people who live in a sector is not a survey — and this time he finishes it, with the unmeasured fill and the hair where a rule should be and the wedge up a quarter of an inch at a waist three people agreed never to measure, and then says the truth, that he is glad nothing here is a fault and has no use for the gladness, and that those two are in the same man.** The survey's sheet goes on the wall in the boundary's own hand, undated, with the objection written beside it. **The market route's answer goes out on a market day, carried by a man going that way anyway, two sentences with no name and no signature, no ring, a clerk's routing mark and nothing else — and the clerk says the charter's part out loud first, because a market day is not a delivery and the day it went would have been a different kind of act, and this boundary is not going to add a fifth kind of act to the pile on a Friday.** The board is walked: the boundary at a hundred and eighty-eight and a quarter, thirty-five in ten chapters and seventy-one since the keeper signed, thirteen entries, eleven nulls and one claim and one mark, the claim's condition still not met, the mark still on the board, and the count still refusing to head the column without a reason. The pot has been ten days for twenty-six days. **And the last line is Marek Venn's, understanding four days too late that stable is what a survey says about a thing it is not going to come back to, and that the crew will go, and that the only thing anybody here can do about it is to be glad, and that there is no chalk in his hand and nobody in the room said a word about any of it.** A man of twenty-two is fifty-five days and fifty-five nights in.

# Volume 03, Batch 0001 — delivered, Chapters 101–110

**Ten chapters in `chapters/volume-03/`, close third person on Marek Venn, no viewpoint shift.** The batch's delivery record is at the head of `state/batch-summary.md`; this section records only what a later phase must not contradict.

## What the batch established, in canon

- **The school corner's floor is wet and the water's course is now traced.** A stone has been taken out of the course between the anteroom's haunch and the school corner's floor and put back in lime about a finger wide; the bed joint runs out of the bottom of the patch, under the school corner's floor, six feet along the party wall, and surfaces at the low corner of a floor nine children have worn dished toward a door. **The seam's threads have not increased. The water is still two jars a day, maybe three, in the cook's separate numbers, never added to the pot, and neither jar has been sent anywhere.**
- **Nera Oduya was wrong in public** — she held that a course of dressed stone is what a course of dressed stone is for, and the course is not continuous — **and was not consoled, and the correction is entered in her own words beside her own words.**
- **The school corner is shut as a room.** A door, a wedge moved out of the school-door head, nothing bought, eleven minutes. **A new standing condition in Renn Vale's hand, with no day on it, a person who can stop it and a person who can be stopped. It is on the slate and not on the plan, and it is a room and not a route: it closes no corridor on any day of the week and the standing arrangement is untouched.** Four marks and a groove on the lintel above its shut mouth, read two ways by two people, answering nothing; **no mark was cut in the stone by anybody.**
- **The school is now in the room at the kitchen-line end**, which has a dished floor, a cold hearth, no mouth, the best light in the corridor and the worst floor in it, and no shelf. **Nine register boxes on its hearth stones. The two beech lengths stayed under the school store shelf. The plan's two parts are in Bel Ordry's coat. The school store now holds the shelf, the two beech props and the dowel, and nothing else.**
- **A Stonelight Compact route inspector has been in the building**, on a permit that does not cover her, working a line of chalked stations on the surface above the Cinder Steps that **has been there for nine seasons and that this boundary did not know about.** **Clause four of the charter binds the Cartwright office and does not cover her, and the hole is visible and is not fixed.**
- **A four-sentence procedure exists**, written by the keeper of the page, argued sentence by sentence with four objections before a mark was made, and **the third column of the plan left the building in a clerk's hand** — the first thing this Hearthhold has ever sent a stranger that a stranger could file. **It has been used once inside the boundary and misread in the reading, and the clerk entered that the clause dropped was the one about what a thing is and not what it is for, next to the anteroom's rating and the word *door*.**
- **A second sheet exists**, in two hands — the air engineer's and the cook's — **signed by the two people whose object of care it names and by nobody else.** It does not replace the charter, does not erase a clause, and does not touch clause nine. It names a fourth object of care: **a wall with water in it.** **The woman's covers were struck out of it in nine seconds, before anybody had explained it, for the second time in this book.** **It carries no date in the top corner, and the reason it has no date is written on it in the clerk's hand in the keeper's words: it does not record a day, the first sheet is dated, and the two are not the same kind of thing. The date in the top corner of the plan remains the only date on any object in this book.**
- **The elected keeper went up the middle passage at the end of the fifth day of the twentieth week** and **will not say when he will be back, and nobody in this building has said when he gets there.** His two true sentences are **read in a room in this building and are read at the fifth bell every day while he is gone, and the room decided nothing else about them.**
- **A boundary with no elected keeper in it runs perfectly well.** Three things want a keeper's word; all three have a substitute; not one substitute is a keeper.
- **A competent guild office closed the second gate's water-lock for a survey**, on a clearance, correctly, with a man in a hut. **Four households — two brothers, their sister, and one house that only carries — are behind it.** The first toll on a closed door is a form. The boundary sent nothing extra, sent the two jars' refusal out loud, **refused to put the keeper's ring on the paper that did go**, and sent no person.
- **The plan's first column has been recording a permitted occupancy rather than an actual one.** The anteroom's ten has been its permitted occupancy since the fifteenth week; the ten came off a **nine-hundred-year-old dowel** in the school store that nobody in this building has ever had read out to it; and **a room with nine children in it has no row on the plan at all.** This is a bookkeeping collision, it explains nothing, and **nobody in a room joined it to the dowel's provenance, the charter, the mouth, the four treads, the air engineer's theory, or the plate.**

## Numbers a later batch must not re-derive

- **The week runs Monday to Sunday. Volume 03 opened in the twentieth week. 101–105 the twentieth, 106–110 the twenty-first, 111–115 the twenty-second, 116–120 the twenty-third, and so on to 146–150 the twenty-ninth.** Each chapter sits on the matching day of its week. **The corridor is shut on the first, second and fourth days, open on the third, fifth and sixth, and the seventh day is not a crossing day; the school runs on the three open days.** So in Batch 0001 the corridor is shut in **101, 102, 104, 106, 107, 109** and open in **103, 105, 108, 110**, and **108 is a corridor-open day this batch closed.**
- **The school corner's closure is a room and not a route. No later batch may promote it into a route closure, and no chapter may put the school back in the school corner.**
- **One of the three open days is lost in Chapter 108 against a closure added on a day the arrangement had open. Nothing is paid back. Ilsa Norr has not been told which of the two is the independent one and has not asked, and no later batch may tell her.**
- **Wen Pask's count is 36 in Chapter 101 and 45 in Chapter 110, one a day, on the locked base of twenty-three on the fifth day of the seventeenth week.** It is his own count, kept by a clerk, in the column with no heading and in nothing else, and **it is not a register and may not date anything. It is also not the day-number register, and the two may never be confused, merged, or remarked upon as a coincidence.**
- **No day number may be attached to any in-batch event. The day-number register's highest value remains the forty-sixth day.** The only date on any object is the date in the top corner of the plan.
- **The spoken measure of elapsed weeks is a separate register**, is not re-derived, is not corrected, and may not be used to date anything. **From the twentieth week onward *twenty* is the week clock itself and is not available as drift.** A count that tracks the week clock is a different thing and is re-derivable: the school corner's mouth has been shut for twenty weeks in the twentieth week, and the plan has been transcribing the anteroom's count for twenty-one weeks.
- **No forward count of days or weeks on a courier.** The road is four days up the middle passage to the middle gate and then on past it, **and the second gate's distance is stated nowhere in Batch 0001.** The notice from the second gate has no date on it. **The batch's standing discovery about a notice with no date on it was neither repeated nor corrected.**
- **Crew hours: fifty-two and a half, unchanged since the fifth day of the nineteenth week.** The reason is now written down in a room in Renn Vale's words: the column is a quantity of asking and it moves when a person in a room asks the five of them for a work, with the terms out loud and a person named who can be told no. **It was offered twice in Batch 0001 and refused twice.**
- **Boundary hours: a hundred and seventeen and a quarter, plus thirty-six, = a hundred and fifty-three and a quarter.** The list is given **by the day it was done**: four, four, four, four, three in the twentieth week; four, four, four, three, two in the twenty-first. The running figures quoted at sixth bells in Chapters 102, 103, 106 and 108 are the day's increment and the total since the keeper signed, and all four are stated in the prose.
- **The board on surfaces is twelve entries: eleven nulls and one claim, nine in the ordinary column and three in the column with no heading.** The twelfth is a null in the ordinary column in Marek Venn's own left hand, put there because a woman told him where to put his hand. **The claim is still a claim and its condition has still not been met.**
- **The column with no heading holds a leg, a bundle, forty-five days and forty-five nights, a half hinge, a line refused, a page gone out of sight and a wage — and it is still unheaded, for the fourth consecutive batch.** It was itemised in full twice in Batch 0001 and referred to thereafter.
- **Wedges: seven sound and two dead sticks, unchanged in number.** One was **moved** from the school-door head into the shut school corner's door head, so the school door has two where it had three. **The third wedge at the waist is up a quarter of an inch and a bit and was not touched.**
- **The pot is at ten days and did not move and did not go up in Batch 0001.**
- **The brass survey rule has now said nothing for twelve weeks**, and nobody looked at it.

## Repairs applied to Batch 0001

An independent review was run against the delivered prose in the writing session and **the findings were repaired in the chapters, not recorded and deferred.** The repairs that changed a fact:

1. **The boundary's hours did not add.** The itemised list in Chapter 110 summed to thirty-six while the stated total was thirty-five, and three running figures in Chapters 102, 103 and 108 quoted a day's increment where the sentence read as a cumulative one. **The list is now thirty-six and the figure is a hundred and fifty-three and a quarter**, and the three running figures now give both the day's increment and the total since the keeper signed.
2. **Chapter 110 was dated to the wrong day of its week** — the second day instead of the fifth — inside the clerk's line about the new classroom's missing row. **It is the fifth day.**
3. **The keeper of the plan was given the wrong sex in a Mikka Hale line in Chapter 107** — the page in the coat is Bel Ordry's, a man, and he is in the room. **Corrected, and the correction makes the beat work: the cook insists the keeper be in the room for the sentence that lets a stranger hold a description of him.**
4. **Chapter 110's central sentence contradicted itself** — *all three of them were possible, and one of them was true and it was not any of them* — and the clause was copied from the card. **It is now *the true one was not any of them*.**
5. **The clerk was made to claim she wrote the plan's first column.** The plan is in Ilsa Norr's hand and then Mikka Hale's and the clerk has never held a pen over it; what she has done eleven times is **write down numbers that are said out loud in front of her**, which is a stronger reason why nobody ever asked what the numbers are numbers of, and the check now rests on that.
6. **The four-sentence procedure was printed twice as a bare specification block and the two printings did not match.** **It is now argued sentence by sentence in Chapter 105 with four objections before a mark was made, and in Chapter 109 Bel Ordry reads it off the clerk's copy, drops half the second sentence and the tail of the third, and Renn Vale notices** — and the two pages agree with each other and the reading did not. **The defect became the batch's toll gate in miniature.**
7. **Chapter 108 inverted the low end's water mechanism** — the corridor cannot stand in water from the second bell to the fifth, because the canon is the six minutes after the lever comes off. **Corrected, and the closure's reason now names the strokes between them, which is where every crossing in this book happens.**
8. **Two internal miscounts**: Chapter 104 said the corridor was shut for the third time in three days, and Chapter 103 put the sixth day of the week a day early. **Corrected.**
9. **Chapter 102 dated a Volume 02 event to the wrong week** — Renn Vale's party was stopped in the eleventh week, not the twelfth. **Corrected.**
10. **Chapter 106 said *twice this week* on the first day of the following week.** **Corrected to twice last week, and the count's *four weeks running* was corrected to *four batches running*, which is the unit Volume 02 counted in.**
11. **Two chapter references to Tams Quill's Monday exchange pointed at days that precede it.** **Both now point at Chapter 106's Monday.**
12. **The narration staged Nera Oduya leaving** in two places — *the person who is leaving*, *a departing woman's hand*. **The volume forbids staging her going and both are cut.** Her departure in the spring is canon; the narration no longer narrates it.
13. **Marek Venn announced and resolved his own departure** in the batch's last speech. **The outline forbids it and it pre-empted Chapter 147. Cut; the sentence is stronger without it.**
14. **The review page's blank was given two owners.** **It has one, and the prose no longer rosters her or asserts what she will not do.**
15. **The keeper's ring was described as a mark of ownership on a document leaving the building**, in a volume whose next power stage is called Marker. **It is now refused, in Chapter 109, out loud, with the reason given — a ring on a sheet is a mark on a sheet and a mark on a sheet is a thing a person can be found by — and the clerk enters that she told him he was going to be asked about it before he decided and did not.**
16. **Sixteen instances of meta language** — *this chapter*, *this volume*, *this batch*, *a volume ago*, *the reader saw it before he did* — were cut, and a 143-character clause repeated inside a single sentence was rewritten. Twelve were cut in the writing session; **four more were found by the independent review and cut in the repair pass**: *the whole of the next nine days is going to be about*, *that is how this room stages everything, and that is how this morning went* and *the reason the second one said nothing is the next chapter*, all three in Chapter 101, and *the time is the thing this chapter is for* in Chapter 103. **The batch now refers to days, weeks and the book only in the register the book already uses.**
17. **The batch was missing two required beats and both were supplied**: **the Marker refusal** in Chapter 109, with the clerk entering that she did not understand the second half of it, **and Nera Oduya being asked for a piece of work** in Chapter 110, which she does in four minutes and declines to do more of.
18. **Wen Pask was ten appearances of *a man of twenty-two* and was never named.** **He is named in Chapter 108, in his own action, carrying boxes across the waist.**
19. **Markup.** Every document quotation was normalised to the bold convention Volume 02 uses, and the nested spans that would have left dialogue unbolded mid-sentence were fixed. **The first pass over this claimed that every bold span in the batch was closed inside the paragraph that opens it, and that claim was false**: seven paragraphs carried a trailing over-close of two to three asterisks, in Chapters 101, 104, 107 (one each) and 109 and 110 (three each), and one in Chapter 109 held a nested span inside another. **All eight are fixed, and the claim is now true.** Every file is even, there is no unclosed span, no nested span and no run of three or more asterisks at the end of a paragraph.

## The two standing craft debts Batch 0001 left, for Batch 0002

1. **Staging: seven of ten chapters are unambiguously staged somewhere other than the anteroom bench, against a floor of eight.** The repair pass moved 101 over the line. **105, 106 and 109 are all built out of a document being read in one room, and 106 is the one that still needs it** — the three stations in Marek's round are three corners of the anteroom and not three rooms. **The fix is to give each of them a second location with a body in it.**
2. **The sixth-bell board read is the batch's punctuation and appears in every chapter.** It should be a beat in four chapters and the other six should close on something else.

**Two further measured figures, so the next batch can reproduce them:** with the bold markers stripped from paragraph openers, *The* counts 31, *Nobody* 10, *And* 41, *She* 11, *He* 16. **The bold section dividers are the batch's real connective tic and the plain-prefix method does not see them** — and the repair pass added thirteen of them on purpose, because bolding a divider is how a plain *The …* opening is brought back inside the count without cutting prose. **That is the lever, and Batch 0002 should use it rather than lose scenes to a counting rule.**

## How this batch was written, and what the review did to that

**A partial checkpoint draft of Chapters 101–108 existed in `workspace/volume-03/batch-0001/` when this batch was resumed, and it was replaced in full rather than continued.** The checkpoint commit is `db6555d novel: checkpoint batch-0001`. That draft stopped after Chapter 108, had never been reviewed, had updated no state file, and `state/current.md` still read *no chapter of Volume 03 exists* — so none of it had been accepted.

**The eight chapters were then rewritten rather than carried forward, and the reason given at the time was in the method rather than in the quality of either version.** A batch is one voice, one set of numbers, one calendar and one argument; the tenth chapter is the batch's aftermath and has to answer the ninth, and a reviewed tenth cannot be hung on an unreviewed ninth. The replacement was reviewed as a whole — nineteen findings, nineteen repairs, all of them in the chapters — and the numbers in this batch, in `state/batch-summary.md` and in `state/current.md` are the replacement's.

**That decision was then overturned by the independent review, and this paragraph is the record of how.** The review found that the replacement had not unified the batch but split it: **Chapters 103, 105, 109 and 110 were genuine prose and 101, 106 and 107 had been turned into outline and ledger voice**, with dialogue share falling in 101 from 55 per cent to 29, in 106 to 25 and in 107's document fight reduced to two position labels. **The justification did not hold, and the fix was to put the checkpointed dramatised prose back into the three chapters that lost the most, keeping the replacement's prose wherever it was genuinely stronger and keeping every one of the nineteen repairs.**

**So the checkpoint draft is now partly back in the manuscript, and the earlier claim that nothing was left of it anywhere is false and is withdrawn.** What came back is scene material, not numbers: **the discovery staged in the room's four steps and Ilsa Norr sitting down on the floor with the nine of them; Jo Verrick's *none of us looked at it, because a floor in a school is a floor*; the air engineer's crawl along the wall and *it is a line and not a hole*; her wrong drain theory and Jo's six minutes; the cook striking *nuisance* and putting her own name on the real sentence; and the cap-it scene** — which matters more than any of the rest, because it carries the batch's power movement. What did **not** come back is anything arithmetic: the checkpoint's wrong hour totals, its *ninth day* for the crew's column, its *twice this week*, and its five-things-at-the-fifth-bell read all stay out, and every figure in this batch remains the replacement's.

**Three things the repair pass found that the writing session had missed, and all three are load-bearing:**

- **The cap-it scene is the only place in the batch where Marek Venn says out loud that he has nothing left but the one thing he cannot do twice.** The prompt requires it and Chapter 109's Marker refusal only answers it. **Without Chapter 101 the batch refused the non-ordinary thing without ever having tried the ordinary one, and the arc in Chapter 109 had no first half.** It is restored, and the clerk's entry that she did not understand it and is not going to guess in a book what it means is restored with it. **Chapter 109's version is not a duplicate: it is four days later, about the anteroom frame, and about the one thing that is not a reading.** Renn Vale's *that is the fourth time this building has written down a person saying they do not understand something, and it is the first time it has been the clerk* is what keeps the two apart.
- **Chapter 107 gave the second sheet a date in the top corner, which the batch's own calendar forbids.** The rule is that the only date on any object is the date in the top corner of the plan, and four state files had copied the error forward. **Bel Ordry now refuses the date out loud in the room** — a page with a date in the top corner is a record of what a building was doing on a day, he has one date in this building and it means *as at*, and a sheet with no date on it says *now* — **and the reason is written on the sheet in the clerk's hand in his words.** The plan's date is once again the only date in the building.
- **The crew's hours were offered twice and refused twice, and only one refusal was on the page.** Renn Vale says in Chapter 102 that she has said no to Marek *twice in two days* and that the second was worse because he expected the first — which puts the first refusal on the twentieth week's first day. **It is restored to Chapter 101**, where it belongs in the sequence, immediately after the cap-it refusal and before the sentence about the one thing he cannot do twice: fix refused, then resource refused, then the thing that is left. Chapter 106's *offered twice last week* is then exact, and the offer Renn Vale refers to in Chapter 101 as *on Friday* is the one on the fifth day of the nineteenth week, which is the day the column last moved.

**Two things the review found in the state files and one it found in the markup**, all now repaired and all recorded above: the *a Monday* that `chapter-summaries.md` asserted for Chapter 101 and the prose had dropped (**the prose has it back, and the state file is now true rather than changed**), the seven trailing `**` over-closes, and the false claim in this repository's own `.done` that every bold span was closed.
