# Volume 04, Batch 0005 — delivered, Chapters 181–185

**Five chapters in `chapters/volume-04/`, close third person on Marek Venn, no viewpoint shift anywhere in the batch, and the protagonist named with interior life in five of five.** The batch's delivery record is at the head of `state/batch-summary.md`; this section records only what a later phase must not contradict.

## What the batch established, in canon

**The guild defector's crew exists and came up the middle passage on foot, and no scene is on a road.** Six people came: five who carry and one who does not, and the one who does not is **Nella Bray, a clerk at a counter at the middle gate, four days up the middle passage, who gave this building her name on the second day of the thirty-fifth week after six weeks in which only her hand was known here.** The foreman is **Emrys Callow, forty-one, shoring, nine years, who held a cleared-risk post-holder's bond in this district until he put it in a hand and did not go back for it, and who said in a room that a man who is not disappointed is not the same as a man who is right before he said it.** They are **not converted and not forgiven.** They will not carry for a man whose name is on two lines of a form, the same post-holder's name in both, and the five of them were on neither line, and when a load came down wrong in the thirty-first week of last year the figure in the district book was a man who was not standing in the passage. They came down for that, and because a store four days up the passage gave forty-one pieces of beech to a boundary and a keeper who can say no. **They were never converted to this boundary's argument and never forgiven by it in this batch, and nothing in these five chapters turns them into collaborators, saints, martyrs or converts.**

**The two reasons not to trust are both true and they are not the same reason, and that is the batch's spine.**
- **The defector crew and the clerk's reason for not trusting this boundary: a number.** Nella Bray cannot find out how many people are in it. Every instrument that reaches her counter about a building is a number of what a building is *permitted*, and in nineteen years she has never been sent one that is a number of what is in it, and she would not have noticed the difference until Bel Ordry put a page on a table beside a stranger's paper on the fourth day of the thirty-fourth week and said out loud that ours is the worst page in the district. **Bel Ordry declined to defend his own page and said the reason first**, and the clerk entered it.
- **This boundary's reason for not trusting them: a name on a line.** Their post-holder's name is in both lines of a form that turned ordinary ground into a working road, and the clerk who filled it in correctly is standing in the room, and if this boundary works with this crew the boundary's work goes under that line too.
- Bel Ordry's own objection to waiting: if the crew stand on a landing another week with nothing to do and no pay, they will take the next work that comes, and the next work comes under a line with a name on it. **Callow said he had no answer to that and asked for it to be entered.**

**Nella Bray's own account of herself, given in her own mouth and not as a defence:** she filled in two lines on a form in the ordinary course of an ordinary morning and did not know what the section under them was for and was not asked, and six weeks ago she took this boundary's form off its board and the rule said the form was wrong. She has been right about both and asked the room to notice what that does to a person. **She is not a hero, does not want to be one, and is doing her job.** Renn Vale refused to hand her a sentence to say about herself.

**The Compact's schedule turns a safe decision into a public concession, and the refusal available is the standing one.** The schedule's first column is **a day of the week and it is a fifth day** — tomorrow when it was put on the table on the fourth day of the thirty-fifth week, and it has been a fifth day since it was printed. Its second column is headed for the person who will be present and is empty against three rooms, two of them struck before the sheet ever reached this room, and the third is the room at the kitchen-line end, not struck. **Nobody wrote a name in it and the covering was struck elsewhere for the second time in six weeks and the clerk entered that she will find out nothing and ask nothing, which is the ninth such entry and is not a number she reads out.** The cheap thing was **proposed in a room by the person with the authority over the air** — keep the day, Nera Oduya's name in the second column, the third room empty, three rooms looked at, nobody hurt, the sheet goes back with a mark on it that says this boundary attended — **and it was correct, and it was entered as proposed and not adopted, and it is the only name this boundary has put in any column in thirty-five weeks and somebody else can read it.** Her reason was that the sentence she wrote a fortnight ago says she will not certify a building that has said no to nothing, and this boundary has said three yeses and no no, and she is not waiting to be asked because a condition nobody asks about is a condition that is only hers. **The half against the concession came from the most competent possible mouth: Nella Bray, who does this work for a living, that not answering a schedule is an answer, it goes in somebody's book, the somebody is not in this room, and the sentence that goes in it will be that this boundary was scheduled and did not attend, and that sentence will be true.**

**And the turn of the chapter is that this boundary neither refused the schedule nor accepted it.** **Dalla Sen refused to write the word *refused* in the space where a reason goes**, on Pettin Rahl's standing sentence — *a regime is not a threat. It is a schedule. And a thing which is scheduled is not a thing that is refused* — **and she entered that she knew what Bel Ordry had said about a visitor's sentence and used it anyway. This boundary has not refused a schedule. It has declined to answer one, and only one of those two acts is a thing an office can act on.** Bel Ordry then said out loud that he put that sentence in this building's book thirty-five weeks ago, that it is the best sentence anybody has brought into this room, and that a room with a good sentence in its book from outside is one step away from having a policy handed to it, and that he wrote the step down.

**The schedule's day came and went. On the sixth day of the thirty-fifth week — a market Saturday — the clerk entered that yesterday was a fifth day, that the corridor was open, that nine children were in a room that is not shut, that a man was expected to walk in and look at three rooms, and that he did not come. Nobody in this building knows what an office does on a Saturday when a boundary does not attend.** The clerk entered what a counter does on a Saturday as a fact about counters and not a finding, and entered that she is not pleased about it, because a boundary that is pleased about a day nothing happened on is a boundary that has begun to want days nothing happens. **This is unresolved and must not be resolved in Batch 0006 without its own chapter.**

**The Warden's first numbered thing was obeyed on the next open morning and a keeper turned an obedience into a decision.** The room at the kitchen-line end was **emptied at the second bell on the third day of the thirty-fifth week** — the next open morning after the instruction was read in — **last one first, the four rooms held as one space, and the clerk entered the compliance with the hour and not with the day.** **At the third bell Ilsa Norr decided the nine go back in at the fourth**, and gave the reason out loud before anybody could enter it: that room has been emptied twice in ten days, once by a woman striking it out of a printed sheet in nine seconds in the twenty-ninth week and once by a number in a numbered list, and a thing that can be emptied twice by two documents is a thing that is being emptied, and the woman who empties it is not in either document and is the only part of the emptying this building has ever been able to trust. Her half against, in the space where a reason goes: nine children beside a two-finger gap four people in this building cannot describe, and she has said the room is not to be used every day and today she said the opposite with the same mouth. **The room is therefore used and is not shut, and the difference is still the one the woman who keeps the corridor gave in Chapter 179.** The keeper wrote the only line in any document this batch that anybody wrote, in the third column, in her own hand, and the clerk read it back and the keeper read it back against her own mouth and the two were the same.

**The school ran on all three open days — the thirty-third, thirty-fourth and thirty-fifth mornings — in the room at the kitchen-line end and nowhere else. It did not run on the two shut days and lost nothing. The school corner is open and is not used. No school day was restored and no closure was removed. On the fifth day of the thirty-fifth week the nine were in that room on purpose, on the day in the schedule's first column, because a keeper who empties a room of nine children because of a sheet on it has let the sheet pick the day.**

**A fact from the party wall changed the arithmetic, and it was a fact about a piece of timber and about two faces of one wall.** On the fifth day of the thirty-fifth week **Jo Verrick went round to the far side of the party wall for the first time since she came into this building and found the same join is a finger wide on the anteroom side and two fingers on the kitchen-line side** — one face twice the other, and she has been reporting one of them for a week as though it were the join. She did not put the folding rule in it. **Marek Venn's three facts, in the order he was sure of them: the wall is not moving; the bad repair is only on one face, because it was put on the face that gets looked at, and it has let go on the face it was put on, and on this face the join has opened about half as far; and the third shore has lost about a finger of its length at the head with its foot unmoved, because there is no spreader under the head of that sill, which is the answer Warden-Officer Karr gave out loud on the first day of the thirty-fifth week and was right about.** **Nobody acted on Karr's answer for four days**, which is the true span: the six shores went up on the first day of the thirty-fifth week, a Monday, and the third shore came out on the fifth day, a Friday. Iven Tallo owned that in a room and asked for no reason to be given him.

**The third shore came out in eleven minutes, and the wall now has five and a half where the district's book says six.** **Leena Orr read it** — she is the only person in this building whose whole trade is reading a thing that is already built, and a shore is one — and her reading is that the head is a finger shorter, the foot has not moved, the mark in the flag is where the foot was, and the head is being crushed for want of a spreader, an eighth of an inch at a time, **and that this is a fault in the ground and not in the timber.** Iven Tallo's sentence from Monday — *a shore with no foot plate crushes its own mark into a floor and takes the floor with it when it lets go* — was read against her two figures and **the two were the same fact said from opposite ends, and the clerk entered that **the carpenter's sentence of four days ago** named the head of that shore in the wrong half of its own sentence.** **The finding entered: five and a half on that wall; the figure in the district book is not corrected by this boundary and is not contradicted by it, because those are two different acts and a clerk who does both at once is making a document.** Emrys Callow will carry the word up the passage himself, because the timber is the district's and the man who chose it should hear it from the crew that found it.

**The shore came out on a Friday morning with nine children in the room on the other side of the wall, and the room knew it and did it anyway.** Mero Senn said the plan was a good plan and the room said so out loud before he said what was wrong with it: **a good plan that depends on nine children being in a room on the other side of a wall while a piece of timber comes out of it.** Renn Vale gave the half against waiting herself, because the third shore has lost a finger of its length in four days and nobody looked, **and Mero Senn stated the bind nobody had stated — the work is only reachable on an open corridor morning, the corridor is shut two days in seven, and the choice was between a morning with nine children next to the wall and no morning at all.** **Ilsa Norr said she is not going to be one of the two people who agrees that the wall can take it**, that she will be in the room with the nine and not within reach of the anteroom, and that she wants it entered that **she decided**, because in four days somebody is going to read that a wall was worked on while nine children were in the next room and want to know who decided. **Renn Vale emptied the anteroom for the length of the work and said its terms first, and entered that a room's rating is a number said to a page and is not a count of the people who cross it — a distinction this boundary has kept for thirty-five weeks and which a woman who keeps a corridor has now said out loud for the first time.**

**The faultform's link is now watched, and not by Marek, and the watcher is a person who can be told to stop.** **The terms between the two crews are six and were written by Dalla Sen on the sixth day of the thirty-fifth week and read back by Emrys Callow, who found nothing to change:** five work the common landing side; the kitchen-line side is not worked and not entered; every person whose hands go on that wall says out loud in a room what they are holding and what stops it; nobody is sent to the low end and the page there stays as it is; nobody goes through the wall and nothing goes into the line of nothing in it; **the person who watches that line is somebody who is not the man who built anything on that wall and not the man who found it, and that person can be told to stop by a person in a room**; none of it goes on the board. **The name in the fifth is left empty on purpose, and the reason is entered: the room already knows who keeps the corridor, and a name in a column in this building is a thing on a column, and a thing on a column is a thing somebody can be sent for.**

**And the answer to a carpenter's question that stood unanswered for two weeks is now in the book, and it is Renn Vale's seventh thing.** On the fifth day of the thirty-third week a woman asked what a person in this building is supposed to do when a piece of beech lets go and answered her own question — it has to be a person who is not the man who built it — **and Iven Tallo asked the next question, which is who that person is, and nobody answered him, and he has now said out loud that he had the answer and held it for two weeks because holding it was easier than handing it over.** His answer: **a person who is not the man who built it, not the man who found it, and who can be told to stop.** Renn Vale took it. She will watch the line at the first bell on open days and the second bell on shut days, and say what she can hear out loud in a room, and not put a rule in it and not put her hand in it and not know what it is about and not pretend to. **Who stops her: Ilsa Norr, the physician, and a room, in that order, and none of the three has to give her a reason and she does not have to accept one.** Bel Ordry's objection is that a woman who decides to take a seventh thing onto herself has become a post, and a post is a thing a person can be moved out of, and there is no page in this building where anybody's hours go. **Her reason, asked for by a stranger and not by the room: the room behind that wall is the room nine children are taught in, and there is no version of her that hears a sound in that wall and waits to be asked.**

**Talla Roke returned deliberately, in one chapter, on her own terms, and not a rescue and not a takeover.** She is in **Chapter 185 only**. **Pell Roke is in none of the five chapters and no chapter puts the two of them in the same room.** She came because she heard on a road that a piece of timber came out of a wall on a Friday morning and because on the fifth day of the thirty-third week she asked a question in this room that a carpenter then asked a better one after. **She has got an answer on a road for two weeks and says it is wrong:** a person who can be told to stop is a person somebody can stop, and the somebody is whoever is holding the pen, and the person holding the pen in this building is a woman who has not written the word *refused* once in a book in six weeks. **Her half against, and the sharpest sentence in the batch: two people can stop you and a room can stop you, and she is not counting the room, because a room is not standing anywhere at the moment that wall does the thing it has been doing — and the two of them will be on the other side of nine children.** The two are Ilsa Norr and the physician; a room is third in that order and can also stop her. **She also now says the word by name and says where her knowledge comes from: the clerk has not written the word *refused* in a book in six weeks, and she knows that from a form and not from the clerk, because the second column of the schedule was empty when it came off the press. She does not claim to have read anybody's book, and no instrument in this building leaves it.** Renn Vale gave the other half and refused to let a new thing be folded into the carpenter's unanswered sentence about a word, which **is still unanswered and is not re-argued.**

**A true fact is going up the middle passage on somebody else's day, and the cost of that is recorded.** The message is a piece of seasoned shore four years old that has lost about a finger of its length at the head, taken out in eleven minutes, five and a half on that wall, and the district's figure neither corrected nor contradicted by this boundary. Bel Ordry's half against: a true fact about a wall that four people in a district know and nobody has written down is a thing that kills somebody in a year, and the only road a fact takes into a district's book is somebody else's paper, and somebody else's paper has a day in it and a column in it. **Renn Vale: send it, because if this boundary holds it back and the man who chose the wood finds it out from a book in a district, this boundary has learned to hold things back from offices, and that is the first sentence of a very short road to a room with a name over the door.** **The clerk writes the day of the week and not the date, on purpose, so that a person in a year can tell the difference between a message and a form** — the plan's top-corner date is the only date available to this building on any instrument and it does not go on this. **The escalation's moral question is now sharper and is not resolved: a boundary that has refused nothing was scheduled, did not answer, and is now sending a true fact up a passage to an office that will answer with a document that has a day in it and a column in it.**

**A third refusal of a nineteenth board entry, with a third and new reason.** The terms between two crews are not going on the board, and the reason is new and is the third distinct shape: **a brace, a store and a plan are things in this building that a person in this building can be asked about, and a term between two crews is not a thing in this building, it is a thing two rooms agreed about, and the day one of those rooms is not in this building any more the term is still on here with nobody left to ask.** Tams Quill gave no reason for the column with nothing over the top of it in any of the five chapters, nothing was manufactured, and **no batch ordinal is restated anywhere in 181–185.**

**What Batch 0005 did not do.** It did not make the comparison or say the sentence that ends it; that is 197's. It did not resolve the void, kill the faultform, name it, measure it, tool it, put a hand or a tool or a tape into it, or go through it. **The line in the party wall is still the width of two fingers on the kitchen-line side, unwatched until Saturday, unmeasured, unnamed, and not joined to the dowel, the charter, the mouth, the four treads, the ninth room, the low end, the air engineer's theory, her twelfth-week name or the plate.** It did not restore a school day or remove a closure. It did not meet Nera's first or second condition, and **nobody asked her about either one in five chapters, and the clerk entered that she noticed herself not asking for the fourth time in a fortnight.** It did not ask the crew for a sixth piece of work, and the reasons are morning-specific in all five days. It did not put a person on the board, did not strike anything out of any document, did not send anybody anywhere, did not approach the review page, did not cut a mark in the stone anywhere in this building, did not raise the capacity of any room, did not resolve the carpenter's word-question, did not resolve who owns a wall, did not stage Nera going — **the going was not raised in this batch at all, which is a choice and not an oversight** — and did not name the One-Seat or Morrowlight or bring Warden-Officer Karr or Cassian Rook into a room.

## Numbers this batch fixed, delivered, and does not want re-derived

- **The week runs Monday to Sunday. 181–185 are the second through sixth days of the thirty-fifth week, Tuesday to Saturday.** The corridor is **shut in 181 and 183 and open in 182, 184 and 185.** The seventh day is not a crossing day and no chapter used it. **The school ran in 182, 184 and 185, for the thirty-third, thirty-fourth and thirty-fifth mornings, in the room at the kitchen-line end and nowhere else.**
- **Wen Pask is 116, 117, 118, 119 and 120 across the five chapters, one a day, every one on the page in the right chapter, and read at the sixth bell in 181, 184 and 185 — in 182 the clerk does not read the day's figures at all and says so in one line, and in 183 they are entered and not read.** It is his own count, kept by a clerk, in the column with nothing over the top of it and in nothing else; it is not a register, it dates nothing, it is not the day-number register, and the two may never be confused or remarked upon as a coincidence. It is at one hundred and twenty, it is not going to be one hundred and twenty-one, and **the roundness of one hundred and twenty was noticed in the room by Tams Quill and answered by the clerk out loud — it is a number of days and it is not a number of anything — and it was not made into anything else.** The count line's own weeks-running clause reads **twenty-five, twenty-six, twenty-seven, twenty-eight and twenty-nine** across 181–185, continuing the twenty-four in 180. **Nothing was made of any of the five figures by anybody else.**
- **No day number is attached to any in-batch event and the day-number register's highest value remains the forty-sixth day.** The only date on any object is the date in the top corner of the plan, and **the clerk deliberately wrote the day of the week and not the date on the message going up the passage, and said why, and the plan's top-corner date did not go on it.** The Compact's *date observed* lie exception was not used.
- **No forward count of days or weeks is put on anybody.** The road is four days up the middle passage to the middle gate and forty days on from the top of it to the guild file; **the second gate carries no figure in this batch.** Callow's *four days* of work is a foreman's own figure about his own five, stated in a room and entered as his and not this boundary's, and it is a term of work and not a count of a road.
- **The spoken measure of elapsed weeks is a separate register**, is not re-derived, is not corrected and was not used to date anything. The bracketed references in this batch are *in a fortnight* (185, two refusals in a fortnight), *two weeks* (185, the carpenter's silence), *ten days* (182, the room emptied twice in ten days; 179's *a week* stands), ***four days* (182 and 184, the Monday instruction and the third shore; this was delivered as *nine days* in five places and is corrected — see the Batch 0005 repair record below), *four days* (183, the page in the coat on the table), *twelve days* (184, the printed schedule down the passage) and *four days* (182, Marek's line about asking to be asked, which is a Saturday)**, *nine weeks* (182, a physician's weeks spent saying a sentence, **which is not his tenure** — see below), *six weeks* (181, the form), *three days* (181, the drawing) and *two days* (181, the light on the flags). **From the thirtieth week onward *thirty* is the week clock itself and was not used as drift.**
- **Crew: seventy-one, unmoved, and no sixth asking in any of the five days.** Five morning-specific reasons, all in the book and all different: 181, six strangers came in and asked for nothing, and asking five people to carry a work in front of six strangers who have not said whether they will stand next to them is asking them to be looked at; 182, a room was deciding whether nine children go back into a room; 183, the cheapest thing in the room was put on the table by the person with the authority over the air and a second thing by a woman who does that work for a living; 184, a wall gave a number and a room has to decide what to do with a number first; 185, a room wrote six terms with a space in the fifth and the clerk refused to fill it. **Walking paper in was not asking and a crew arriving from outside was not asking.**
- **Boundary hours: base 117.25 constant, the day's list chosen by day and stated by day, and it sums.** **181 three, 182 two, 183 two, 184 four, 185 three = fourteen.** Running since the keeper signed **246, 248, 250, 254, 257**, continuing from 243. Totals on the constant base of 117.25 of **363.25, 365.25, 367.25, 371.25, 374.25**. **Both columns reconcile and the counter is carried at seventeen and is not re-derived.** The day's increment and the total are on the page in all five chapters; **read out loud in 181, 184 and 185, and entered and not read in 182 and 183**, each with a distinct morning-specific reason: 182, nine children went back through a door in this building for the first time in a fortnight; 183, a room spent the morning deciding what it was not going to answer.
- **Board: eighteen entries, nine ordinary and nine in the column with nothing over the top of it. No nineteenth entry was earned.** Three refused candidates in three weeks, all with reasons, and the third reason is new: a printed map, a Warden crew's count, and **the terms between two crews.** The board is walked in **181, 182, 184 and 185** — four chapters, which is one more than the two-or-three the previous prompt allowed and is recorded here as a deliberate change, because three of the four walks are a refusal rather than a reading and the fourth is the walk that carries the roundness beat. It is passed over in **183** with a reason. **No chapter closes on the board.**
- **Brass survey rule silent twenty-six weeks and the wrapped plate unopened thirty-five through the whole batch**, on the ninth-week origin `outline/volume-04.md` fixes. Chapter 150's sixteen was not quoted and no closed-chapter quote was made. Neither instrument was in a room in any of the five chapters.
- **Scarcity, worse, as contracted.** **The pot is eight days in 181, 182 and 183 and seven in 184 and 185.** The seam gave nothing on Monday and Tuesday, **one on the Thursday of the thirty-fifth week and not two**, and a cook said the arithmetic out loud in the middle of a stranger's work and in the middle of a morning's argument and would not say the word, and the clerk entered the two next to each other with nothing between them and did not write the word beside either. **The seam is at four threads. Four households at a second gate have nothing and no figure is attached to that gate by anybody.** The wall's reading is a quarter of an inch and it is the same as eleven, and the bed under the ninth hearth stone is unmentioned this batch and uncaused, and the clerk's standing refusal to write what caused either stands.
- **Capacity unchanged: ten including one litter for no more than two hours, said in 181, 182, 183 and 184 and not changed in any of them, and the brace still redistributes and never adds.** No chapter in this batch restates it at 185 and that is a change of pattern and not a change in the figure.
- **The hands.** Right hand lost for fine control, unrecovered. **The left hand did not close, was used once and coarsely on the head of the fourth shore in 184, and was not used for or against anybody.** The load echo is not named in this batch. **The marker is spent, the Reader reading is not repeatable, the Chapter 99 claim's condition is unmet, no mark was cut in the stone anywhere in this building, and no stage beyond the standing Bracer advanced and no panel of any kind appears in five chapters.**
- **Four strict read-against-original comparisons in five chapters, with the object varied each time, a second person in each, and a room-accepted reason in each: 181, a slate of six names taken from a stranger's mouth and read back by Jo Verrick and then by the stranger herself; 182, the keeper's own line in the third column, read out of the clerk's book and read back against her own mouth by the woman who wrote it; 183, the air engineer's concession sentence, written out at her own request and read back to her; 184, Iven Tallo's Monday sentence read against Leena Orr's two figures; 185, the six terms read back by Emrys Callow against what the clerk said with her mouth.** **The brace's condition and the four terms of the fourth asking were not used at all in this batch, so neither is near its cap. The fifth of the anteroom's six terms is named in 181, 182 and 183 as a term among six and is never read out and never compared; the *fifth of the six* in Chapter 185 is the fifth of the crews' terms and is a different document.**

## Repairs applied in a review-fix phase, after Batch 0005's independent review

**Volume 04 Batch 0005 was reviewed by a phase this writer did not control. All five chapters were revised in place. Every plot fact, figure, date, guardrail and hand-off above stands and has been re-verified against the repaired files. What changed is that two errors had been promoted into this file and into `state/current.md` as canon, and that the batch's own review record made six measurable claims that do not survive its own method. Nothing was restarted, no beat was moved, and the batch's ending is unchanged.**

- **The Monday-to-Friday span is four days and it is now four days everywhere.** Delivered as *nine days* in 182:85, 184:35, 184:45, 184:59 and 184:83, and promoted into this file and into `state/current.md`. **A later phase must not write nine and must not re-derive this.**
- **The page in the coat on the table is four days old in 181 and six in 183**, delivered as nine in 181:77, 183:7 and 183:45. The schedule down the passage is **twelve** days old in 184, delivered as five weeks. **Marek's own line about asking to be asked is a Saturday**, delivered as nine days ago in 182:43; the line is his in Chapter 178, the sixth day of the thirty-fourth week.
- **The day-of-week column was wrong in six places** and is now consistent with `state/current.md`'s calendar: 181 opens on the second day and Callow now says the second day; 182's Bel Ordry now says the room is to be used again on a **fifth** day, which is what the corridor rule and his own next line require; 182's Callow crew came up the nine steps on **Tuesday** and the printed schedule came down the passage on **Tuesday**; 184's Bel Ordry asked two mornings ago and the hours have been argued for two mornings.
- **181 counted seven strangers where six came up the steps**, and 181's Dalla Sen was speaking *Say your own* and the line was attributed to Callow. Both corrected.
- **185 contradicted itself on the count line's weeks clause** — twenty-five in one paragraph, twenty-nine six paragraphs later. Twenty-five is 181's figure. **It is twenty-nine in 185 and in every state file.**
- **Nera Oduya is twenty-eight and is not a counter clerk.** The thesis paragraph of 183 had her claiming nineteen years at a counter, which is **Nella Bray's** credential, given to her thirty lines earlier in 181. **Her credential is now her own trade: nine rooms of this Hearthhold, since she was nineteen, and not one of the nine has ever said no.** **Nella Bray's nineteen years is hers alone and no later phase may give it to anybody else.**
- **The *this book* clock was inside a character's mouth twice** (185:73, 185:77) and is now *the weeks we have been standing in it* and *in this room*. The narrator may still say *this book*; a person may not.
- **Chapter 185's sharpest sentence was also its weakest.** *That word* had no antecedent, and *I have read that book on a road* asserted access to an instrument that never leaves this building. **She now names the word — *refused* — and gets her knowledge from a form: the second column of the schedule was empty when it came off the press.** The argument is unchanged and the sentence is now the strongest thing in the batch rather than the weakest, and `state/current.md`'s claim that it is the sharpest sentence is earned.
- **Chapter 185's courier said *two people* where the room had named three stoppers.** **She is now explicit that she is not counting the room, and why: a room is not standing anywhere at the moment that wall does the thing.** Ilsa Norr and the physician are the two; a room is third.
- **Chapter 182's closing ledger duplicated Chapter 179's keeper line in twenty-eight identical words**, the same woman in the same room, and the closing ledger paragraph ran in one fixed shape in four of five chapters. **Both closed. 182 and 183 now close on the room, and the ledger runs in three shapes across the five.**
- **Two chapter-level motivation defects are closed and neither changed a plot point.** **184**: the work is only reachable on an open corridor day, and Mero Senn now says so — the corridor is shut two days in seven, and the choice was between a morning with nine children next to the wall and no morning at all. **183**: the concession rested on a premise Chapter 182 had demolished, and Bel Ordry now says that in the room; Nera Oduya answers that she is asking the keeper to be in the building, not to empty it, and picked the request that costs nothing.
- **Six sentences of ninety words or more are zero.** Six remained as delivered and **all six were speech, not narration**, which the batch's own record reported as the opposite. Two are now split in place, 181's and 184's, and the figures are in the review record with the method.
- **The ritual moved from dialogue into narration and was not broken.** *Half against / the other half / the half of that* ran twenty-four times in five chapters, always in the same shape and always followed by an entry. **It is now twenty-two, in the same five mouths, with the most mechanical instances re-shaped and no beat removed.** The half against remains canon and must be in every chapter; what is retired is opening a speech with the same four words.
- **The manuscript's real filler is the tag *said*.** It ran at 35, 34, 48, 39 and 59 lines per chapter as a bare attribution between consecutive speech paragraphs. **Roughly thirty attributions across the five chapters were converted into a small physical beat, a location, or a different verb, and the remaining ones are short interjections where a bare tag is correct English. The method and the counted figures are in the review record.**
- **One unattributed fully-bold one-line paragraph in 185** — the batch's only one, and its only rule-1 blemish — **is now attributed and is no longer the retired bare-imperative shape.**
- **The batch's own review record is corrected where it was wrong**, in six places, with the method beside each figure. **`workspace/volume-04/batch-0006/PROMPT.md` no longer carries the false versions as binding craft baseline.**

**What a later phase must not do with any of this.** Do not re-derive the four days, the four days, the six days, the twelve days, the six days or the six weeks. Do not re-derive Wen Pask's five figures, the boundary's five day-increments, the crew's seventy-one, the board's eighteen or the count's weeks clause. **Do not re-derive anything this file already fixes.**

## Open hand-off to Batch 0006 (Chapters 186–192)

The comparison is owed and is not made, and the room that can hear it still does not exist. The schedule's day came and went unanswered and nobody knows what an office does about that. A true fact about a piece of timber is going up the middle passage on somebody else's day and the answer will have a day in it and a column in it. Six people came down a passage with two true and different reasons for not trusting this boundary and neither crew has converted or been forgiven. A wall with five and a half shores where a district's book says six, a brace of a school's own beech pushing on it from the other side, a bad repair on one face only, and a line of nothing about two fingers wide on the other face that is now watched by a woman who can be told to stop by three people and who is not a post and has no page. A keeper with nine children in a room that is not shut and is emptied when a document says so and filled when she says so. A crew that cannot be paid out of a pot at seven days. A clerk who will not write the word *refused*. A man who keeps a page who has admitted he wrote a step toward a policy and has not said which step. A carpenter who held an answer for two weeks and handed it over and has a piece of paper four and a half days up a road with a route-holder's name in the second line and nothing in the second line, and nobody asked him for a second time. And a pot at seven, four households with nothing and no figure, the low end, the ninth room, the four treads, the market form, the plate, the brass rule, the four words about who owns a wall, the carpenter's word-question, and the air engineer's two unmet conditions and a theory and a name that nobody has asked about.

# Batch 0004's movement, recorded at the end of Chapters 131–140

*This section is the Batch 0004 record and supersedes nothing above it; the Batch 0003 record above is left standing because it is what the twenty-fourth and twenty-fifth weeks did.*

### Marek Venn

- **Named in ten of ten chapters, with interior life in ten of ten — and this line was false when the writing session wrote it.** The batch was contracted to close third person on him throughout and he was named in seven chapters on delivery: absent from 135, 136 and 137. **A review run outside the writing session found it, and the writing session's own review had not, because that review measures paragraphs, openers, markup, staging and length and had never measured viewpoint presence.** Both absences were repaired with a beat each rather than by rewriting a chapter: he is against the anteroom wall through Chapter 135, listening to a man from four days up a passage describe accurately the thing he did in the twenty-fourth week; and he is in the room for all of Chapter 136, with his hand flat on the back of the bench when a physician says that a promise about a place where nobody can stand is a lie told in a column. He was already present and unnamed in Chapter 137 and is now named once. **A viewpoint-presence check is now part of the craft baseline and a later batch may not certify this figure without measuring it.** His beats, in order: the ordinary fact that a room with nobody's condition on it is a room nobody is watching, and a room nobody is watching finds out about itself from a stranger; the asking in Chapter 132 includes him and he is one of the two who can be asked, and he notices that he was glad to be asked, which is new and which he does not say out loud; the third answer on the market form, which is that they do not fill it in and forty-one people do not go anywhere; the limit of the anteroom, repeated in front of eleven people, **with the admission that he has no reading for it and will not pretend he has**; a room full of people and a word nobody in it can say; **the sentence the batch is built on, said and then half taken back in the same breath**; a proposal into the second column of a row he does not keep, written as a proposal and not a change because a man who writes a change to a room he does not keep is a stranger on a page about a room; and the secondary route, laid out with a piece of spent rope, with five reasons why it is a place a person can be killed and the fifth of them being his own refusal.
- **The book of his own** was used once: at the seventh bell of the fourth day of the twenty-seventh week he wrote the number of people in the anteroom in it and gave it to a woman and not to a page, **because that is what he does, and the number is not on the plan and the plan's first column does not say it.**
- **What he said that is new and load-bearing:** that being right about five walls stopped being the same fact as being right about a floor, and that the cheapest protection anything in this Hearthhold has ever had is a word that cannot be carried. **And that a plan with no signature is a plan with nobody in it, and that the name is the only protection anything here has ever had, and that he wants somebody to hold him to the second half for the rest of his life.** Renn Vale did.
- **Board: fifteen entries — eleven nulls, one claim, one mark, one row and a plan; nine in the ordinary column and six in the column with nothing over the top of it.** The plan is not his entry.
- **Immediate choice:** the leaving is unchanged and unscheduled, **and he did not raise it and did not answer it in this batch.** He said in Chapter 137 that a boundary that has to be looked after by somebody who is not standing in it is the day he is afraid of, and that is a different sentence and it is not an answer.

### Leena Orr

- **Position:** the anteroom and the lower level, this side of the waist. **She is one of the three named in Chapter 132 as not askable, with the reason given out loud in a room, and the reason is not her shoulder: it is that there is no version of the work that is on this side of the waist.**
- **Two beats, both earned and neither a decoration.** **In Chapter 136 she found the shape of the refusal of a row for the low end of the corridor — every row on that page is a place somebody is going to be, and that is the only place in this building nobody ever will be — and Renn Vale said in the room that she was borrowing it.** And **in Chapter 140 she said *a list is not a location* and stopped a man who had laid a length of rope on a floor and called it a way out.** That sentence was held back through Batch 0003 and used once, by her, on the only ground that earns it.
- **Body:** right shoulder slinged, takes no weight, unchanged.

### Iven Tallo

- **Asked for two hours of a piece of work and named the split himself, and asked to be put on the other side of the door he would not pack.** **He said the hard part out loud in a room: that a man who is the only person who knows what is under a room gets asked about that room by somebody four days up a road, that it is still true, that nothing about today made it less true, and he asked for his refusal from the twenty-fourth week to stand afterwards. It stands.**
- **He put his knee in the floor joint and named a figure and a week and said he has no idea what happens after the week.** He laid the sill and said the joint is in the sill and the sill is in the door and the door is not wedged, and said it while he was in the room.
- **In Chapter 137 he offered a joiner's mark for the plan because it was his and he did not look at it, and withdrew it in a carpenter's own words when a clerk read back the sentence he had said about a mark in Chapter 122.** He said *I offered a thing because it was mine and I did not look at it.* **He is not a defector, not a martyr, not a saint and not redeemed, he is not a signatory of anything, and nothing in this batch made him any of those four things.**

### Pell Roke

- **His work in this batch is reading numbers aloud, and it is all of his work.** He read the market form's two lines out loud for a courier, at her request, **and said what they are, and said he does not know anything about that and that he reads numbers and that is the end of what he does.** In Chapter 137 he read all twelve numbers in the plan's first column in one breath, including two new ones, and said nothing about any of them, and read the second column, the third column and the empty fourth column, and said **there was nothing in it** for the third time in this book.
- **A courier who is his older sister was in the building for eight chapters and he was on the bench at the top of the nine steps for all of them, and she did not go up to him, and he was not used as a route to her, and nobody in the building made anything of it, and the clerk entered that she entered that restraint on purpose.** She said thank you once, at the same volume she said everything else.
- **He did not go down the steps, into the corridor, or over the waist, in any chapter he appears in, and nobody asked him to.** He was named as not askable, with the reason, in Chapter 132.

### Tams Quill

- **The right hand is still open, flat, and still not a working hand, and nobody let it be.** He never took a bar, a chisel, a lever or a packing. He was named as one of the three who could not be asked, with the reason given out loud: his hand is not a working hand, and he keeps the water record and the count, and a man cannot be in a channel and at a sixth bell.
- **He gave the seventh reason for refusing to head the column with nothing over the top of it, and it is worse than the six before it and it is not about a word: a heading says what goes in a column, and the moment it says what goes in, a person can work out what would have to be left out to make room, and this column has been making room for twenty-seven weeks, and eleven nulls is not a list of nothing but a list of things that could not be filed anywhere else — and the worst version of a heading on that column is not a clerk four days up the passage, it is a person in this building, in a bad month, deciding that a room is not a wage.** When a cook asked him what the unheaded column has that a headed one has not, he said one thing: the doorway in it.
- **He entered the fifteenth entry on the board — a plan — into the column with nothing over the top of it, and said it is the second thing on that board that is not about a wall and the first that anybody in this building wrote and then refused to sign.** He named no day and gave no reason for not naming one. **In Chapter 140 the board is not walked at all, and he gives no reason for that either, and the clerk does not ask.**
- **In Chapter 130's successor beat he read the crew's column and Wen Pask's count in the same breath and did not make anything of it, twice, and in Chapter 138 the board took four minutes because the count was in a short mood and nobody said so out loud except the clerk.**

### Nera Oduya

- **The second of Volume 03's five acts of trust is spent, and it is the one the batch prompt named as the stronger of the two: she countersigned his revision in her own hand, on a page, with an objection stated first, in her own hand, above it, in a room with other people in it.** She came down a step nobody asked her to. **Her objection is the best argument anybody made in the batch and it is against him: a page that shows a condition being lifted is a page that says every condition on it can be lifted, and the second column's entire claim is that its conditions are not set aside.** She said the half against herself unasked — a condition that has never been lifted is a sentence, and this boundary had a page of sentences for twenty-seven weeks and shut a room with eleven people in it while every sentence on it was true. **Then the person who keeps the room wrote a stronger condition than the one he proposed to replace, and then she put her hand under his.**
- **She was right in public three times and wrong in public once and was not consoled for either.** She said the anteroom is not to be slept in or kept in, said its fifth condition has been broken for a fortnight, said a room with a word for a second way out is a room relying on everybody inside it having said the right thing in the right order in a room with the pump running, and **said that the day the word is not enough the room says so before anybody is in it and not after.**
- **Her theory was not said. She said in a room that she has had half of it since the fourth day of the eleventh week, did not give it, and that half of what she knows is about a room and what was asked is about a road.** Her condition is not met and **no room asked her.** She says her condition is not met and that a plan with twelve rows in it and a river at the waist is not the thing that meets it.
- **She struck the wash-room line out of the boundary's own evacuation sheet in nine seconds, before anybody asked, and did not give a reason at all, and nobody asked.** That is the fifth instrument and the first time the reason was withheld entirely.
- **She is not leaving in this volume, no chapter stages her going, and the question of her going is not raised.** **The remaining act — she stops checking his arithmetic out loud and somebody notices and she gives an answer about the work — is unspent and is Batch 0005's. She asked for his figures to be read against an original four times in this batch and never once asked him how he knows, and nobody has noticed yet.**
- **Relationship:** no intimacy, no recognition scene, no acceleration, and no scene whose only content is the two of them. **Their closest moment in this batch is a working moment in front of a room in which she is right about a page and he has to take it, and then she signs under a hand that has been corrected.**

### The Hearthhold boundary maintainers

- **Renn Vale:** keeper of the shore, the road and the lead terms. **She said the volume's answer to *for how long* — as long as the person who is able to say no is able to say it — and refused to put a name on a row for any reason, and refused the row for the low end of the corridor, and then wrote a stronger condition than the man who proposed it, in her own hand, read out twice and compared.** She lifted a condition in the twenty-fifth week and in this batch said out loud what lifting it is worth. She shut the waist on the fourth day of the twenty-seventh week and said she was the person who shuts it. She said *I will hold you to it* about a man's own argument against himself and meant it.
- **Dalla Sen:** repair ledger, route record, work-bell relay, cost witness. **She named the three who could not be asked before she asked anybody anything; she entered a broken condition of the anteroom's rating three times and said she knew on the day and did not write it down; she doubted the keeper of the plan in a room with a reason and entered afterwards that she had arranged it; she entered that nobody in a room with a stranger in it said the number in the room; she entered five reasons for not signing a plan and read them out twice; she decided not to put two questions next to each other when she was asked to, and entered that she was not going to.** She keeps writing a dead man's count every day and has said out loud in three weeks running that she is going to keep writing it.
- **Jo Verrick:** trial pump maintainer. **She found water in three places at once and said she can say they are the same warmth and cannot say they are the same joint; she said the only repair that would have kept that floor dry needs a wall in lime; she said she could take five jars out of the haunch and nobody would find out for about a week, and did not, in her own words on the page; she gave the reason the three of them have never measured the fill at the waist, out loud, for the first time, and said the reason was good and the rule was right and the water is on the ground anyway; and she corrected a courier in front of everybody and was thanked by nobody.**
- **Mikka Hale:** kitchen, the second hand of the plan. **She wrote a second permission and said out loud that she did not count anybody for the second time either and that she is the worst person in this room twice over; she wrote a fourth striking-out of a document; and she asked the count one question about the unheaded column and got one sentence, the doorway in it.** The pot is at ten days and has not gone up since the fifth day of the nineteenth week.
- **Ilsa Norr (nine children and herself):** the person who keeps the room. **She said the children are cold and will not have the cold left out of the record; she will not write a figure on a thing and will not stand up and agree to a page; she told a room from a surface federation that this building has a count and that she was not going to tell them the number; she said a third column is what a person does and a signature is what a person agrees to; and in Chapter 140 she said that a building like this one is not a thing people live in, it is a thing they are in, and that the page with no row for the hole is part of it.** She taught in the room eighteen mornings with a propped stone under one of nine and a child in it who sits.
- **Bel Ordry:** thirty-five, keeper of the boundary's public maintenance plan. **His plan has twelve rows and two of them are places rather than rooms. He asked for a third row for a hole and was refused in a room. He was doubted by the clerk with a reason and admitted which of his two answers was older. He asked five people to sign a plan and accepted five refusals. He said the plan does not leave this building and that there is no procedure for the two people who came up the passage, and that if that is a hole then it is the hole.** His half hinge is his own and is in a bag. He has still not raised his leaving and nobody has asked.
- **The woman from the wash rooms:** **not named, not asked, not rostered, not sent for.** Her covers were struck out of a fifth instrument in nine seconds, before anybody had asked, **and the reason was not given at all for the first time in twenty-six weeks, and nobody asked.** The floor was not approached, nobody went near it, and nobody was sent. Her two sentences on the review page are read out of the page in Chapter 140 as one of five reasons a hole is a place a person can be killed, and she is not in the room, is not used, is not asked, and the page is still blank.
- **Wen Pask: age twenty-two. Paid, kept, seventy-five days and seventy-five nights at the end of Batch 0004, and dead.** His count is at seventy-five and is not going to be seventy-six and the clerk has said so out loud in a room in three weeks running. **He is not a martyr, not a lesson and not an argument in this batch, and a chapter of this batch used the fact of his death and did not use him.**
- **Mero Senn: age forty-five.** In the building, not a rescue, not a saint, not a rebuke. **Asked three times in four days whether a plan with a number in it is acceptable, gave the same answer three times, refused to sign a number, said he would sign a condition, gave the half of the refusal of a row that is against the people who wanted the row, said a condition that has never been lifted is a sentence, and said that a page with four columns and no signature moved forty people in fifty minutes and that he cannot tell you whether that is the best thing this Hearthhold has done or the reason one of them is not here in a year.** Wrong in public about the anteroom, and said so first, and not consoled.
- **Orla Kern: age nine.** **In the room on all four school days and sitting down. Her bone is where a physician put it, it has moved, and two people have not said in a room that it has not moved, and that is entered as a condition not met.** The set is crate board bound with a piece of an old apron and a physician has said the set is correct and bad and that both are true.
- **Talla Roke: age twenty-two.** **In the building for eight chapters, on her own terms, with Bevin Tace, Osha Kell and Merrit Amm, and not a rescue.** She said before she said anything else that she is not here about the water, the school, or a boy, and that nobody is to use her to get to him. She brought the fact that the market road's form has become a pass and said her rule. She asked the boy on the bench to read two lines for her. She was wrong about a fill and was corrected and was not consoled. She asked the volume's question out loud and nobody answered it. **Her mark on a paper is a courier's mark and not a guild's, and she said that is the only thing she has got and it is three people's.**
- **Hollis Ashe: forty-one, sixteen years, Stonelight Compact route inspection.** Came up the passage a second time and brought the four pages she said she would write, and said she could not write a procedure for a boundary that does not want to be looked at. Sat through clause four being read against the original. Called the boundary's answer a bad answer and said it was the correct one, and said she would write it in a form a room can be looked at without being taken. **Not an antagonist, not defeated, and not consoled.**
- **Pettin Rahl: fifty-two, twenty-six years, Stonelight Compact, continuity. New in this batch.** **He is right, out loud, about a permitted occupancy that has to be believed instead of counted, and he has a room on the Rim side whose page said six with thirty-one people in it and four dead, and he was the reason the number was on the page, and he said he has not been able to walk into a room like that without looking at the first column first.** He wrote down that this boundary will not give a count and said that is his whole problem. He said out loud, before anybody else said it in that room, that his office will want a regime and that a regime is not a threat. **He is not a villain and nothing in this batch made him one.**
- **A Quiet Hands cell:** at least two and probably three. **Unchanged and uncaught. Nothing in this batch recruited anybody, nothing turned their reason into a riddle or a voice, and their argument was not restated.** The one new fact beside them is a sentence about a fill nobody measures. The One-Seat protocol and Cassian Rook remain the destination.

### The stair, the plans, the plate, and the evidence

The stair is **restricted, corded, and in service on its near side only**, with two timber shores on the common landing, **a lip that is still not measured by the people who own it**, and a third party's measurement of the ground at the waist that says the fill has moved a finger and a bit in three years. **The fill has now been measured for the first time in twenty-seven weeks and what was measured is that the water is standing on it and nobody has a number for it.** **The four treads behind the rail are dry, nobody has been on them, and it is said in Chapter 140 that nobody went down them. The eighth term is not touched, the ninth line is *none*, the ninth room has no row on the plan and is not in the charter and is not on the second sheet, and no mark is cut in its stone. The far wall of the throat is eleven feet down and has still never been seen.** **The board on surfaces now holds fifteen entries, of which eleven are nulls, one is a claim whose condition has not been met, one is a mark, one is a row on a page, and one is a plan.** The plan on a dowel is a nine-row maintenance schedule in a locked school store and did not leave the store and was not unrolled. **The plan on butcher's paper is one document in four parts in a coat, it does not leave the building, and it has twelve rows, of which two are places rather than rooms and one of which carries three hands and an objection.** The fourth column is empty and unheaded with a reason in it in two hands. The tenth row's second column now carries a **harder** condition than the one it replaced. **The wrapped empty-seat plate** lies in a knotted bundle of work cloth on the shelf above the anteroom bench, unexplained, unidentified, unused, unclaimed, and unopened, and Marek Venn said in a room that it is on that shelf and that is the whole of what he is going to say about it. **The brass survey rule** is in the pocket of the coat on the anteroom's hook, **has said nothing for longer than fifteen weeks**, and was not put on a table. The four marks and the groove on the lintel above the open school corner's mouth **are damaged, were read two ways by two people in Chapter 140, answered nothing, and no mark was cut in the stone.**
